questions.stem: PLYWOOD is always made up of an ODD number of veneer plies, with the grain of successive plies at right angles, principally so that:
options: The board is BALANCED about its central ply and the two faces have their grain in the SAME direction, so the board does not warp and its strength is more nearly equal in both directions
Less adhesive is required
The board can be cut more easily
The plies can be of different timber species
questions.solution:
**So that the board is BALANCED about its central ply**, with both faces having their grain running the same way — which prevents warping and equalises the strength in the two directions.

**Why an ODD number is essential:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **Successive plies are laid with their grain at RIGHT ANGLES** ← | **Cross-lamination — the basis of plywood** ← |
| **With an ODD number, the outermost plies on both faces run the SAME way** ← | **3, 5, 7 plies — the first and last are parallel** ← |
| **The construction is then SYMMETRICAL about the central ply** ← | **Equal numbers of plies in each direction on either side of the centre** ← |
| **An EVEN number would be UNBALANCED** ← | **The two faces would run at right angles to one another, and the board would CUP or WARP as it took up or lost moisture** ← |

> **THE WARPING MECHANISM IN THE LAST ROW IS THE PRACTICAL REASON AND IT IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING: timber moves a great deal ACROSS the grain and hardly at all ALONG it.**

> **In a balanced board, a change in humidity makes both faces try to move by the same amount in the same direction, and the board stays flat.**

> **In an unbalanced board, one face would try to expand while the other stayed put, and the board would curl — exactly as a bimetallic strip bends when heated.**

> **Symmetry about the centre is therefore not an aesthetic preference but the condition for dimensional stability, and it is the same principle that requires a laminate's layup to be symmetric in composite engineering.**

**What cross-lamination achieves:**

| Benefit | Note |
|---|---|
| **Strength more nearly EQUAL in both directions** ← | **Solid timber is several times stronger along the grain than across it; plywood evens this out** ← |
| **Greatly reduced SPLITTING** ← | **A split cannot run far, because the next ply's grain crosses it** ← |
| **Nails and screws can be driven near the edge** | **Which would split solid timber** ← |
| **Dimensional stability with humidity** | **The cross plies restrain the movement of their neighbours** ← |
| **Large sheets from small logs** ← | **Veneer is peeled continuously from a rotating log, so a wide board needs no wide tree** ← |
| **Defects are dispersed** | **Knots in one ply are backed by sound material in the next** ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE ECONOMIC REASON PLYWOOD EXISTS AT ALL and it is easily overlooked: a 1.2 × 2.4 m sheet of solid timber would require an enormous tree and would be prohibitively expensive and unstable.**

> **Rotary peeling produces a continuous ribbon of veneer from a modest log, and gluing the ribbon into sheets converts a small tree into a large board — which is a much better use of the material as well as a cheaper one.**

**The grades and their uses:**

| Grade | Adhesive | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **BWR / BWP (boiling water resistant/proof), "marine"** ← | **PHENOL formaldehyde — waterproof** ← | **Exterior work, formwork, boats, kitchens, wet areas** ← |
| **MR (moisture resistant), "commercial"** | **UREA formaldehyde — resists humidity, not immersion** ← | **Interior furniture and panelling** ← |
| **Fire-retardant and preservative-treated grades** | ← | **Where required** |

> **CHOOSING MR PLYWOOD FOR AN EXTERIOR OR WET APPLICATION IS THE COMMONEST AND MOST EXPENSIVE MISTAKE WITH THIS MATERIAL: urea formaldehyde adhesive breaks down with prolonged moisture, and the board DELAMINATES — the plies separate and it falls apart.**

> **The two grades look identical, cost noticeably different amounts, and are frequently substituted on site.**

> **In a bathroom, a kitchen, a shuttering panel or anything exposed to weather, the failure appears within a year or two, and by then the board is built in.**

> **Which is why the grade marking on the board should be checked on delivery rather than taken on the supplier's word — one of those small inspections that costs nothing and prevents a wholly avoidable failure.**

examTip.trick: **An ODD number puts both face plies in the same grain direction and makes the board SYMMETRIC about its centre** — so it does not cup as humidity changes.
examTip.trap: **An even-ply board would curl like a bimetallic strip** — one face expanding across the grain while the other stays put. Symmetry is a stability requirement, not a preference.
examTip.mnemonic: **BWP/marine uses PHENOL (waterproof); MR uses UREA (humidity only).** They look identical, and MR used in a wet area DELAMINATES within a year or two — check the grade marking on delivery.

questions.stem: FLY ASH used as a partial replacement for cement in concrete improves the concrete principally because it:
options: Sets faster than cement, giving higher early strength
Increases the water demand of the mix
Reacts POZZOLANICALLY with the CALCIUM HYDROXIDE liberated by cement hydration to form additional binding gel, improving long-term strength, workability and durability
Acts as an inert filler with no chemical effect
questions.solution:
**It reacts POZZOLANICALLY with the calcium hydroxide liberated by cement hydration**, forming additional calcium silicate hydrate gel — the same binding material that gives concrete its strength.

**The chemistry, which explains every one of its benefits:**

| Step | Reaction |
|---|---|
| **Cement hydrates, producing C-S-H gel AND CALCIUM HYDROXIDE, Ca(OH)₂** ← | **The calcium hydroxide is a by-product; it contributes little strength and is soluble and vulnerable** ← |
| **Fly ash is rich in reactive SILICA and ALUMINA** | ← |
| **The silica reacts with the calcium hydroxide, in the presence of water** ← | **SiO₂ + Ca(OH)₂ → C-S-H gel** ← |
| **So a weak, soluble by-product is converted into MORE of the strong binding gel** ← | **Which is the whole idea of a pozzolan** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE KEY INSIGHT: fly ash is not merely a diluent or a filler. It CONSUMES the weakest constituent of hydrated cement and turns it into the strongest.**

> **That single fact explains why the strength continues to develop for months rather than weeks, why the permeability falls so markedly, and why durability improves.**

**The benefits, and the mechanism behind each:**

| Benefit | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Higher LONG-TERM strength** ← | **The pozzolanic reaction continues for months** ← |
| **Much LOWER PERMEABILITY** ← | **The additional gel fills the capillary pores, and removing the soluble Ca(OH)₂ closes leaching paths** ← |
| **Better resistance to SULPHATE attack and to chloride ingress** ← | **A direct consequence of the lower permeability, and of consuming the Ca(OH)₂ that sulphates attack** ← |
| **Reduced ALKALI-SILICA reaction** | **Fly ash binds the alkalis** ← |
| **IMPROVED WORKABILITY at the same water content** ← | **The particles are SPHERICAL, and act as tiny ball bearings — so option (b) is exactly backwards** ← |
| **LOWER HEAT of hydration** ← | **Valuable in mass concrete, where the temperature rise causes cracking** ← |
| **Lower cost and a large environmental benefit** | **It is a waste product, and it displaces cement whose manufacture releases about a tonne of CO₂ per tonne** ← |

> **THE SPHERICAL PARTICLE SHAPE IN THE FIFTH ROW IS WORTH KNOWING BECAUSE IT IS COUNTER-INTUITIVE: a fine powder would normally be expected to INCREASE the water demand, since fine particles have a large surface area to wet.**

> **Fly ash does the opposite, because it forms in a furnace as molten droplets that solidify into smooth glassy SPHERES.**

> **Those spheres roll past one another and past the angular cement grains, lubricating the mix — the "ball bearing effect" — so a fly ash concrete needs LESS water for the same workability, and less water means more strength.**

**The limitations, stated fairly:**

| Limitation | Note |
|---|---|
| **SLOWER early strength gain** ← | **The pozzolanic reaction cannot begin until the cement has produced some calcium hydroxide — so formwork stays longer and cold-weather work is slower** ← |
| **Needs LONGER CURING to realise its benefit** ← | **Cut the curing short and fly ash concrete is worse than plain concrete, not better** ← |
| **Quality varies between sources** | **Loss on ignition and fineness must be checked** ← |
| **Not suited where very high early strength is required** | ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE MOST IMPORTANT PRACTICAL WARNING AND IT IS REGULARLY IGNORED: fly ash concrete's advantages all depend on a reaction that continues for months, and that reaction requires WATER to be available.**

> **A fly ash mix cured for three days and then left to dry has a lower strength than an equivalent plain cement mix, because the fly ash has diluted the cement and has not yet had the opportunity to compensate.**

> **So specifying fly ash without also specifying and enforcing extended curing converts a durability improvement into a strength reduction — which is a good general caution about substituting materials: the benefit usually comes with a condition attached, and the condition is the part that gets left out on site.**

examTip.trick: **Fly ash converts the weak, soluble Ca(OH)₂ from cement hydration into more C-S-H gel** — consuming the weakest product of hydration and making the strongest.
examTip.trap: **It REDUCES water demand, it does not increase it** — the particles are smooth glassy SPHERES formed from molten droplets, and they act as ball bearings in the mix.
examTip.mnemonic: **Fly ash concrete cured for three days is WORSE than plain concrete** — the pozzolanic reaction needs months and water. Specify the fly ash and the extended curing together, or don't specify it at all.

questions.stem: For the concrete of a heavily reinforced beam or column section, compacted by mechanical vibration, the slump generally specified is of the order of:
options: 75 to 125 mm
0 to 25 mm
175 to 200 mm
No slump requirement applies to reinforced concrete
questions.solution:
**Of the order of 75 to 125 mm** for heavily reinforced sections compacted by vibration.

**Typical slump values by application:**

| Type of work | Slump (mm) | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Roads, mass concrete, pavements — VIBRATED** | **0 to 25** ← (option b) | **Very stiff; compacted by heavy vibration or rolling** ← |
| **Mass concrete, lightly reinforced sections, canal linings** | **25 to 50** | ← |
| **Normal reinforced work: slabs, beams, columns, walls — VIBRATED** | **50 to 100** ← | **The common range** |
| **HEAVILY reinforced sections; thin sections; congested cages** ← | **75 to 125** ← | **This question — the concrete must flow around dense reinforcement** ← |
| **Sections where vibration is DIFFICULT or impossible** | **100 to 150** | ← |
| **TREMIE concrete, underwater placing, deep foundations** ← | **150 to 200** ← | **Must flow and self-level without any compaction** ← |
| **Self-compacting concrete** | **Slump flow, measured differently** | **500 to 700 mm spread** ← |

> **THE PATTERN THROUGHOUT IS CONSISTENT AND WORTH GRASPING RATHER THAN MEMORISING: the slump required rises with how DIFFICULT it is to place and compact the concrete, and falls as the available compaction effort rises.**

> **A road slab with a heavy vibrating roller over open ground needs almost no workability. A pile bored fifteen metres down through a tremie, with no possibility of compaction at all, must flow into place under its own weight.**

> **Everything in between grades between the two.**

**The rule that governs all of it, and the reason it matters:**

| Principle | Note |
|---|---|
| **Use the LOWEST slump that permits full compaction in the circumstances** ← | **Because water is the enemy of strength and durability** ← |
| **Never add water on site to increase the slump** ← | **It raises the water-cement ratio and reduces the strength directly, by Abrams' law** ← |
| **If more workability is genuinely needed, use a PLASTICISER** ← | **Which increases the slump at the SAME water content — the only legitimate way** ← |
| **A high slump also increases SEGREGATION and BLEEDING** | **And shrinkage, and permeability** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW DESCRIBES THE COMMONEST AND MOST DAMAGING ACT ON ANY CONCRETING SITE, and it is worth stating without qualification: adding water to a load of concrete because it is "too stiff" destroys the concrete's strength.**

> **A modest addition — say 10 litres to a cubic metre — can raise the water-cement ratio enough to cut the 28-day strength by several newtons per square millimetre.**

> **It is done because it makes the labourers' work easier and because the effect is entirely invisible until the cubes are tested, by which time the concrete is in the structure.**

> **It is why water addition after batching is prohibited, why the slump is tested at the point of PLACING rather than at the plant, and why a load whose slump exceeds the specification should be rejected rather than accepted with a shrug.**

**What the slump test does and does not tell you:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **It measures CONSISTENCY, one aspect of workability** ← | **How readily the concrete deforms under its own weight** ← |
| **It does NOT measure cohesion, segregation resistance or compactability** ← | **Two mixes of the same slump can behave quite differently** ← |
| **It is insensitive at both extremes** ← | **A very dry mix gives zero slump whatever its consistency; a very wet one collapses** ← |
| **For a very DRY mix, use the COMPACTING FACTOR or VEE-BEE test instead** ← | **Which apply a measured compactive effort** ← |
| **Its real virtue is as a CONSISTENCY CHECK between batches** ← | **A sudden change of slump signals a change in the aggregate moisture, the batching, or the mix — which is worth far more than the absolute value** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE MOST USEFUL THING TO KNOW ABOUT THE TEST: its value on site lies less in the number itself than in the CHANGE in the number.**

> **A batch that suddenly slumps 40 mm more than the previous one has more water in it, and something has changed — wetter sand after rain, a mis-set batcher, or somebody adding water.**

> **That signal arrives within minutes, while the concrete can still be rejected, whereas the cube result arrives in 28 days when it can only be regretted.**

examTip.trick: **0-25 roads and mass concrete, 50-100 normal RC, 75-125 heavily reinforced, 150-200 tremie and underwater.** The slump rises with placing difficulty and falls with available compaction.
examTip.trap: **Never add water on site to raise the slump** — it cuts strength directly by Abrams' law and is invisible until the cubes fail. Use a PLASTICISER, which raises slump at the same water content.
examTip.mnemonic: **The slump test's value is the CHANGE, not the number** — a batch suddenly 40 mm wetter means something changed, and it arrives in minutes while the load can still be rejected.

questions.stem: The SPLIT TENSILE STRENGTH test on concrete is carried out by:
options: Pulling a cylinder apart with grips at each end
Applying a COMPRESSIVE line load along the length of a cylinder laid on its SIDE, which induces a nearly uniform TENSILE stress across the vertical diameter
Loading a beam at its third points until it cracks
Applying a torque to a cylindrical specimen
questions.solution:
**By applying a compressive LINE LOAD along the length of a cylinder laid on its side** — which induces a nearly uniform TENSILE stress across the vertical diametral plane, splitting the cylinder along it.

**Why an INDIRECT test is used:**

| Difficulty with direct tension | Note |
|---|---|
| **Gripping a concrete specimen to pull it is very hard** ← | **The grips themselves crush or crack the concrete, and failure occurs at the grips rather than in the specimen** ← |
| **Any eccentricity in the pull introduces BENDING** ← | **And concrete is so weak in tension that a small bending stress dominates the result** ← |
| **The result is highly variable** | ← |
| **So the tension is generated INDIRECTLY, by compression** ← | **Which testing machines apply easily and concentrically** ← |

> **THE ELEGANCE OF THE SPLIT CYLINDER TEST IS EXACTLY THIS: it produces a clean tensile stress field using nothing but a compression machine and a cylinder, both of which every concrete laboratory already has.**

**The formula and the three tensile measures:**

| Test | Formula | Relative value |
|---|---|---|
| **DIRECT tension** | **Hard to perform** | **The lowest — the true tensile strength** ← |
| **SPLIT tensile (Brazilian) test** | **f_ct = 2P / (π L D)** ← | **10 to 15 per cent higher than direct** ← |
| **FLEXURAL strength (modulus of rupture)** ← | **f_cr = P L / (b d²) for third-point loading** ← (option c describes this test) | **The HIGHEST — 1.5 to 2 times the direct tensile strength** ← |

> **THE ORDERING IS CONSISTENT AND THE REASON FOR IT IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING: the flexural test gives the highest value because the modulus of rupture is computed from ELASTIC beam theory, assuming a linear stress distribution to the extreme fibre.**

> **In reality concrete's stress-strain curve is not linear near failure, so the actual extreme fibre stress is lower than the elastic formula predicts.**

> **The formula therefore OVERSTATES the true tensile strength — and the flexural test also stresses only a thin surface layer at the extreme fibre, where a weak flaw is less likely to be found than in the whole volume stressed by a direct pull.**

> **Both effects push the same way, which is why the three tests give three different numbers for one property, and why a tensile strength must always be quoted with the test that produced it.**

**Why concrete's tensile strength matters, since it is never relied on for strength:**

| Use | Note |
|---|---|
| **CRACKING is governed by tensile strength** ← | **Every crack in concrete is a tensile failure, and crack control is a serviceability requirement** ← |
| **SHEAR and TORSION capacity depend on it** ← | **Diagonal tension is what cracks a beam in shear** ← |
| **The modulus of rupture governs the design of RIGID PAVEMENTS** ← | **A concrete slab is a beam in bending, and it is designed on flexural strength, not compressive** ← |
| **Bond, anchorage and splitting around bars** | ← |
| **IS 456 relates it to the compressive strength: f_cr = 0.7 √f_ck N/mm²** ← | **Which is used where no test result is available** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE MOST IMPORTANT APPLICATION AND EXPLAINS WHY THE TEST EXISTS AS A ROUTINE ONE: a concrete road slab fails by cracking in bending, so its design depends entirely on the flexural strength.**

> **Specifying and testing the compressive strength of a pavement concrete, and inferring the flexural strength from a formula, is an approximation — and for an important pavement the flexural strength is measured directly on beam specimens.**

> **THE IS 456 RELATION IN THE LAST ROW IS WORTH REMEMBERING FOR ITS FORM AS MUCH AS ITS VALUE: tensile strength goes as the SQUARE ROOT of compressive strength.**

> **So doubling the compressive strength raises the tensile strength by only about 40 per cent — the two do not improve together.**

> **A high-strength concrete is therefore proportionately MORE brittle than an ordinary one: it is much stronger in compression and only a little stronger in tension, so the gap between the two widens.**

> **That is one reason high-strength concrete requires more careful attention to confinement and ductility, and it is a good illustration of why a single "grade" does not describe a material fully.**

examTip.trick: **A compressive LINE load along a cylinder on its side generates tension across the vertical diameter: f_ct = 2P/(πLD).** Option (c) is the flexural (modulus of rupture) test.
examTip.trap: **Direct < split (by 10-15 %) < flexural (1.5-2×)** — the flexural value is highest because elastic beam theory overstates the extreme fibre stress and only a thin surface layer is stressed.
examTip.mnemonic: **f_cr = 0.7√f_ck — tensile goes as the SQUARE ROOT of compressive.** So doubling f_ck raises tension only 40 %, which is why high-strength concrete is proportionately MORE brittle.

questions.stem: As per IS 456, the minimum period before the formwork SUPPORTING the SOFFIT of a beam spanning more than 6 m may be removed, where ordinary Portland cement is used and no strength test is made, is:
options: 24 hours
7 days
14 DAYS for the props to the span, and 21 days for the props to a cantilever over 6 m
60 days
questions.solution:
**14 days for the props under a beam soffit spanning more than 6 m** (and 21 days for a cantilever exceeding 6 m).

**The minimum striking periods (ordinary Portland cement, no strength test):**

| Formwork | Minimum period |
|---|---|
| **VERTICAL faces of walls, columns and beam sides** ← | **16 to 24 HOURS — they carry no load, only the concrete's own pressure while fluid** ← |
| **SOFFIT of slabs, props LEFT under** | **3 days** ← |
| **Soffit formwork to slabs, props REMOVED, span up to 4.5 m** | **7 days** ← |
| **Props to slabs, span OVER 4.5 m** | **14 days** ← |
| **Soffit formwork to BEAMS, props left under** | **7 days** ← |
| **Props to BEAMS and arches, span UP TO 6 m** | **14 days** ← |
| **Props to beams and arches, span OVER 6 m** ← | **21 days** ← |
| **Props to CANTILEVERS** | **14 days up to 1 m; 28 days beyond** ← |

> **The exact figures differ slightly between editions and are sometimes tabulated differently, and the PATTERN is what matters: vertical faces come off within a day, and load-bearing props stay for one to four weeks depending on the span.**

> **The essential distinction, and the one this question turns on, is between formwork that merely SHAPES the concrete and formwork that SUPPORTS it.**

**Why the periods lengthen with SPAN:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **A longer span carries a larger self-weight moment** ← | **And the concrete's own weight is the first load it must carry** ← |
| **DEFLECTION at early age is largely irreversible** ← | **Young concrete creeps heavily, so a sag taken up at 7 days is largely permanent** ← |
| **The concrete gains strength with time, so waiting is the cheapest form of strengthening** | ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE REASON THE RULE IS ABOUT MORE THAN COLLAPSE, and it is often missed: striking props too early rarely causes a failure, and frequently causes a permanent SAG.**

> **Concrete at 7 days has perhaps two thirds of its 28-day strength but a much lower modulus and a very high creep rate. A beam propped and then released early deflects immediately and then goes on creeping, and the deflection never recovers.**

> **The structure is safe and it looks wrong — a visible sag in a long beam, a floor that is not level, doors that bind — and there is no remedy short of demolition.**

> **So early striking is a serviceability risk far more often than a safety one, and it is a permanent one.**

**The practical qualifications:**

| Qualification | Note |
|---|---|
| **These are MINIMUM periods for OPC in normal weather** ← | **They assume proper curing throughout** ← |
| **In COLD weather, strength gains far more slowly** ← | **The periods must be extended — maturity, not the calendar, governs** ← |
| **RAPID HARDENING cement permits shorter periods** | ← |
| **Where CUBE TESTS are made, striking may be based on the actual strength achieved** ← | **The proper method for a project where the programme matters — test, do not guess** ← |
| **BACK-PROPPING is used where props must be removed early** ← | **The formwork is struck and props immediately replaced, so the slab is not left to carry its full load unaided** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE ANSWER FOR A PROJECT UNDER SCHEDULE PRESSURE AND IT IS UNDERUSED: casting extra cubes and testing them at 7 or 10 days establishes the actual strength, and the props can be struck as soon as it is adequate.**

> **That is both safer and often faster than the calendar rule, because the calendar rule is deliberately conservative — it must cover the worst plausible combination of cement, temperature and curing.**

> **THE BACK-PROPPING IN THE LAST ROW DESERVES A CAUTION THOUGH: it is frequently done badly, with props removed from several floors at once, or replaced loosely so they carry nothing until the slab has already deflected.**

> **A back-prop that is not wedged tight is not a prop, and multi-storey construction has collapsed from exactly that — the load from several freshly cast floors finding its way onto one young slab because the props between them were not doing their job.**

examTip.trick: **Vertical faces 16-24 hours; props to beams up to 6 m span 14 days; over 6 m, 21 days; cantilevers over 1 m, 28 days.** The distinction is formwork that SHAPES versus formwork that SUPPORTS.
examTip.trap: **Early striking causes a permanent SAG far more often than a collapse** — young concrete has a low modulus and high creep, and the deflection never recovers. There is no remedy.
examTip.mnemonic: **Cast extra cubes and strike on measured STRENGTH, not the calendar** — safer and usually faster. And a back-prop that is not wedged tight is not a prop; multi-storey collapses have started there.

questions.stem: SINGLE (bricklayer's or putlog) SCAFFOLDING differs from DOUBLE (mason's or independent) scaffolding in that single scaffolding:
options: Has ONE row of standards, with the inner ends of the putlogs supported in HOLES LEFT IN THE WALL itself
Uses only one plank as a working platform
Can be used only for single-storey buildings
Is erected by a single worker
questions.solution:
**It has ONE row of standards (vertical members), and the inner ends of the putlogs rest in HOLES left in the wall itself.**

**The two types compared:**

| Feature | SINGLE (putlog, bricklayer's) | DOUBLE (independent, mason's) |
|---|---|---|
| **Rows of STANDARDS** | **ONE, about 1.2 m from the wall** ← | **TWO — one near the wall and one further out** ← |
| **Support of the putlogs' inner end** | **In HOLES left in the wall's joints** ← | **On the SECOND row of ledgers — no wall support at all** ← |
| **Depends on the wall** | **YES, completely** ← | **NO — it is free-standing (independent)** ← |
| **Used for** | **BRICK masonry, where holes can be left and later filled** ← | **STONE masonry, plastering, painting, repairs, and any wall that must not be pierced** ← |
| **Material and cost** | **Less** ← | **More — twice the standards** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE ESSENTIAL DISTINCTION AND EXPLAINS THE NAMES: a single scaffold LEANS ON the building, and a double scaffold stands on its own.**

> **The word "independent" is the clearest of the several names for the second type, because it says exactly what the difference is.**

**Why single scaffolding cannot be used for stone masonry:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **Putlog holes must be left and later FILLED** ← | **Straightforward in brickwork, where a hole is a missing brick and the fill is invisible** ← |
| **In STONE masonry a hole cannot be neatly made or filled** ← | **The stones are irregular and individually placed; a hole disrupts the bond and the filling always shows** ← |
| **Nor in fair-faced or finished work** | **Where the patch would be visible** ← |
| **Nor where the wall is too weak to carry the putlog's reaction** ← | **A freshly built or a rubble wall** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE SAFETY CONSIDERATION AND IT IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS MOST: a putlog transfers the scaffold's load — workers, materials, the platform itself — into a wall that may have been built the same day.**

> **Green masonry has very little strength, and a putlog bearing on a joint laid that morning is bearing on mortar that has barely set.**

> **Which is why single scaffolding is limited to brickwork of sufficient maturity, and why the safe alternative for any doubtful wall is the independent scaffold that does not touch it structurally at all.**

**The parts of a scaffold, since the terminology is examined:**

| Part | Function |
|---|---|
| **STANDARDS** | **The VERTICAL members carrying the load to the ground** ← |
| **LEDGERS** | **HORIZONTAL members running PARALLEL to the wall, connecting the standards** ← |
| **PUTLOGS** | **Horizontal members running at RIGHT ANGLES to the wall, carrying the platform** ← |
| **TRANSOMS** | **The equivalent of putlogs in a double scaffold, spanning between the two rows of ledgers** ← |
| **BRACES** | **DIAGONAL members giving stability — longitudinal (cross) and transverse** ← |
| **BOARDING / battens** | **The working platform** |
| **GUARD RAIL and TOE BOARD** | **Fall protection — a rail at about 1 m and a board at the platform edge** ← |
| **BASE PLATES and SOLE PLATES** | **Spreading the standards' load onto the ground** ← |

> **THE LAST TWO ROWS ARE THE ITEMS MOST OFTEN OMITTED ON SITE AND THEY ARE THE TWO THAT PREVENT DEATHS.**

> **A GUARD RAIL and TOE BOARD stop a worker falling and stop a tool or brick falling onto whoever is below — and falls from height are the largest single cause of construction fatalities everywhere in the world.**

> **SOLE PLATES matter for a different reason: a standard bearing directly on soft or wet ground settles, the scaffold racks, and the bracing is overloaded. On a monsoon site, ground that carried the scaffold in the morning may not carry it in the afternoon.**

> **Both are cheap, both are visible from the ground, and both are among the first things a competent inspection looks for — which makes their absence a reliable indicator of how the rest of the site is being run.**

examTip.trick: **Single scaffold: ONE row of standards, putlog ends in HOLES IN THE WALL — it leans on the building. Double (independent): TWO rows, free-standing.**
examTip.trap: **Single scaffolding cannot be used on stone masonry, fair-faced work, or green walls** — the holes cannot be neatly filled, and the putlog loads mortar that may have been laid that morning.
examTip.mnemonic: **Standards vertical, LEDGERS parallel to the wall, PUTLOGS at right angles to it.** And guard rails, toe boards and sole plates are the cheap items whose absence tells you how the whole site is run.

questions.stem: A rectangular section is 100 mm wide and 200 mm deep. Its POLAR moment of inertia about the centroidal axis perpendicular to the plane of the section is:
questions.solution:
**83.33 × 10⁶ mm⁴.**

**The computation, using the PERPENDICULAR AXIS theorem:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Perpendicular axis theorem** | **I_zz = I_xx + I_yy, for a PLANE lamina** ← |
| **I_xx (about the axis parallel to the width)** | **b d³/12 = 100 × 200³/12 = 66.67 × 10⁶ mm⁴** ← |
| **I_yy (about the axis parallel to the depth)** | **d b³/12 = 200 × 100³/12 = 16.67 × 10⁶ mm⁴** ← |
| **Polar (I_zz)** | **66.67 + 16.67 = 83.33 × 10⁶ mm⁴** ← |

> **Options (a) and (c) are the two component values I_yy and I_xx — offered separately, since forgetting to add them is the obvious error.**

**The perpendicular axis theorem and its restriction:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Statement** | **I_zz = I_xx + I_yy, where z is PERPENDICULAR to the plane and x, y lie IN it, all three meeting at a point** ← |
| **Applies ONLY to a PLANE LAMINA** ← | **A flat area of negligible thickness — NOT to a three-dimensional body** ← |
| **The three axes must be MUTUALLY perpendicular and CONCURRENT** | **They need not pass through the centroid, but they must all meet at one point** ← |

> **THE PLANE LAMINA RESTRICTION IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE THEOREM'S ONE REAL LIMITATION and it is worth knowing why it exists: the proof depends on r² = x² + y², which is true only when z = 0 for every element of the body.**

> **For a solid three-dimensional body, each element has a z coordinate as well, the identity fails, and the theorem does not hold.**

> **Contrast the PARALLEL axis theorem, which has no such restriction and applies to any body whatever — a point of difference between the two that examinations like.**

**The polar moment of inertia and what it is used for:**

| Use | Note |
|---|---|
| **TORSION of a circular shaft: τ/r = T/J = Gθ/L** ← | **The polar moment J is what resists twisting** ← |
| **For a solid circle, J = π d⁴/32** ← | **Which is exactly twice I about a diameter (πd⁴/64) — as the perpendicular axis theorem requires, since I_xx = I_yy for a circle** ← |
| **For a hollow circle, J = π(D⁴ − d⁴)/32** | ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS A NEAT SELF-CHECK: for any section with two axes of symmetry at right angles and equal I about both — a circle, a square — the polar moment is simply twice the diametral one.**

> **The rectangle in this question does NOT have equal I about its two axes, which is why the two components had to be computed separately.**

**AND A CAUTION THAT MATTERS FOR NON-CIRCULAR SECTIONS, since it is a genuine trap:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The torsion formula T/J = Gθ/L is valid ONLY for CIRCULAR sections** ← | **Solid or hollow, but circular** ← |
| **For a non-circular section, plane cross-sections WARP out of plane when twisted** ← | **The assumption underlying the formula fails** ← |
| **So the polar moment of inertia does NOT give the torsional stiffness of a rectangle** ← | **A separate torsion constant J_t, from Saint-Venant's theory, must be used — and it is considerably SMALLER** ← |
| **For a thin-walled CLOSED section, Bredt's formula applies** | **And a closed tube is enormously stiffer in torsion than an open one of the same material** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW CONTAINS THE MOST USEFUL PRACTICAL FACT ABOUT TORSION AND IT IS DRAMATIC: a closed hollow tube may be HUNDREDS of times stiffer in torsion than the same tube with a longitudinal slit cut in it.**

> **The material is almost unchanged; the slit destroys the closed shear flow path, and the section must then resist torsion by the far weaker mechanism of warping.**

> **This is why box girders are used where torsion matters — a curved bridge deck, a crane runway — and why an open I-section is a poor torsional member despite being an excellent bending one.**

> **It is also why an accidental cut or opening in a closed section is far more serious than its size suggests, and why torsion is the one action in which the SHAPE of the section matters more than the quantity of material in it.**

examTip.trick: **I_zz = I_xx + I_yy = 66.67 + 16.67 = 83.33 × 10⁶ mm⁴.** The two wrong options are the individual components.
examTip.trap: **The PERPENDICULAR axis theorem applies only to a PLANE LAMINA** (its proof needs z = 0), whereas the PARALLEL axis theorem applies to any body. A favourite distinction.
examTip.mnemonic: **T/J = Gθ/L holds only for CIRCULAR sections** — others warp. And a closed tube is hundreds of times stiffer in torsion than the same tube with a slit: shape beats quantity.

questions.stem: A trapezoidal section has parallel sides of 200 mm (bottom) and 100 mm (top), with a height of 150 mm between them. The centroid lies, measured from the BOTTOM (200 mm) side, at:
questions.solution:
**66.67 mm from the 200 mm side.**

**The computation, by the standard formula:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **For a trapezium of parallel sides a (top) and b (bottom) and height h** | **ȳ from the side b = h (2a + b) / [3 (a + b)]** ← |
| **Substituting a = 100, b = 200, h = 150** | **ȳ = 150 (200 + 200) / [3 × 300]** |
| **Numerator** | **150 × 400 = 60,000** |
| **Denominator** | **900** |
| **ȳ** | **= 66.67 mm** ← |

> **Option (c) 75.00 mm is h/2 — correct only for a rectangle, that is when a = b; and it is the value obtained by assuming the section is symmetric about mid-height, which a trapezium is not.**

> **Option (d) 83.33 mm is the distance from the OTHER side — the complement, 150 − 66.67 — which is what you get by measuring from the wrong end.**

**Checking it by DECOMPOSITION, which is worth doing since it needs no formula:**

| Part | Area | ȳ from base | A·ȳ |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Rectangle 100 × 150** | **15,000** | **75** | **1,125,000** |
| **Triangle, base 100, height 150** ← | **7,500** | **150/3 = 50** ← | **375,000** |
| **TOTAL** | **22,500** | ← | **1,500,000** |

> **ȳ = 1,500,000 / 22,500 = 66.67 mm ✓**

> **THE DECOMPOSITION METHOD IS WORTH PREFERRING IN AN EXAMINATION, and not merely as a check: it needs no memorised formula, it works for any composite shape, and each step is simple enough to be verified by inspection.**

> **A trapezium is a rectangle plus a triangle. An L-section is two rectangles. An I-section is three. A section with a hole is a solid minus the hole, with the hole's area taken as NEGATIVE — which is the one refinement worth remembering, and it makes hollow sections just as easy.**

**A SANITY CHECK, which should be applied to every centroid answer:**

| Check | Note |
|---|---|
| **The centroid must lie between the two ends** | **0 < 66.67 < 150 ✓** |
| **It must lie on the side of mid-height where MORE AREA is** ← | **The section is wider at the bottom, so the centroid must be BELOW mid-height (75 mm) — and 66.67 is ✓** ← |
| **As a → b the answer must tend to h/2** | **With a = b = 200: 150(400+200)/(3×400) = 75 ✓** ← |
| **As a → 0 (a triangle) it must tend to h/3** | **150(0+200)/(3×200) = 50 ✓** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE FASTEST CHECK AND IT WOULD IMMEDIATELY ELIMINATE OPTIONS (C) AND (D): the section has more material at the bottom, so its centroid must sit below the middle.**

> **75 mm is exactly the middle and 83.33 mm is above it, so both are impossible before any arithmetic is done.**

> **THE THIRD AND FOURTH ROWS ARE A DIFFERENT AND EQUALLY VALUABLE HABIT: checking a formula at its LIMITING CASES.**

> **A trapezium formula must reduce to the rectangle's h/2 when the two parallel sides are equal, and to the triangle's h/3 when one of them vanishes.**

> **If a remembered formula fails either test, it has been remembered wrongly — and this takes ten seconds and catches the transposed-term errors that are otherwise invisible.**

> **It is a habit worth applying to every formula in the syllabus: check it against the cases whose answer you already know.**

examTip.trick: **ȳ = h(2a + b)/[3(a + b)] from the side b = 150(400)/900 = 66.67 mm.** Or decompose into a rectangle plus a triangle and take moments of area.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) 75 mm is h/2, right only for a rectangle; option (d) 83.33 is measured from the wrong side.** More area at the bottom means the centroid must be BELOW mid-height.
examTip.mnemonic: **Check a formula at its LIMITING CASES** — a → b must give h/2 (rectangle), a → 0 must give h/3 (triangle). Ten seconds, and it catches transposed terms that are otherwise invisible.

questions.stem: BOWDITCH'S RULE is used in surveying to:
options: Compute the area enclosed by a traverse
Correct for local attraction of the compass
DISTRIBUTE the CLOSING ERROR of a traverse among its legs IN PROPORTION TO THEIR LENGTHS
Determine the true bearing from the magnetic bearing
questions.solution:
**To DISTRIBUTE the closing error of a traverse among its legs in proportion to their LENGTHS.**

**The rule and its assumption:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **Correction to the latitude of a leg** | **= total error in latitude × (length of that leg ÷ perimeter of the traverse)** ← |
| **Correction to the departure of a leg** | **= total error in departure × (length of that leg ÷ perimeter)** ← |
| **The corrections are applied with the OPPOSITE sign to the error** ← | ← |
| **The assumption** | **That the errors in ANGLES and in LENGTHS are of the same order of accuracy** ← |

> **THE ASSUMPTION IN THE LAST ROW IS WHAT DETERMINES WHEN THE RULE IS APPROPRIATE, and it is the reason the alternative rule exists:**

| Rule | Assumption | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **BOWDITCH (compass) rule** ← | **Angular and linear measurements are equally precise** ← | **COMPASS traverses, and modern total station work where both are good** ← |
| **TRANSIT rule** ← | **ANGLES are measured MORE precisely than lengths** ← | **THEODOLITE traverses where the lengths were chained or taped** ← |

> **The transit rule distributes the error in proportion to the LATITUDES and DEPARTURES themselves rather than to the lengths, which has the effect of adjusting the longer components more and disturbing the bearings less — which is what you want when you trust your angles more than your distances.**

> **With modern EDM the distances are usually at least as accurate as the angles, so BOWDITCH is now the normal choice, and the transit rule is largely historical.**

**THE CLOSING ERROR itself, and how it is judged:**

| Quantity | Note |
|---|---|
| **Error in LATITUDE, ΣL** | **The algebraic sum of the latitudes, which should be ZERO for a closed traverse** ← |
| **Error in DEPARTURE, ΣD** | **Likewise zero** ← |
| **CLOSING ERROR e = √(ΣL² + ΣD²)** ← | **The distance by which the traverse fails to close** ← |
| **Its direction** | **tan θ = ΣD / ΣL** |
| **RELATIVE error = e ÷ perimeter** ← | **Expressed as 1 in N — this is the figure by which the work is judged** ← |

> **THE RELATIVE ERROR IN THE LAST ROW IS THE MEANINGFUL MEASURE AND THE ABSOLUTE ERROR IS NOT, which is the point worth carrying:**

> **A closing error of 100 mm is excellent on a 5 km traverse (1 in 50,000) and unacceptable on a 100 m one (1 in 1,000).**

| Standard of work | Acceptable relative closure |
|---|---|
| **Rough compass traverse** | **1 in 300 to 1 in 600** ← |
| **Ordinary theodolite traverse** | **1 in 3,000 to 1 in 5,000** ← |
| **Precise traverse, total station** | **1 in 10,000 or better** ← |

> **AND THE MOST IMPORTANT PROFESSIONAL POINT ABOUT THE WHOLE PROCEDURE: adjustment is NOT a substitute for checking the work.**

> **Bowditch's rule assumes the error is the accumulation of many small RANDOM errors, spread through the traverse — and on that assumption, distributing it proportionally is a reasonable thing to do.**

> **If instead the closing error is caused by ONE MISTAKE — a leg measured 10 m short, a bearing booked as 47° instead of 74°, a station occupied out of order — then the error is not random at all, it is concentrated in one place, and spreading it across every leg is precisely the wrong response.**

> **It CONCEALS a blunder by smearing it thinly over the whole survey, leaving every station slightly wrong instead of one station badly wrong — and the resulting plan looks perfectly consistent while being wrong everywhere.**

> **So an unexpectedly large closing error must be INVESTIGATED before it is adjusted. If the error is roughly equal to one leg's length, or lies along one leg's bearing, that leg is where to look — and only when the work has been checked and no blunder found is it legitimate to adjust.**

examTip.trick: **Correction to a leg = total error × (leg length ÷ perimeter)**, applied to both latitude and departure with the opposite sign.
examTip.trap: **BOWDITCH assumes angles and lengths are equally accurate; the TRANSIT rule assumes angles are better** and suits theodolite-plus-chain work. With EDM, Bowditch is now standard.
examTip.mnemonic: **Judge the work by the RELATIVE closure (1 in N), never the absolute error.** And investigate a large closing error before adjusting it — Bowditch smears a BLUNDER over every leg and hides it.

questions.stem: A SUPPLEMENTARY estimate differs from a REVISED estimate in that a supplementary estimate:
options: Is prepared before the detailed estimate
Is prepared when the original estimate is found to be arithmetically wrong
Replaces the original estimate entirely
Is prepared for ADDITIONAL WORK found necessary while the original work is in progress, and is submitted TOGETHER WITH the original estimate as an addition to it
questions.solution:
**A supplementary estimate covers ADDITIONAL WORK found necessary while the original work is in progress**, and it is submitted alongside the original estimate as an addition to it.

**The two compared:**

| Aspect | REVISED estimate | SUPPLEMENTARY estimate |
|---|---|---|
| **Prepared when** | **The original estimate is EXCEEDED, or is likely to be, by more than a stated percentage (commonly 5 %)** ← | **ADDITIONAL work, not in the original scope, becomes necessary** ← |
| **Covers** | **The SAME work, at a revised cost** ← | **NEW work, in addition to the original** ← |
| **Relationship to the original** | **REPLACES it** ← | **ADDS to it — the two are considered TOGETHER** ← |
| **Must be accompanied by** | **A comparative statement showing the original and revised figures item by item, WITH REASONS for each excess** ← | **A full description of why the additional work is needed** ← |
| **Cause** | **Rate increases, quantity variations, design changes, delay** ← | **Genuine additional requirement discovered during execution** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE CLEANEST WAY TO REMEMBER THE DIFFERENCE: a REVISED estimate replaces; a SUPPLEMENTARY estimate is added.**

> **Option (b) describes neither — an arithmetical error is corrected, not made the subject of a new estimate.**

**The COMPARATIVE STATEMENT in the fourth row deserves emphasis, because it is the point of the whole procedure:**

> **A revised estimate is not merely a larger number. It must show, item by item, what was originally allowed, what is now required, and WHY.**

> **That requirement exists so that the approving authority can distinguish between legitimate causes — a genuine rise in material prices, ground conditions worse than could have been foreseen, a change of scope directed by the client — and illegitimate ones, principally an original estimate that was too low.**

> **The first three are nobody's fault. The fourth is, and it will not be identified unless the comparison is set out.**

**The full family of estimates, so this pair is in context:**

| Estimate | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **PRELIMINARY (approximate, rough cost)** | **At the planning stage, to decide whether to proceed — by plinth area, cubic content or per unit** ← |
| **PLINTH AREA / cube rate estimate** | **A form of the above** |
| **DETAILED estimate** ← | **Item by item, from the drawings and the schedule of rates — the basis of sanction and of tendering** ← |
| **REVISED estimate** | **When the sanctioned amount is exceeded** ← |
| **SUPPLEMENTARY estimate** | **For additional work — this question** ← |
| **ANNUAL REPAIR / maintenance estimate** ← | **The yearly provision to keep an existing asset in order** ← |
| **COMPLETE estimate** | **Covering all ancillary items as well as the main work** |
| **EXTENSION AND IMPROVEMENT estimate** | **For enlarging or upgrading existing works** ← |

> **THE ANNUAL REPAIR ESTIMATE IN THE SIXTH ROW IS WORTH ENDING ON, because it is the one that is most often cut and least often defended:**

> **It is the routine yearly provision for keeping an existing road, building or irrigation system serviceable, and it produces nothing new or visible.**

> **It is therefore the first item reduced when a budget is tight, and the consequence — as with road maintenance, canal maintenance and drainage — appears years later as a rehabilitation estimate several times larger.**

> **The estimating framework itself contains no defence against that. It is a matter of institutional discipline, and the strongest practical protection is the one adopted for roads: a dedicated maintenance fund, ring-fenced from the annual budget negotiation, so that the money cannot be moved to new construction.**

> **The recurring theme is worth stating plainly, since it has appeared in road maintenance, canal drainage and reservoir sedimentation alike: the works that fail are rarely the ones that were badly designed. They are the ones that were not maintained.**

examTip.trick: **REVISED replaces (same work, higher cost); SUPPLEMENTARY adds (new work, considered together with the original).**
examTip.trap: **A revised estimate must carry a COMPARATIVE STATEMENT with reasons item by item** — so the approving authority can tell a genuine price rise from an original estimate that was simply too low.
examTip.mnemonic: **The ANNUAL REPAIR estimate is the one always cut and never defended** — and its absence returns years later as a rehabilitation estimate several times the size. Ring-fence it, as the Roads Board does.

questions.stem: In the Unified (and IS) soil classification system, a soil designated SP is:
options: A well-graded sand
A POORLY GRADED (uniform) SAND
A silty sand
A sandy clay of low plasticity
questions.solution:
**A POORLY GRADED (uniformly graded) SAND.**

**The two-letter system:**

| First letter — the principal soil type | Second letter — the qualifier |
|---|---|
| **G — GRAVEL** | **W — WELL graded** ← |
| **S — SAND** | **P — POORLY graded (uniform or gap graded)** ← |
| **M — SILT (from the Swedish "mo")** | **M — with SILT (non-plastic fines)** ← |
| **C — CLAY** | **C — with CLAY (plastic fines)** ← |
| **O — ORGANIC soil** | **L — LOW plasticity (LL below 35, or below 50 in some versions)** ← |
| **Pt — PEAT (used alone)** | **I — INTERMEDIATE plasticity (35 to 50) — in the IS system** ← |
| — | **H — HIGH plasticity (above 50)** ← |

> **THE SECOND LETTER'S MEANING DEPENDS ON THE FIRST, which is the point that causes confusion and is worth stating explicitly:**

> **For COARSE soils (G and S), the second letter describes the GRADING (W or P) or the type of FINES present (M or C).**

> **For FINE soils (M, C and O), the second letter describes the PLASTICITY (L, I or H).**

> **So "SM" is a silty SAND, while "ML" is a SILT of low plasticity — the M means different things in the two positions.**

**Reading the common symbols:**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **GW / GP** | **Well-graded / poorly graded GRAVEL, clean** ← |
| **GM / GC** | **Gravel with silty / clayey fines** |
| **SW / SP** | **Well-graded / poorly graded SAND, clean** ← (this question) |
| **SM / SC** | **Silty sand / clayey sand** ← |
| **ML / MI / MH** | **Silt of low / intermediate / high plasticity** ← |
| **CL / CI / CH** | **Clay of low / intermediate / high plasticity** ← |
| **OL / OI / OH** | **Organic soil, by plasticity** |
| **Pt** | **PEAT and other highly organic soils** ← |

**How the classification is actually made:**

| Step | Criterion |
|---|---|
| **1. COARSE or FINE?** | **More than 50 % retained on the 75 μm sieve → COARSE-grained** ← |
| **2. If coarse: GRAVEL or SAND?** | **More than half of the coarse fraction retained on 4.75 mm → GRAVEL** ← |
| **3. How much passes 75 μm?** | **Under 5 % → clean, so use W or P. Over 12 % → use M or C. Between → a dual symbol such as SP-SM** ← |
| **4. For clean coarse soils, judge the GRADING** | **WELL graded needs Cu > 6 (sand) or > 4 (gravel), AND Cc between 1 and 3 — BOTH conditions** ← |
| **5. For fine soils, use the PLASTICITY CHART** | **Above the A-line → CLAY; below → SILT. The liquid limit gives L, I or H** ← |

> **THE "BOTH CONDITIONS" REQUIREMENT IN STEP 4 IS THE DETAIL MOST OFTEN MISSED and it is the reason many sands classify as SP: a soil must satisfy the uniformity coefficient AND the coefficient of curvature to be called well graded.**

> **A soil with Cu = 10 but Cc = 0.4 is GAP-graded — it has a wide range of sizes with a whole band missing — and it fails the Cc test, so it is classed as POORLY graded despite its wide range.**

> **The Cu test asks whether the range is wide; the Cc test asks whether the range is CONTINUOUS. Both are needed, and "poorly graded" therefore covers both uniform and gap-graded soils.**

**Why the classification matters at all:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **It COMMUNICATES the soil's engineering behaviour in two letters** ← | **An engineer told "CH" immediately expects high compressibility, low strength, high swelling and slow drainage** ← |
| **It predicts SUITABILITY as fill, subgrade or foundation** | ← |
| **It permits published correlations to be applied** | **Permeability, compaction characteristics, likely CBR** ← |
| **It is NOT a substitute for testing** ← | **A classification is a starting point and a communication tool, not a design parameter** ← |

> **The last row deserves the emphasis: the symbol tells you what KIND of soil you have and roughly how it will behave, which is enough to plan an investigation and to anticipate problems — and it is never enough to design a foundation on.**

examTip.trick: **S = sand, P = poorly graded.** First letter is the soil type; the second is the GRADING for coarse soils and the PLASTICITY for fine ones.
examTip.trap: **M means different things in the two positions** — SM is a silty SAND, ML is a SILT of low plasticity. And well graded needs BOTH Cu and Cc to pass.
examTip.mnemonic: **Cu asks if the range is WIDE; Cc asks if it is CONTINUOUS.** A gap-graded soil passes Cu and fails Cc, so "poorly graded" covers both uniform and gap-graded.

questions.stem: A clay compacted at a water content WET of optimum, compared with the same clay compacted DRY of optimum to the same dry density, will generally have:
options: A higher permeability and greater swelling potential
A flocculated structure and greater brittleness
Identical properties, since the dry density is the same
A DISPERSED (oriented) structure, LOWER permeability, LOWER swelling potential and MORE ductile behaviour, but lower strength at low strain
questions.solution:
**A DISPERSED, oriented structure** — with lower permeability, lower swelling potential and more ductile behaviour, but lower strength at small strains.

**The two structures:**

| Aspect | Compacted DRY of optimum | Compacted WET of optimum |
|---|---|---|
| **Particle arrangement** | **FLOCCULATED — particles randomly oriented, edge-to-face** ← | **DISPERSED — particles ORIENTED parallel to one another** ← |
| **Why** | **Little water, so the electrical repulsion between particles is suppressed and they clump** ← | **More water, thicker double layers, particles repel and slide into a parallel arrangement under the compactive effort** ← |
| **PERMEABILITY** | **HIGHER — the random structure leaves larger interconnected voids** ← | **LOWER, often by an order of magnitude** ← |
| **SWELLING potential** | **HIGHER — the soil is water-deficient and will take up more** ← | **LOWER — it is already near its equilibrium water content** ← |
| **SHRINKAGE on drying** | **LOWER** | **HIGHER** ← |
| **Strength at LOW strain** | **HIGHER — stiffer and stronger initially** ← | **LOWER** ← |
| **Strength at LARGE strain** | **Similar or lower** | **Similar** |
| **Stress-strain behaviour** | **BRITTLE — a peak followed by a drop** ← | **DUCTILE — deforms without a sharp peak** ← |
| **Compressibility at high stress** | **HIGHER** | **Lower** |

> **THE SAME SOIL AT THE SAME DRY DENSITY BEHAVES QUITE DIFFERENTLY DEPENDING ON WHICH SIDE OF OPTIMUM IT WAS COMPACTED, which is why option (c) is wrong and why this is worth knowing at all.**

> **Dry density is only one measure of a compacted soil's state. The STRUCTURE — how the particles are arranged — is a second, independent one, and it governs permeability, swelling and ductility more than the density does.**

**Choosing the side of optimum deliberately:**

| Application | Compact | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **CORE of an earth dam; a canal or landfill LINER** ← | **WET of optimum** ← | **LOW PERMEABILITY is the objective, and ductility lets the core deform with settlement WITHOUT CRACKING** ← |
| **SHELLS of an earth dam; a road SUBGRADE; structural fill** ← | **DRY of optimum, or at optimum** ← | **STRENGTH and STIFFNESS are wanted, and permeability does not matter** ← |
| **Under a floor slab in an expansive clay** | **WET of optimum** | **To minimise subsequent swelling** ← |
| **Where the fill must be trafficked immediately** | **Dry of optimum** | **A wet-compacted clay is unworkable under construction traffic** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE MOST IMPORTANT APPLICATION AND THE DUCTILITY REASON IS THE ONE USUALLY OMITTED, so it is worth expanding:**

> **An earth dam's core sits on a foundation that settles, between shells that settle by different amounts, and the whole embankment deforms over the years.**

> **A core compacted dry of optimum is strong and BRITTLE — it resists the deformation until it CRACKS, and a crack through the core of a dam is a concentrated leakage path and a piping failure waiting to happen.**

> **A core compacted wet of optimum is weaker and DUCTILE — it deforms with the settlement, and it does not crack.**

> **The weaker material makes the safer dam, which is a genuinely counter-intuitive result and one of the more instructive conclusions in earthwork engineering.**

**And why the compaction curve has a peak at all, since it underlies all of this:**

| Water content | What happens |
|---|---|
| **Very DRY** | **High friction between particles; the compactive effort cannot rearrange them, so the density is low** ← |
| **Increasing** | **Water LUBRICATES the particles, they pack more closely, and the dry density RISES** ← |
| **At OPTIMUM** | **The best compromise — maximum dry density for that compactive effort** ← |
| **Beyond optimum** | **The extra water occupies VOLUME that soil solids could have occupied, and air cannot be expelled fast enough — the dry density FALLS** ← |
| **The ZERO AIR VOIDS line** | **The theoretical maximum, at 100 % saturation — the curve approaches it but can never reach or cross it** ← |

> **The last row gives a valuable check on any laboratory compaction curve: a plotted point lying ON or ABOVE the zero air voids line is impossible, and indicates an error in the specific gravity used or in the measurements themselves.**

examTip.trick: **Wet of optimum → DISPERSED, oriented particles → low permeability, low swelling, DUCTILE. Dry of optimum → FLOCCULATED → higher permeability, higher swelling, BRITTLE and stiffer.**
examTip.trap: **Same dry density does NOT mean same properties** — structure is a second, independent variable, and it governs permeability and ductility more than density does.
examTip.mnemonic: **Dam CORE wet of optimum (ductile, so it deforms without cracking); SHELLS dry of optimum (strong).** The weaker material makes the safer dam. And no point can lie above the zero-air-voids line.

questions.stem: CONSOLIDATION differs from COMPACTION of a soil in that consolidation is:
options: The GRADUAL reduction in volume of a SATURATED soil under a sustained load, caused by the EXPULSION OF PORE WATER over time
The instantaneous densification of a soil by mechanical energy
A reduction in volume caused by the expulsion of AIR
Only applicable to sands and gravels
questions.solution:
**The GRADUAL reduction in volume of a SATURATED soil under a sustained load, caused by the slow expulsion of PORE WATER.**

**The two processes compared:**

| Aspect | COMPACTION | CONSOLIDATION |
|---|---|---|
| **What is expelled** | **AIR** ← (option c) | **WATER** ← |
| **Soil state** | **PARTIALLY saturated** ← | **SATURATED** ← |
| **Cause** | **Applied mechanical ENERGY — rolling, ramming, vibrating** ← | **A sustained STATIC load** ← |
| **Timescale** | **INSTANTANEOUS — a few roller passes** ← | **SLOW — months to years in clay** ← |
| **Where it happens** | **A construction operation, deliberately performed** ← | **A NATURAL process that happens to the ground under a load** ← |
| **Governing soil** | **Any soil, but especially fills** | **CLAYS — sands consolidate almost instantly, so it is not an issue for them** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE CLEANEST DISTINCTION AND IS WORTH FIXING: COMPACTION EXPELS AIR; CONSOLIDATION EXPELS WATER.**

> **Everything else follows from it — air is compressible and can be driven out quickly, while water is incompressible and must physically FLOW out through the soil's pores, which in a clay takes a very long time.**

> **Option (d) is wrong but points at something true: sands DO consolidate, so quickly that the settlement is complete almost as soon as the load is applied, and it is treated as "immediate" settlement rather than as consolidation.**

**Why clay consolidation is so slow:**

| Factor | Note |
|---|---|
| **Clay's PERMEABILITY is extremely low** ← | **Of the order of 10⁻⁹ m/s — the water can barely move** ← |
| **The water must travel to a DRAINAGE BOUNDARY** ← | **The top or bottom of the clay layer, wherever a permeable stratum exists** ← |
| **Time varies with the SQUARE of the drainage path** ← | **t = T_v d²/c_v — so DOUBLING the drainage path length QUADRUPLES the time** ← |
| **A layer drained on BOTH faces has d = HALF its thickness** ← | **So it consolidates FOUR TIMES faster than the same layer drained on one face only** ← |

> **THE LAST TWO ROWS TOGETHER GIVE THE MOST USEFUL RESULT IN THE WHOLE TOPIC AND THE ONE MOST OFTEN GOT WRONG IN CALCULATION: d is the length of the longest drainage path, NOT the layer thickness.**

> **A 4 m clay layer with sand above and below has d = 2 m. The same layer resting on rock has d = 4 m and takes four times as long.**

> **Using the thickness where the half-thickness applies produces an answer four times too large, and it is the standard error in these problems.**

> **It is also the entire basis of VERTICAL DRAINS: installing sand or band drains at, say, 2 m centres replaces a vertical drainage path of several metres with a horizontal one of about 1 m — and since time goes as d², the consolidation period collapses from years to months.**

**Terzaghi's model, which is worth holding as a picture:**

| Element | Represents |
|---|---|
| **A SPRING in a cylinder of water, with a piston and a small valve** ← | **The classic analogy** ← |
| **The SPRING** | **The soil skeleton** ← |
| **The WATER** | **The pore water** |
| **The small VALVE** | **The soil's permeability** ← |
| **Load applied, valve shut** | **The WATER carries all of it — pore pressure equals the applied stress, and the spring carries nothing** ← |
| **Valve opened slightly** | **Water escapes slowly; the load TRANSFERS gradually from water to spring** ← |
| **Eventually** | **All the excess water is gone, the pore pressure is back to zero, and the SPRING carries the whole load** ← |

> **THE TRANSFER IN THE SIXTH ROW IS THE ESSENCE OF CONSOLIDATION AND EXPLAINS WHY IT IS INSEPARABLE FROM EFFECTIVE STRESS: the settlement is not caused by the water leaving as such.**

> **It is caused by the effective stress RISING as the pore pressure falls — and it is the effective stress that compresses the soil skeleton.**

> **So consolidation settlement and strength GAIN are the same process seen from two sides: as the effective stress rises, the soil both compresses and gets stronger.**

> **That is exactly why staged construction works, and why a clay foundation that has consolidated under one embankment lift can safely carry the next.**

examTip.trick: **COMPACTION expels AIR (instant, mechanical, partly saturated); CONSOLIDATION expels WATER (slow, sustained load, saturated).** Everything else follows from that.
examTip.trap: **t ∝ d², and d is the longest DRAINAGE PATH, not the layer thickness** — drained both faces, d = half the thickness and it consolidates FOUR times faster. The standard calculation error.
examTip.mnemonic: **Settlement is caused by the effective stress RISING as pore pressure falls** — so consolidation settlement and strength GAIN are one process seen from two sides. Hence staged construction.

questions.stem: A field PUMPING TEST is preferred to a laboratory permeability test for determining the permeability of a soil stratum principally because it:
options: Is quicker to perform
Requires no boreholes
Measures the permeability of a LARGE MASS of soil IN PLACE, including the effects of its stratification, fissures and natural fabric, which a small laboratory sample cannot represent
Gives a lower and therefore safer value
questions.solution:
**Because it measures the permeability of a LARGE MASS of soil in place**, including stratification, fissures and natural fabric that a small laboratory specimen cannot represent.

**Why the laboratory value is so often wrong:**

| Problem | Note |
|---|---|
| **A laboratory specimen is TINY — perhaps 75 mm across** ← | **And permeability is governed by the most permeable path available, which a small sample may not contain** ← |
| **The natural FABRIC is disturbed by sampling** ← | **Fissures, root holes, sand partings and laminations are destroyed or unrepresented** ← |
| **Stratification is missed entirely** ← | **A clay with thin sand seams may be a thousand times more permeable HORIZONTALLY than the clay alone — and a vertical sample will never show it** ← |
| **The flow direction in the test may not match the field** | ← |
| **Discrepancies of one to three ORDERS OF MAGNITUDE are common** ← | **Not a small error** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE DECISIVE ONE AND IT IS WORTH DWELLING ON: natural soils are almost always LAYERED, and layering makes permeability strongly ANISOTROPIC.**

> **Horizontal flow takes the easiest route — along the most permeable layer, which dominates the average.**

> **Vertical flow must cross EVERY layer, so it is controlled by the LEAST permeable one.**

> **The result is that k_horizontal can exceed k_vertical by a factor of tens or hundreds in a stratified deposit, and a single laboratory specimen tells you about neither reliably.**

> **A pumping test, drawing water from a large volume of the actual stratum, gives the value that actually governs a dewatering scheme or a seepage calculation.**

**How the test is performed:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **A well is bored fully into the aquifer and pumped at a CONSTANT rate** ← | ← |
| **The drawdown is measured in two or more OBSERVATION wells at known distances** ← | **Two are needed to determine k without assuming the radius of influence** ← |
| **Pumping continues until STEADY STATE — the drawdowns stop changing** ← | **Which may take hours or days** ← |
| **k is computed from the discharge and the two drawdowns** | **By the Dupuit equation for an unconfined aquifer, or Thiem's for a confined one** ← |
| **UNCONFINED aquifer** | **k = Q ln(r₂/r₁) / [π (h₂² − h₁²)]** ← |
| **CONFINED aquifer of thickness b** | **k = Q ln(r₂/r₁) / [2π b (h₂ − h₁)]** ← |

> **THE TWO OBSERVATION WELLS IN THE SECOND ROW MATTER MORE THAN THEY APPEAR TO: with only the pumped well, the radius of influence must be ASSUMED, and it is a quantity nobody can estimate well.**

> **With two observation wells the radius of influence cancels out of the equation entirely, and the result depends only on measured quantities.**

> **Designing the test so that an unknowable parameter cancels is worth a great deal more than estimating it carefully, and it is a good general principle in field measurement.**

**The test's own limitations, stated fairly:**

| Limitation | Note |
|---|---|
| **EXPENSIVE and slow** ← | **A well, observation wells, a pump, and days of running — which is why laboratory tests survive** ← |
| **Needs a substantial aquifer and somewhere to discharge the water** | ← |
| **Gives an AVERAGE over a large volume** ← | **Which is usually what is wanted, but it conceals local variation** ← |
| **Not practicable in a clay** ← | **The yield is far too small to pump — so for clays, laboratory tests or in-situ falling-head tests in a borehole must be used** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW SETS THE PRACTICAL DIVISION BETWEEN THE METHODS AND IS THE THING TO REMEMBER: PUMPING tests for permeable strata (sands and gravels), where the value matters for dewatering and water supply; LABORATORY tests for clays, where the value matters for consolidation rate.**

> **And in both cases the number obtained should be treated as an ORDER OF MAGNITUDE rather than a precise value.**

> **Permeability is the soil property with by far the widest natural range — from 10⁻¹ m/s in a clean gravel to 10⁻¹¹ in a dense clay, ten orders of magnitude — and the one that is hardest to measure reliably.**

> **A design that is sensitive to whether k is 10⁻⁶ or 3 × 10⁻⁶ is a design resting on a number nobody can supply, and it should be reconsidered rather than refined.**

examTip.trick: **It tests a LARGE MASS in place, with its fissures, sand partings and layering** — features a 75 mm laboratory specimen cannot contain. Discrepancies of 1-3 orders of magnitude are routine.
examTip.trap: **Layering makes permeability ANISOTROPIC** — horizontal flow follows the MOST permeable layer, vertical flow is controlled by the LEAST. k_h can exceed k_v by a factor of hundreds.
examTip.mnemonic: **Two observation wells make the radius of influence CANCEL** — designing a test so the unknowable parameter drops out beats estimating it. And pumping tests suit sands; clays yield too little.

questions.stem: The RESIDUAL shear strength of an over-consolidated clay is:
options: The strength measured immediately after sampling
The strength remaining after VERY LARGE shear displacement, once the clay particles along the shear surface have become ORIENTED parallel to it — substantially LOWER than the peak strength
The strength at zero effective stress
The average of the peak and the undrained strengths
questions.solution:
**The strength remaining after VERY LARGE shear displacement**, once the clay particles along the failure surface have become oriented parallel to it — and it is substantially LOWER than the peak strength.

**The stress-displacement behaviour of a stiff clay:**

| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| **Small displacement** | **Strength rises to a PEAK** ← |
| **At the peak** | **The maximum the intact clay can carry, with a cohesion intercept c′ and a friction angle φ′_peak** ← |
| **Beyond the peak** | **Strength FALLS — the clay STRAIN-SOFTENS** ← |
| **Larger displacement** | **Falls further, to a CRITICAL STATE (constant volume) value with c′ ≈ 0** ← |
| **VERY LARGE displacement — tens or hundreds of mm** ← | **The plate-like clay particles rotate into PARALLEL alignment along the shear plane — the RESIDUAL condition** ← |
| **Residual strength** | **c′_r = 0 and φ′_r substantially lower — often 10° or less in a highly plastic clay, against a peak of 20-25°** ← |

> **THE PARTICLE ALIGNMENT IN THE FIFTH ROW IS THE PHYSICAL MECHANISM AND IT EXPLAINS WHY THE DROP IS SO LARGE IN PLASTIC CLAYS: clay minerals are flat plates.**

> **Randomly arranged, they interlock and resist sliding. Aligned face-to-face along a polished shear surface, they slide over one another with very little resistance.**

> **The more plastic the clay — that is, the higher its clay fraction and the flatter its particles — the greater the drop, which is why residual strength matters most in exactly the soils that are already most troublesome.**

> **In a sand, where the grains are bulky and cannot align, peak and residual differ far less.**

**Why it matters — PROGRESSIVE FAILURE:**

| Step | What happens |
|---|---|
| **A slope is stressed non-uniformly** ← | **Some part of the potential failure surface is more heavily stressed than the rest** ← |
| **That part reaches its PEAK strength first, and then SOFTENS** ← | ← |
| **The load it can no longer carry is shed to the adjacent soil** ← | **Which is then overstressed, reaches its peak, and softens in turn** ← |
| **The failure PROPAGATES along the surface** ← | **Like a zip opening** ← |
| **By the time the whole surface has failed, much of it is at RESIDUAL, not peak** ← | **So the slope's actual strength was never the peak value the designer used** ← |

> **THIS IS WHY A SLOPE DESIGNED WITH PEAK PARAMETERS CAN FAIL AT A CALCULATED FACTOR OF SAFETY WELL ABOVE 1, and it is the central practical lesson of the topic:**

> **Peak strength can only be mobilised everywhere at once if the soil reaches its peak everywhere simultaneously — and in a real, non-uniformly stressed slope it does not.**

**When residual strength must be used:**

| Situation | Note |
|---|---|
| **A slope containing a PRE-EXISTING slip surface** ← | **An old landslide, whether recognised or not — the surface is already at residual and can never regain its peak** ← |
| **REACTIVATION of an ancient landslide** ← | **Extremely common in the Himalaya, where much of the terrain has failed before** ← |
| **Bedding-plane shears in folded or tectonically disturbed strata** | **Which the Himalaya has in abundance** ← |
| **Highly plastic clays and clay shales** | ← |
| **Any surface where large displacement has already occurred** | ← |

> **THE FIRST TWO ROWS DEFINE THE MOST IMPORTANT SLOPE STABILITY PROBLEM IN NEPAL AND ONE THAT IS ROUTINELY MISSED: an ancient landslide, long since revegetated and looking like ordinary hillside, retains a shear surface at RESIDUAL strength.**

> **Cut into its toe for a road, load its head with spoil, or raise its water table — and it reactivates at a strength far below what a laboratory test on intact samples would suggest.**

> **The clue is geomorphological rather than geotechnical: hummocky ground, back-tilted benches, a bulging toe, springs emerging along a line, tension cracks, and trees leaning uphill.**

> **Recognising an old landslide on the ground is therefore worth more than any amount of testing, because it tells you WHICH strength to use — and using the peak strength on a reactivated slide is not a conservative error but a fundamental one.**

examTip.trick: **After very large displacement the plate-like clay particles align along the shear plane and slide easily** — c′_r = 0 and φ′_r can be 10° or less against a peak of 20-25°.
examTip.trap: **PROGRESSIVE FAILURE means peak strength is never mobilised everywhere at once** — the overstressed part softens and sheds load to its neighbour, so a slope can fail at a calculated FoS above 1.
examTip.mnemonic: **An old landslide keeps its shear surface at RESIDUAL forever** — hummocky ground, back-tilted benches, a bulging toe, trees leaning uphill. Recognising it on the ground beats any laboratory test.

questions.stem: A TENSION CRACK forming at the crest of a clay slope reduces the slope's stability because it:
options: Increases the weight of the sliding mass
Allows sunlight to reach the failure surface
Reduces the slope angle
SHORTENS the length of the failure surface over which shear strength can act, and — if it FILLS WITH WATER — adds a horizontal HYDROSTATIC THRUST driving the slide
questions.solution:
**It shortens the failure surface over which shear strength acts, and if it fills with water it adds a horizontal HYDROSTATIC THRUST driving the slide.**

**The two effects, each significant on its own:**

| Effect | Note |
|---|---|
| **1. The RESISTING arc is SHORTENED** ← | **No shear strength can be mobilised across an open crack — so the length of surface contributing resistance is reduced by the crack's depth** ← |
| **2. WATER filling the crack exerts a horizontal FORCE** ← | **P_w = ½ γ_w z_c², acting at z_c/3 above the crack's base and pushing the mass outward** ← |
| **The disturbing moment increases and the resisting moment decreases — simultaneously** ← | **Both terms of the factor of safety move the wrong way** ← |

> **THE SIMULTANEITY IN THE THIRD ROW IS WHY A WATER-FILLED TENSION CRACK IS SO DAMAGING: most influences on slope stability affect either the driving side or the resisting side. This one attacks both at once.**

**THE ARITHMETIC OF THE WATER THRUST IS WORTH DOING, because the magnitude surprises people:**

| Crack depth | Water thrust per metre run |
|---|---|
| **2 m** | **½ × 9.81 × 4 = 19.6 kN/m** |
| **3 m** | **½ × 9.81 × 9 = 44.1 kN/m** ← |
| **5 m** | **½ × 9.81 × 25 = 123 kN/m** ← |

> **The force goes as the SQUARE of the depth, so a deep crack full of water applies an enormous horizontal push — comparable with the entire resisting force on a marginal slope.**

> **This is the direct mechanical explanation of why slope failures occur DURING or immediately after heavy rain, and often within hours of a storm: a crack that has been open and dry all season fills in a few hours, and the thrust appears almost instantly.**

**THE THEORETICAL DEPTH of a tension crack:**

| Relation | Note |
|---|---|
| **z_c = 2c / (γ √K_a)** ← | **For a cohesive soil behind a vertical face** ← |
| **The soil above this depth is in TENSION** | **And soil has essentially no tensile strength, so it cracks** ← |
| **Which is also why an unsupported vertical cut can stand to a limited height** ← | **H_c = 4c/(γ √K_a) = 2 z_c — twice the tension crack depth** ← |

> **THE RELATION IN THE LAST ROW IS ELEGANT AND WORTH KNOWING: the critical height of an unsupported vertical cut in clay is exactly TWICE the depth of the tension crack.**

> **And it carries a serious practical warning: that critical height is a THEORETICAL collapse height with a factor of safety of exactly 1.0.**

> **It also relies on the clay's COHESION, which is a temporary property — it depends on suction in the unsaturated soil, and it is lost when the soil wets up.**

> **A trench that stood open perfectly well for a week can collapse without warning after rain, and trench collapses kill more construction workers than almost any other single cause, because a cubic metre of soil weighs about two tonnes and a buried worker cannot be dug out in time.**

> **Which is why trench support is required by depth (typically beyond 1.2 m) regardless of how stable the ground appears — the rule deliberately ignores the engineer's judgement about cohesion, because that judgement has been wrong too often.**

**And what to do about tension cracks in practice:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **SEAL the crack — fill it with clay, or cover it with polythene** ← | **The cheapest and most effective emergency measure on a moving slope, and it can be done in an afternoon** ← |
| **Provide surface drainage to divert water AWAY from the crest** ← | **So the crack does not fill** ← |
| **Monitor crack width and length** | **A widening or lengthening crack is a moving slope, and it is the clearest warning available** ← |
| **Unload the crest, or load the toe** | **The classic geometric remedies** ← |
| **Include the crack in the stability analysis** ← | **Both effects — the shortened arc and, in the design case, a FULL crack of water** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE MOST VALUABLE PIECE OF PRACTICAL ADVICE HERE AND IT IS OFTEN OVERLOOKED IN AN EMERGENCY: when tension cracks appear above a slope, sealing them against rainfall is immediate, cheap, requires no design, and removes the single largest destabilising force.**

> **It buys the time in which a proper investigation and remedy can be arranged, and on a Nepali hillside during the monsoon that time is worth a great deal.**

examTip.trick: **It shortens the resisting arc AND, when full of water, pushes with ½γ_w z_c².** Both terms of the factor of safety move the wrong way at once.
examTip.trap: **The thrust goes as the SQUARE of the depth** — a 5 m crack full of water gives 123 kN/m. That is why slopes fail within hours of heavy rain.
examTip.mnemonic: **z_c = 2c/(γ√K_a), and the critical vertical cut height is exactly TWICE it** — but that FoS is 1.0 and relies on cohesion that vanishes when wet. Support trenches by depth, not by judgement.

questions.stem: COULOMB'S theory of earth pressure differs from RANKINE'S in that Coulomb's theory:
options: TAKES ACCOUNT of the FRICTION between the wall and the soil, and can handle an inclined wall face and a sloping or irregular backfill, by considering the equilibrium of a trial wedge
Assumes the wall is frictionless and vertical
Applies only to cohesive soils
Gives the same result as Rankine's in every case
questions.solution:
