**It takes account of WALL FRICTION**, and can handle an inclined wall face and an irregular backfill, by analysing the equilibrium of a trial WEDGE.

**The two theories compared:**

| Aspect | RANKINE | COULOMB |
|---|---|---|
| **Approach** | **A STRESS field — the state of stress throughout the soil mass** ← | **A rigid WEDGE sliding on a plane, in force equilibrium** ← |
| **WALL FRICTION δ** | **NEGLECTED — the wall is assumed SMOOTH** ← (option b describes Rankine) | **INCLUDED** ← |
| **Wall face** | **Assumed VERTICAL** | **May be INCLINED** ← |
| **Backfill surface** | **Horizontal, or uniformly sloping** | **Any shape, including irregular and with surcharges** ← |
| **Failure surface** | **A PLANE, from the theory itself** | **ASSUMED to be a plane, and the critical one found by TRIAL** ← |
| **For ACTIVE pressure** | **Conservative — it OVERESTIMATES, since neglecting wall friction ignores a helpful effect** ← | **More realistic and slightly lower** ← |
| **For PASSIVE pressure** | **Conservative — it UNDERESTIMATES** | **UNCONSERVATIVE and can be seriously so at high φ** ← |

> **THE LAST TWO ROWS CONTAIN THE PRACTICALLY IMPORTANT WARNING, and it is worth being precise about the direction of each error:**

> **For ACTIVE pressure, ignoring wall friction is SAFE. Wall friction acts upward on the soil wedge as it slides down, helping to hold it up, so including it reduces the pressure. Rankine, which omits it, therefore gives a higher and safer answer.**

> **For PASSIVE pressure the situation reverses and becomes dangerous: Coulomb's assumption that the failure surface is a PLANE is a poor one in the passive case, where the real surface is markedly CURVED.**

> **The plane assumption OVERESTIMATES the passive resistance, and the error grows with φ and with wall friction — at φ = 40° with full wall friction the overestimate can exceed 100 per cent.**

> **So Coulomb's active values may be used freely, and Coulomb's PASSIVE values must not be used for high friction angles: a curved-surface method (log-spiral) or a reduced coefficient is required.**

**THE TRIAL WEDGE METHOD, since it is Coulomb's essential idea:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Assume a PLANE failure surface at some angle** ← | **Through the base of the wall** |
| **Consider the equilibrium of the WEDGE between that plane and the wall** ← | **Under its own weight W, the reaction R on the failure plane (at φ to its normal), and the force P from the wall (at δ to the wall's normal)** ← |
| **Draw the TRIANGLE OF FORCES and solve for P** | **Three forces, two known directions — determinate** ← |
| **REPEAT for other trial planes** ← | **P varies with the assumed angle** ← |
| **The ACTIVE pressure is the MAXIMUM of those values** ← | **The wall must resist the worst wedge** ← |
| **The PASSIVE resistance is the MINIMUM** ← | **The soil will fail on whichever surface requires the least force** ← |

> **THE MAXIMUM-FOR-ACTIVE, MINIMUM-FOR-PASSIVE RULE IN THE LAST TWO ROWS IS THE PART MOST OFTEN CONFUSED, and the logic is worth holding:**

> **In the ACTIVE case, the soil is pushing and the wall must be strong enough for the worst wedge that could form — so take the largest P.**

> **In the PASSIVE case, the wall is pushing and the soil will fail along whichever surface it finds easiest — so the available resistance is the smallest P.**

> **In both cases nature chooses the easiest route, and the designer must take the unfavourable end of it.**

**And CULMANN'S graphical construction, which is Coulomb's method made practical:**

> **It is a graphical solution of the same trial wedge problem, and its virtue is that it handles ANY backfill shape and ANY arrangement of surcharge loads — irregular ground, a building near the wall, a stockpile — which closed-form equations cannot.**

> **In an age of computers its graphical nature is no longer an advantage, but the underlying idea remains the standard one: define the geometry, try many failure surfaces, and take the critical result.**

> **That is precisely how every modern slope stability and earth pressure program works — thousands of trial surfaces instead of a dozen, and the same principle of searching for the critical one.**

examTip.trick: **Coulomb includes WALL FRICTION and handles inclined walls and irregular backfill via a trial WEDGE. Rankine assumes a smooth vertical wall and works from a stress field.**
examTip.trap: **Coulomb's ACTIVE values are fine; its PASSIVE values are UNCONSERVATIVE** — the real passive failure surface is curved, and the plane assumption can overestimate resistance by over 100 % at high φ.
examTip.mnemonic: **Active = the MAXIMUM trial wedge force; passive = the MINIMUM.** Nature takes the easiest route, and the designer takes the unfavourable end of it.

questions.stem: A REINFORCED EARTH (mechanically stabilised earth) retaining wall carries the earth pressure by:
options: The bending strength of the precast facing panels
A massive concrete gravity section behind the panels
FRICTION between horizontal reinforcing strips or geogrids and the compacted granular fill, which allows the reinforced block to act as a COHERENT GRAVITY MASS
A row of piles driven behind the facing
questions.solution:
**By FRICTION between horizontal reinforcement and the compacted granular fill**, which makes the reinforced block behave as a coherent gravity mass.

**How it works:**

| Element | Function |
|---|---|
| **Horizontal REINFORCEMENT — steel strips, steel mesh, or polymer GEOGRIDS** ← | **Laid in layers as the fill is placed and compacted** ← |
| **The fill tries to spread laterally under its own weight** ← | **Generating TENSION in the reinforcement** ← |
| **That tension is resisted by FRICTION (and bearing, for grids) along the reinforcement** ← | **Which restrains the fill** ← |
| **The reinforced block then behaves as a single coherent MASS** ← | **Which resists the earth pressure from the retained fill behind it, by its own weight** ← |
| **The FACING panels merely retain the soil at the face** ← | **They carry very little load — which is why option (a) is wrong and why the facing can be thin** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE CONCEPTUAL HEART OF IT: reinforced earth is not a structural wall holding soil back. It is a block of soil that has been given INTERNAL TENSILE STRENGTH, so that it can act as a gravity wall.**

> **Soil is strong in compression and shear and has essentially no tensile strength. Adding reinforcement supplies the missing tension, in exactly the way steel bars supply it in concrete.**

> **The analogy with reinforced concrete is close and not accidental: a strong-in-compression, weak-in-tension material combined with a tensile element to make a composite that is good in both.**

**Its advantages, which have made it very widely used:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **FLEXIBLE — it tolerates differential settlement that would crack a rigid wall** ← | **So it suits poor and variable foundations, and it needs no piled foundation** ← |
| **Fast to build; no formwork, no curing, no skilled concrete work** | **Each layer is fill, compact, place reinforcement, repeat** ← |
| **CHEAPER than a reinforced concrete wall, increasingly so with height** ← | **A concrete wall's cost rises steeply with height; a reinforced earth wall's rises nearly linearly** ← |
| **Excellent SEISMIC performance** ← | **Its flexibility and ductility absorb ground motion that cracks rigid walls** ← |
| **The facing can be architecturally treated** | ← |
| **Uses locally available granular fill** | ← |

> **THE SEISMIC PERFORMANCE IN THE FOURTH ROW IS WELL DOCUMENTED AND WORTH KNOWING: reinforced earth walls have repeatedly survived earthquakes that destroyed rigid concrete walls nearby.**

> **A rigid wall must resist the dynamic thrust without moving, and if it cannot, it cracks or overturns. A reinforced earth wall deforms, absorbs energy, and settles into a new position still functioning.**

> **For Nepal's hill roads — poor foundations, high seismicity, difficult access for concrete, and abundant granular material — the case is strong, and gabion and reinforced-earth solutions are for the same reasons often preferable to masonry gravity walls.**

**The requirements and limitations, which are real:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **The fill MUST be GRANULAR and free-draining** ← | **Friction is the whole mechanism; a clay fill provides little friction, holds water, and creeps** ← |
| **Adequate DRAINAGE behind and beneath** | **Water pressure would defeat the design and corrode the reinforcement** ← |
| **CORROSION protection for steel reinforcement** ← | **Galvanising, plus a sacrificial thickness for the design life — and the fill's chemistry (chlorides, sulphates, pH, resistivity) must be tested** ← |
| **A sufficient reinforcement LENGTH** | **Typically 0.7 times the wall height, to extend beyond the active wedge into the resistant zone** ← |
| **Careful compaction close to the facing** ← | **But not with heavy plant, which would push the panels out of line** ← |
| **The facing connection is a critical detail** | **It is where failures concentrate** ← |

> **THE CORROSION ISSUE IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE PRINCIPAL LONG-TERM CONCERN WITH STEEL-REINFORCED WALLS AND IT IS INVISIBLE: the reinforcement is buried in the fill and cannot be inspected.**

> **A wall whose strips are corroding gives no warning until it deforms, and by then the reinforcement is inaccessible.**

> **Hence the requirement to test the fill's aggressiveness before construction, the sacrificial thickness allowance, and the growing preference for POLYMERIC geogrids where the fill's chemistry is doubtful or the design life is long — they do not corrode, though they must be checked for creep and for construction damage instead.**

examTip.trick: **Friction between reinforcement and granular fill gives the soil block internal TENSILE strength, so it acts as a coherent gravity mass.** The facing panels carry almost nothing.
examTip.trap: **The fill MUST be granular and free-draining** — friction is the entire mechanism, and a clay fill gives little friction, holds water and creeps.
examTip.mnemonic: **Flexible, so it tolerates settlement and survives earthquakes that crack rigid walls** — ideal for Nepali hill roads. But steel strips corrode invisibly: test the fill's chemistry, or use geogrid.

questions.stem: A STATIC PILE LOAD TEST is regarded as a more reliable measure of a pile's capacity than a dynamic driving formula because it:
options: Can be performed more quickly
MEASURES the pile's actual load-settlement behaviour under a SUSTAINED static load, which is the condition the pile will experience in service
Requires no reaction system
Is applicable only to bored piles
questions.solution:
**Because it MEASURES the pile's actual load-settlement behaviour under a sustained static load** — which is precisely the condition the pile will experience in service.

**The comparison:**

| Aspect | STATIC load test | DYNAMIC formula (Engineering News, Hiley) |
|---|---|---|
| **What is measured** | **Load against SETTLEMENT, directly** ← | **The pile's SET per blow during driving** ← |
| **Condition tested** | **The SERVICE condition — sustained static load** ← | **A dynamic impact of a few milliseconds** ← |
| **Applies to** | **Any pile — driven, bored, cast in situ** ← | **DRIVEN piles only** ← (so option (d) is backwards) |
| **Reliability** | **HIGH — it is a direct measurement** ← | **Poor; scatter against measured capacity of ±50 % or more is common** ← |
| **Cost and time** | **EXPENSIVE and slow — days, with a large reaction load** ← | **Free — the data are obtained while driving** ← |
| **Practice** | **One or two piles on a site, typically 0.5 to 2 per cent** ← | **Every pile, as a construction control** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW DESCRIBES HOW THE TWO ARE ACTUALLY USED TOGETHER, and it is the sensible answer rather than a choice between them:**

> **A static test on one or two piles establishes the true capacity and CALIBRATES the dynamic formula for that site and that hammer.**

> **The calibrated formula is then applied to every remaining pile as a driving control — giving both the reliability of a direct measurement and the coverage of a universal check, at an acceptable cost.**

> **Using either alone is worse: dynamic formulae alone are unreliable, and static tests on every pile are unaffordable.**

**Why dynamic formulae are so unreliable:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **They equate the hammer's ENERGY to the work done in penetrating** ← | **Ignoring the wave propagation that actually occurs in a long slender pile** ← |
| **Energy is lost in ways the formula cannot account for** | **Elastic compression of the pile, the cushion, the helmet and the soil; heat; hammer inefficiency** ← |
| **Dynamic resistance is NOT static resistance** ← | **A rapidly loaded soil, especially a clay, is much stronger — so the driving resistance overstates the long-term capacity** ← |
| **SET-UP and RELAXATION occur after driving** ← | **Clays typically GAIN capacity over days or weeks as the disturbed soil reconsolidates; some dense sands and shales LOSE it** ← |

> **THE SET-UP EFFECT IN THE LAST ROW IS LARGE AND IS THE REASON A RE-DRIVE OR A DELAYED TEST IS SPECIFIED: a pile driven into soft clay may show a capacity at the end of driving that DOUBLES or TREBLES over the following weeks, as the excess pore pressures generated by driving dissipate.**

> **Judging such a pile by its end-of-driving resistance is therefore extremely conservative, and driving it to refusal to achieve the design capacity immediately is both wasteful and may damage the pile.**

> **The opposite case — RELAXATION, a loss of capacity after driving — is less common but far more dangerous, since the pile appeared satisfactory when driven and is not.**

> **Both are reasons to test after a delay rather than at the end of driving.**

**How the static test is performed and interpreted:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Load applied by jacking against KENTLEDGE (dead weight) or against REACTION PILES** ← | **Reaction piles must be far enough away not to interact — usually 3 diameters or 2.5 m** ← |
| **Load applied in increments, each held until the settlement rate is small** | ← |
| **Test to 1.5 × working load (routine) or 2.5 × (initial/ultimate test)** ← | **A routine test proves the pile; an initial test establishes the capacity** ← |
| **Safe load taken as the LESSER of: two thirds of the load causing 12 mm settlement, and half the load at which settlement equals 10 % of the pile diameter** ← | **A settlement-based criterion, because a pile rarely shows a clean plunging failure** ← |

> **THE SETTLEMENT-BASED CRITERION IN THE LAST ROW REFLECTS SOMETHING IMPORTANT ABOUT PILES: most do not fail suddenly.**

> **The load-settlement curve bends over gradually, and there is no unambiguous "ultimate load" to read from it.**

> **So the capacity is DEFINED by an acceptable settlement rather than by a failure — which means that a pile's "safe load" is a serviceability quantity, not a strength one.**

> **That is a useful thing to understand: for most foundations, what limits the load is not the risk of collapse but the amount of movement the structure above can tolerate.**

examTip.trick: **It measures load against settlement under the SERVICE condition** — a sustained static load — whereas a dynamic formula infers capacity from a few milliseconds of impact.
examTip.trap: **Use both: a static test on 1-2 piles CALIBRATES the dynamic formula, which then controls every other pile.** Neither alone is satisfactory.
examTip.mnemonic: **SET-UP: clays can double or treble their capacity in the weeks after driving; some sands RELAX and lose it.** Test after a delay, not at the end of driving. And safe load is defined by SETTLEMENT, not failure.

questions.stem: A clay whose PRESENT effective overburden pressure is LESS than the maximum pressure it has carried at some time in the past is described as:
options: Normally consolidated
Under-consolidated
Sensitive
OVER-CONSOLIDATED, with an over-consolidation ratio greater than 1
questions.solution:
**OVER-CONSOLIDATED**, with an over-consolidation ratio (OCR) greater than 1.

**The definitions:**

| State | Definition | OCR |
|---|---|---|
| **NORMALLY CONSOLIDATED (NC)** | **The present effective stress is the HIGHEST the soil has ever carried** ← | **OCR = 1** ← |
| **OVER-CONSOLIDATED (OC)** | **The soil has carried a HIGHER stress in the past** ← | **OCR > 1** ← |
| **UNDER-CONSOLIDATED** | **The soil is still consolidating under its present overburden — it has not yet reached equilibrium** ← | **OCR < 1** ← |

> **OCR = preconsolidation pressure (p_c) ÷ present effective overburden pressure (p₀).**

**What causes over-consolidation:**

| Cause | Note |
|---|---|
| **EROSION of overlying soil** ← | **The classic case — the load was there and has been removed** ← |
| **Melting of an ICE SHEET** | **Which pressed down on the soil during a glaciation** ← |
| **A FALL and subsequent RISE of the water table** ← | **A low water table raises the effective stress; when it rises again the effective stress falls, leaving the soil over-consolidated** ← |
| **DESICCATION — drying of the surface** ← | **Suction in the drying soil acts as an effective stress, and it can be very large — which is why the crust of almost every clay deposit is over-consolidated** ← |
| **AGEING and secondary compression** | **Producing an apparent preconsolidation without any past load** ← |
| **Removal of a structure** | ← |

> **THE DESICCATED CRUST IN THE FOURTH ROW IS THE MOST COMMONLY ENCOUNTERED CASE AND IT HAS A PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE THAT MISLEADS PEOPLE: almost every soft clay deposit has a stiff, over-consolidated crust a metre or two thick at the surface.**

> **A trial pit or a shallow investigation encounters that crust, finds a satisfactory stiff clay, and reports good ground.**

> **Beneath it lies soft, normally consolidated clay of much lower strength and much higher compressibility, and a foundation whose stress bulb reaches into it will settle badly.**

> **The crust is a trap for shallow investigation, and it is one more argument for boring to a depth related to the loaded WIDTH rather than to a fixed figure.**

**Why the distinction matters so much:**

| Behaviour | NORMALLY consolidated | OVER-consolidated |
|---|---|---|
| **COMPRESSIBILITY** | **HIGH — every increment of load causes substantial settlement** ← | **LOW, until the preconsolidation pressure is exceeded** ← |
| **Settlement under a new load** | **Large** | **SMALL — while the total stress stays below p_c** ← |
| **Strength** | **Lower** | **Higher** ← |
| **Behaviour in shear** | **CONTRACTS; generates POSITIVE pore pressure** ← | **DILATES; generates NEGATIVE pore pressure and shows a peak strength followed by softening** ← |
| **K₀ (at rest pressure coefficient)** | **1 − sin φ′, typically about 0.5** ← | **HIGHER, and can EXCEED 1 at high OCR — the soil pushes sideways harder than it does downward** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW GIVES THE MOST IMPORTANT DESIGN CONSEQUENCE AND IT IS WHY THE PRECONSOLIDATION PRESSURE IS DETERMINED AT ALL: an over-consolidated clay settles very little while the applied stress keeps the total below p_c, and settles a great deal once p_c is exceeded.**

> **The settlement calculation therefore has a KINK in it: use the recompression index C_r for the part of the load below p_c, and the much larger compression index C_c for whatever lies above it.**

> **Using C_c throughout grossly overestimates the settlement of an over-consolidated clay; using C_r throughout grossly underestimates it once p_c is passed. Both errors are large, and finding p_c from the consolidation test — by Casagrande's construction — is what avoids them.**

> **THE HIGH K₀ IN THE LAST ROW IS A LESS FAMILIAR BUT IMPORTANT CONSEQUENCE: a heavily over-consolidated clay retains locked-in horizontal stresses from the load it once carried.**

> **A retaining wall or a basement in such a clay may attract lateral pressures far above the active value — approaching or exceeding the at-rest value, and in extreme cases the vertical stress itself.**

> **Designing such a wall for Rankine active pressure, on the assumption that it will move enough to relieve the stress, can be seriously unsafe, and this is one of the situations in which the difference between active and at-rest pressure genuinely matters.**

examTip.trick: **OCR = preconsolidation pressure ÷ present effective overburden.** OCR = 1 normally consolidated, > 1 over-consolidated, < 1 still consolidating.
examTip.trap: **Almost every soft clay has a stiff DESICCATED CRUST** — a shallow trial pit finds good ground and misses the soft, compressible clay beneath. Bore to a depth related to the loaded WIDTH.
examTip.mnemonic: **Settlement has a KINK at p_c: use C_r below it and C_c above.** And a heavily over-consolidated clay retains locked-in horizontal stress, so K₀ can exceed 1 — active pressure may be unsafe there.

questions.stem: An oil has a dynamic viscosity of 1.2 poise and a density of 900 kg/m³. Its KINEMATIC viscosity is:
questions.solution:
**1.33 × 10⁻⁴ m²/s (equivalently 1.33 stokes).**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Convert the dynamic viscosity to SI** | **1 poise = 0.1 N·s/m² (Pa·s), so 1.2 poise = 0.12 Pa·s** ← |
| **Kinematic viscosity** | **ν = μ / ρ** ← |
| **Substituting** | **ν = 0.12 / 900** |
| **ν** | **= 1.333 × 10⁻⁴ m²/s** ← |
| **In CGS units** | **1 stoke = 10⁻⁴ m²/s, so ν = 1.333 stokes** ← |

> **Option (b) uses 1.2 poise as though it were 1.2 Pa·s but then divides correctly by 1,000 rather than 900 — the sort of near-miss that a units check catches.**

> **The DECIMAL PLACE is where most errors occur here, and the unit conversions are the reason: poise and stokes are CGS units still in everyday use for viscosity, and both must be converted before anything else is done.**

**The units, gathered, since they are the whole difficulty:**

| Quantity | SI unit | CGS unit | Conversion |
|---|---|---|---|
| **DYNAMIC viscosity μ** | **Pa·s = N·s/m² = kg/(m·s)** ← | **POISE = dyne·s/cm²** ← | **1 poise = 0.1 Pa·s** ← |
| **KINEMATIC viscosity ν** | **m²/s** ← | **STOKE = cm²/s** ← | **1 stoke = 10⁻⁴ m²/s** ← |
| **Also used** | — | **centipoise, centistoke** | **1 cP = 10⁻³ Pa·s; water at 20 °C is almost exactly 1 cP** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW GIVES THE MOST USEFUL REFERENCE VALUE IN THE WHOLE TOPIC AND IS WORTH MEMORISING: water at 20 °C has a dynamic viscosity of almost exactly 1 centipoise = 10⁻³ Pa·s, and a kinematic viscosity of almost exactly 10⁻⁶ m²/s (1 centistoke).**

> **That single pair of numbers lets any viscosity answer be sanity-checked: an oil should be tens or hundreds of times more viscous than water, and an answer that comes out less viscous than water is wrong.**

> **Here 1.33 × 10⁻⁴ is 133 times water's kinematic viscosity — entirely plausible for an oil ✓**

**The distinction between the two viscosities, which is the concept behind the arithmetic:**

| Viscosity | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **DYNAMIC (absolute) μ** | **The fluid's resistance to shear — the constant in τ = μ du/dy** ← |
| **KINEMATIC ν = μ/ρ** | **The resistance to shear relative to the fluid's INERTIA** ← |

> **THE PHYSICAL MEANING OF DIVIDING BY DENSITY IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING RATHER THAN ACCEPTING: viscous forces resist motion, and inertia resists changes in motion.**

> **Kinematic viscosity is the ratio of the two, so it measures how quickly viscous effects DIFFUSE through the fluid relative to how much the fluid resists being moved.**

> **It appears in the Reynolds number — Re = VD/ν — precisely because Re is the ratio of inertial to viscous forces, and ν has already combined both into one quantity.**

> **A striking illustration: AIR has a dynamic viscosity about 55 times SMALLER than water's, and a kinematic viscosity about 15 times LARGER — because air's density is some 800 times less.**

> **So air is much "thinner" in the everyday sense and diffuses momentum much faster, and for the same velocity and size the Reynolds number in air is LOWER than in water.**

> **That is why the two viscosities cannot be used interchangeably, and why the formula being used must be checked for which one it wants.**

examTip.trick: **1 poise = 0.1 Pa·s, so 1.2 poise = 0.12; ν = μ/ρ = 0.12/900 = 1.33 × 10⁻⁴ m²/s = 1.33 stokes** (1 stoke = 10⁻⁴ m²/s).
examTip.trap: **Convert the CGS units FIRST** — poise and stokes are still in everyday use, and the errors here are all decimal places.
examTip.mnemonic: **Water at 20 °C: μ ≈ 1 cP = 10⁻³ Pa·s and ν ≈ 10⁻⁶ m²/s.** Any oil must come out more viscous than that. And air has LOWER dynamic but HIGHER kinematic viscosity than water.

questions.stem: A fluid whose apparent viscosity INCREASES as the rate of shear increases — such as a dense suspension of sand in water — is described as:
options: DILATANT (shear-thickening)
Pseudoplastic (shear-thinning)
Newtonian
An ideal fluid
questions.solution:
**DILATANT**, or shear-thickening — its apparent viscosity RISES with the rate of shear.

**The classification of fluids by their shear stress-shear rate behaviour:**

| Type | Behaviour | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **NEWTONIAN** | **τ = μ (du/dy) — a STRAIGHT LINE through the origin; the viscosity is constant** ← | **Water, air, most oils, glycerine** ← |
| **DILATANT (shear-thickening)** | **Apparent viscosity RISES with shear rate — the curve is CONCAVE UPWARD** ← | **Dense suspensions of sand or starch in water; wet beach sand; some slurries** ← |
| **PSEUDOPLASTIC (shear-thinning)** | **Apparent viscosity FALLS with shear rate — CONCAVE DOWNWARD** ← | **Paint, blood, polymer solutions, ketchup, most drilling muds** ← |
| **BINGHAM PLASTIC** | **Requires a YIELD STRESS before it flows at all; then behaves like a Newtonian** ← | **Toothpaste, sewage sludge, fresh concrete, some drilling muds** ← |
| **THIXOTROPIC** | **Viscosity falls with TIME under constant shear, and recovers at rest** ← | **Bentonite drilling mud; some paints and gels** ← |
| **RHEOPECTIC** | **Viscosity rises with time under shear** | Rare |

> **THE FIRST FOUR ARE DISTINGUISHED BY THE SHAPE OF THE CURVE AND THE LAST TWO BY TIME DEPENDENCE, which is the organising distinction worth carrying: dilatant and pseudoplastic depend on the RATE of shear; thixotropic and rheopectic depend on how LONG shearing has continued.**

**Why dilatancy occurs, since the mechanism is intuitive once seen:**

| Step | What happens |
|---|---|
| **At rest, the particles in a dense suspension are packed as closely as they can be** ← | **With just enough liquid to fill the voids** ← |
| **To SHEAR the suspension, particles must ride over one another** ← | **Which requires the packing to LOOSEN — that is, the volume to INCREASE** ← |
| **That volume increase is DILATANCY** ← | **The same word, and the same phenomenon, as the dilatancy of a dense sand in soil mechanics** ← |
| **But there is no extra liquid to fill the new voids** ← | **So the liquid is drawn in, suction develops, and the mixture resists — strongly, and more so the faster you try to shear it** ← |

> **THE CONNECTION TO SOIL MECHANICS IN THE THIRD ROW IS EXACT AND WORTH NOTICING: a DENSE sand must expand to be sheared, and that is why it shows a peak strength and generates negative pore pressure in an undrained test.**

> **A dilatant suspension is the same material behaviour observed in a fluid mechanics setting, and the SPT dilatancy correction met earlier arises from the same cause.**

> **One phenomenon appearing in three parts of the syllabus, which is worth recognising as one thing rather than three.**

> **A familiar demonstration: WET BEACH SAND. Press it slowly with a foot and it yields; strike it sharply and it feels solid, and the sand around the footprint goes momentarily DRY as the dilating voids suck the water down.**

**Where these fluids matter in civil engineering:**

| Fluid | Relevance |
|---|---|
| **Fresh CONCRETE — a Bingham plastic** ← | **It has a yield stress, which is why it holds a slump instead of levelling out, and why the slump test works at all** ← |
| **Bentonite DRILLING MUD — thixotropic** ← | **It flows freely when pumped and GELS when circulation stops, holding the cuttings in suspension instead of letting them settle onto the bit** ← |
| **Sewage SLUDGE — Bingham plastic** | **Its yield stress governs pumping and pipe sizing** ← |
| **Debris flows and mudflows** | **Highly non-Newtonian, which is why they behave so differently from clear water floods** ← |

> **THE DRILLING MUD IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE MOST ELEGANT ENGINEERING USE OF NON-NEWTONIAN BEHAVIOUR, and it is worth appreciating: a thixotropic mud is asked to do two contradictory things.**

> **While circulating it must be FLUID, so it can be pumped down the drill pipe and back up the annulus without excessive pressure.**

> **When circulation stops — for a pipe connection, or a breakdown — it must become a GEL, so the rock cuttings it is carrying do not settle and jam the bit.**

> **A Newtonian fluid cannot do both. A thixotropic one does exactly this: shear it and it thins, leave it and it sets, and the transition is reversible and immediate.**

> **The same behaviour is exploited in bentonite slurry for diaphragm walls and bored piles, where the slurry must support the excavation's walls while remaining pumpable.**

examTip.trick: **DILATANT = shear-THICKENING (viscosity rises with shear rate); PSEUDOPLASTIC = shear-THINNING.** Bingham needs a yield stress first; thixotropic depends on TIME, not rate.
examTip.trap: **Dilatancy is the same phenomenon as a dense sand's dilatancy in soil mechanics** — particles must ride over one another, the packing must loosen, and there is no extra liquid to fill the new voids.
examTip.mnemonic: **Thixotropic drilling mud does two contradictory things: FLUID while pumped, GEL when stopped** so cuttings don't settle. Same trick for bentonite slurry in diaphragm walls.

questions.stem: For a plane surface submerged in a liquid, the CENTRE OF PRESSURE always lies BELOW the centroid of the area because:
options: The pressure INCREASES with depth, so the lower part of the area carries a greater share of the total force
The liquid is denser at greater depth
The surface is always inclined
Of the surface tension acting at the free surface
questions.solution:
**Because pressure INCREASES linearly with depth**, so the lower part of the area carries a disproportionate share of the total force, and the resultant acts below the area's geometric centre.

**The relation:**

| Quantity | Expression |
|---|---|
| **Total force on the surface** | **F = γ h̄ A, with h̄ the depth of the CENTROID** ← |
| **Depth of the CENTRE OF PRESSURE** | **h_cp = h̄ + I_G sin²θ / (A h̄)** ← |
| **For a VERTICAL surface (θ = 90°)** | **h_cp = h̄ + I_G / (A h̄)** ← |
| **The second term is always POSITIVE** ← | **So the centre of pressure is ALWAYS below the centroid** ← |

> **THE ALWAYS-POSITIVE SECOND TERM IS THE ANSWER IN ALGEBRAIC FORM: I_G, A and h̄ are all positive quantities, so the correction can never be negative and the centre of pressure can never be above the centroid.**

> **Note also that the FORCE uses the depth of the CENTROID while its POSITION is at the centre of pressure — two different depths, and confusing them is the classic error in these problems.**

**How the two separate with depth, which is the useful behaviour:**

| Situation | I_G/(A h̄) | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **The surface is close to the free surface (h̄ small)** ← | **LARGE** | **The centre of pressure is well below the centroid** ← |
| **The surface is DEEPLY submerged (h̄ large)** ← | **SMALL** ← | **The two nearly coincide** ← |
| **In the limit of very great depth** | **→ 0** | **The pressure is almost uniform over the area, so the resultant acts at the centroid** ← |

> **THE DEEP-SUBMERGENCE LIMIT IS PHYSICALLY OBVIOUS ONCE STATED AND IT IS A GOOD CHECK ON THE FORMULA: a small gate 100 m down experiences almost the same pressure at its top and bottom, so there is nothing to shift the resultant away from the centre.**

> **A gate whose top is at the water surface experiences zero pressure at the top and full pressure at the bottom, and the resultant sits at the third point — as far from the centroid as it ever gets.**

**The standard case, worth having at hand:**

| Case | h̄ | h_cp |
|---|---|---|
| **A vertical rectangle of height d with its TOP AT the free surface** ← | **d/2** | **h̄ + (bd³/12)/(bd × d/2) = d/2 + d/6 = 2d/3** ← |
| **In words** | ← | **The resultant acts at ONE THIRD of the depth from the BOTTOM** ← |

> **THAT RESULT — the resultant of a triangular pressure distribution acting at the third point — is the one to have memorised, because it covers dams, retaining walls, gates at the surface, and every hydrostatic pressure diagram that starts from zero.**

> **It also generalises: for any TRIANGULAR distribution the resultant acts at one third of the height from the base, which is the same result met in earth pressure on a retaining wall and in the water thrust in a tension crack.**

**And the practical consequence for gate and dam design:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **The OVERTURNING MOMENT depends on where the resultant acts, not merely on its size** ← | **So the centre of pressure determines the stability calculation** ← |
| **A gate's hinge or trunnion must be positioned with the centre of pressure in mind** | ← |
| **For a dam, the resultant of the water thrust at the third point sets the overturning moment about the toe** ← | **And it is why the elementary profile of a gravity dam works out as it does** ← |
| **As the water level changes, the centre of pressure MOVES** ← | **So the check must be made at several water levels, not only at the maximum** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW REPEATS A THEME THAT HAS APPEARED SEVERAL TIMES — with the hydraulic jump's tailwater, with spillway energy dissipation, and with reservoir levels — and it is worth stating as a general habit:**

> **The maximum load is not always the critical case. Check the structure across the full range of conditions it will actually experience, because an intermediate state can combine a moderate force with an unfavourable position or an absent counterbalance.**

examTip.trick: **h_cp = h̄ + I_G/(A h̄) for a vertical surface** — the second term is always positive, so the centre of pressure is ALWAYS below the centroid.
examTip.trap: **The FORCE uses the centroid depth; its POSITION is the centre of pressure.** Two different depths, and confusing them is the standard error.
examTip.mnemonic: **Deeply submerged, the two nearly coincide** (the pressure is almost uniform). **Top at the surface, the resultant is at the THIRD point** — the same triangular-distribution result as earth pressure.

questions.stem: A TRIANGULAR (V-notch) weir is preferred to a rectangular one for measuring SMALL discharges principally because:
options: It is cheaper to construct
Its discharge varies as H^2.5 rather than H^1.5, so a small change in discharge produces a much LARGER and more readable change in head
It requires no approach channel
Its discharge coefficient is exactly 1.0
questions.solution:
**Because its discharge varies as H^2.5 rather than H^1.5**, so at small flows a given change in discharge produces a much larger — and therefore more readable — change in head.

**The two discharge relations:**

| Notch | Discharge formula |
|---|---|
| **RECTANGULAR** | **Q = (2/3) C_d √(2g) L H^1.5** ← |
| **TRIANGULAR (V-notch), total angle θ** | **Q = (8/15) C_d √(2g) tan(θ/2) H^2.5** ← |
| **For a 90° V-notch, tan 45° = 1** | **Q = (8/15) C_d √(2g) H^2.5 ≈ 1.4 H^2.5 (SI units)** ← |

> **THE HIGHER POWER IS THE ENTIRE ADVANTAGE, and the arithmetic makes it concrete:**

| Discharge falls to | Head falls to (rectangular, H^1.5) | Head falls to (V-notch, H^2.5) |
|---|---|---|
| **1/10 of the original** | **(0.1)^(1/1.5) = 0.215, so 21.5 % of H** ← | **(0.1)^(1/2.5) = 0.398, so 39.8 % of H** ← |
| **1/100** | **4.6 % of H — a tiny, unreadable head** ← | **15.8 % of H — still comfortably measurable** ← |

> **AT ONE HUNDREDTH OF THE DESIGN FLOW, A RECTANGULAR NOTCH IS SHOWING A HEAD OF A FEW MILLIMETRES AND A V-NOTCH IS STILL SHOWING A USEFUL DEPTH.**

> **Since the head is the quantity actually measured, and it can be read to perhaps ±1 mm, the V-notch retains its accuracy over a far wider range of flows.**

> **The reason is geometric and easy to see: as the water level in a V-notch falls, the WIDTH of the flowing section falls too. In a rectangular notch the width stays the same, so the flow area shrinks only in proportion to the depth.**

> **The V-notch's area shrinks in proportion to the depth SQUARED, which is where the extra power comes from.**

**The trade-off, stated fairly:**

| Aspect | RECTANGULAR | TRIANGULAR |
|---|---|---|
| **Sensitivity at LOW flow** | **Poor** | **EXCELLENT** ← |
| **Capacity at HIGH flow** | **Good — the head rises slowly** ← | **POOR — the head rises very steeply, and the notch must be made deep** ← |
| **Range of flows handled well** | **Moderate to high** | **Low to moderate** ← |
| **Where used** | **Canals, larger streams, treatment plants** ← | **Laboratory work, small streams, seepage measurement, spring yields** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE MIRROR IMAGE OF THE ADVANTAGE AND IS WHY V-NOTCHES ARE NOT USED FOR EVERYTHING: the same H^2.5 relation that makes them sensitive at low flow makes the head climb alarmingly at high flow.**

> **A tenfold increase in discharge raises a V-notch's head by a factor of 2.5 against a rectangular notch's 4.6 — so the V-notch needs a much greater depth of channel and much more freeboard.**

> **A CIPOLLETTI (trapezoidal) notch is the compromise: its sides slope at 1 horizontal to 4 vertical, and the additional area they provide compensates for the end contractions, so its discharge follows the simple rectangular H^1.5 law without a length correction.**

**The practical requirements for accurate weir measurement, which are frequently neglected:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **The head H is measured UPSTREAM of the drawdown** ← | **At least 3 to 4 times H back from the notch — measuring at the crest gives a value well below the true head** ← |
| **The nappe must be fully VENTILATED** ← | **Air must reach beneath the falling sheet; if it cannot, the nappe clings, the pressure beneath falls, and the discharge is greater than the formula gives** ← |
| **A sharp, clean CREST** | **A rounded or damaged crest changes the coefficient** ← |
| **The approach flow must be smooth and the velocity of approach small** | **Or it must be allowed for** ← |
| **Free discharge — the downstream level must be BELOW the crest** ← | **A drowned weir does not obey the formula at all** ← |

> **THE VENTILATION POINT IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE COMMONEST SOURCE OF ERROR IN PRACTICE AND IS EASILY MISSED: a nappe with no air beneath it entrains the air, the space below is partly evacuated, and the sheet is pulled downward.**

> **The weir then discharges more than its formula predicts — by several per cent — and worse, the nappe oscillates between clinging and free, so the reading is unsteady.**

> **A simple air pipe through the side wall, below the crest, cures it entirely, and it costs nothing.**

examTip.trick: **Q ∝ H^2.5 for a V-notch against H^1.5 for a rectangular one** — at 1/100 of the flow, the rectangular head is 4.6 % of H and the V-notch's is 15.8 %, still readable.
examTip.trap: **The same power makes the V-notch POOR at high flow** — the head climbs steeply and the notch must be deep. A CIPOLLETTI (1:4 sides) is the compromise, following the simple H^1.5 law.
examTip.mnemonic: **Measure H at 3-4 H upstream of the notch, and VENTILATE the nappe** — an unventilated nappe clings, over-discharges by several per cent, and oscillates. An air pipe costs nothing.

questions.stem: A pipe surface is described as HYDRAULICALLY SMOOTH when:
options: Its roughness projections have been polished away entirely
The pipe is made of plastic rather than steel
The surface ROUGHNESS projections are SUBMERGED within the LAMINAR SUB-LAYER, so they do not disturb the turbulent flow and the friction factor depends on the Reynolds number alone
The Reynolds number exceeds 4,000
questions.solution:
**When the roughness projections are entirely SUBMERGED within the LAMINAR SUB-LAYER**, so they do not disturb the turbulent core — and the friction factor then depends on the Reynolds number alone.

**The mechanism:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **Even in fully turbulent pipe flow, a very thin LAMINAR SUB-LAYER persists against the wall** ← | **The no-slip condition forces the velocity to zero at the wall, and viscosity dominates in that thin film** ← |
| **Its thickness δ′ DECREASES as the Reynolds number rises** ← | **Faster flow scours it thinner** ← |
| **If the roughness height k is LESS than δ′, the projections are buried in it** ← | **The turbulent core never "sees" them — the surface is HYDRAULICALLY SMOOTH** ← |
| **If k is much GREATER than δ′, the projections stick out into the turbulent flow** ← | **Generating eddies and form drag — the surface is fully ROUGH** ← |

> **THE CRUCIAL POINT, AND THE ONE THE QUESTION IS TESTING, IS THAT "SMOOTH" IS NOT A PROPERTY OF THE PIPE ALONE.**

> **The same pipe can be hydraulically smooth at a low velocity and hydraulically rough at a high one, because the sub-layer thins as the flow speeds up while the roughness stays the same.**

> **So the classification depends on the FLOW as well as on the surface — which is why option (a) is wrong: a pipe need not be polished to behave as smooth, it need only be smoother than the sub-layer is thick.**

**The three regimes on the Moody diagram:**

| Regime | Condition | f depends on |
|---|---|---|
| **LAMINAR (Re < 2,000)** | **Viscous flow throughout** | **Re ALONE: f = 64/Re. Roughness is IRRELEVANT** ← |
| **Hydraulically SMOOTH turbulent** | **k < δ′** ← | **Re alone — all the curves collapse onto one line** ← |
| **TRANSITIONAL turbulent** | **k comparable with δ′** | **BOTH Re and the relative roughness k/D** ← |
| **Fully ROUGH turbulent** | **k ≫ δ′** ← | **Relative roughness k/D ALONE — the curves become HORIZONTAL, and f is independent of Re** ← |

> **THE LAMINAR ROW CONTAINS A RESULT THAT SURPRISES PEOPLE AND IS WORTH STATING: in LAMINAR flow, the pipe's roughness makes no difference whatever to the friction factor.**

> **The fluid moves in smooth layers, the roughness is buried in a slow-moving film, and f = 64/Re regardless of whether the pipe is polished glass or rusted iron.**

> **THE FULLY ROUGH ROW CONTAINS THE MIRROR RESULT AND IT IS THE ONE WITH PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCES: once the flow is fully rough, the friction factor is independent of the Reynolds number.**

> **The Moody curves become horizontal, and f depends only on k/D. That is why, for most practical water pipelines — which operate in or near the fully rough zone — the friction factor can be taken as a constant for a given pipe, and why the head loss then varies almost exactly as V².**

> **It is also why the empirical formulae that assume h_f ∝ V^1.85 or V² — Hazen-Williams, Manning — work as well as they do: they are implicitly assuming the fully rough regime, and they become inaccurate outside it.**

**The practical consequences of ageing, which is where this matters most:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **A new pipe may be hydraulically SMOOTH; the same pipe after 20 years is ROUGH** ← | **Corrosion, tuberculation and deposits raise k by an order of magnitude** ← |
| **The friction factor can DOUBLE over the pipe's life** ← | **And the effective diameter falls as well** ← |
| **So the discharge falls, or the pumping cost rises, or both** | **Steadily and invisibly** ← |
| **Design must therefore use an AGED roughness value, not the new-pipe value** ← | **A pipeline sized on new-pipe roughness will fail to deliver within a decade** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE PRACTICAL CONCLUSION AND IT IS ROUTINELY IGNORED IN FAVOUR OF THE MANUFACTURER'S FIGURE: designing a gravity main on the roughness of a brand-new pipe produces a scheme that works perfectly at commissioning and under-delivers for the remaining forty years of its life.**

> **The conservative and correct approach is to check the design at both extremes — the new condition, which governs the maximum velocity and any surge, and the aged condition, which governs whether the design discharge can still be delivered at the end of the design period.**

examTip.trick: **Roughness buried inside the LAMINAR SUB-LAYER** — so the turbulent core never sees it and f depends on Re alone. "Smooth" is a property of the FLOW as well as the pipe.
examTip.trap: **In LAMINAR flow roughness is irrelevant (f = 64/Re); in FULLY ROUGH flow the Reynolds number is irrelevant (f depends on k/D alone).** Each regime ignores one variable.
examTip.mnemonic: **Design on AGED roughness, not the new-pipe value** — f can double over 20 years. Check the new condition for velocity and surge, the aged one for delivering the design discharge.

questions.stem: The maximum height of the SUMMIT of a siphon above the upstream water surface is limited in practice to about 7 to 8 metres because:
options: Above that height the pressure at the summit would fall to the water's VAPOUR PRESSURE, the water would boil and the siphon would break
The pipe would burst under the internal pressure
The friction loss becomes infinite
The flow would become supercritical
questions.solution:
**Because above that height the pressure at the summit would fall to the water's VAPOUR PRESSURE**, the water would boil, a vapour pocket would form, and the siphon would break.

**The reasoning:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **The siphon is driven by ATMOSPHERIC pressure acting on the upstream surface** ← | **About 10.3 m of water at sea level** ← |
| **Applying Bernoulli from the upstream surface to the summit** | **The pressure at the summit falls BELOW atmospheric by the summit's height, plus the velocity head, plus the friction loss to that point** ← |
| **The ABSOLUTE limit is the point at which the summit pressure reaches the vapour pressure** ← | **About 0.24 m of water at 20 °C — so the theoretical maximum height is roughly 10.3 − 0.24 ≈ 10 m** ← |
| **In PRACTICE the limit is 7 to 8 m** ← | **Because the velocity head, the friction losses and the release of dissolved air all reduce it further** ← |

> **THE GAP BETWEEN THE THEORETICAL 10 m AND THE PRACTICAL 7 TO 8 m IS ACCOUNTED FOR BY REAL EFFECTS, and the most important of them is the one least often mentioned:**

> **DISSOLVED AIR comes out of solution as the pressure falls, long before the water actually boils.**

> **That air collects at the summit, where the pressure is lowest and the velocity may be low, and it accumulates. As the pocket grows it reduces the flow area, then breaks the continuous column of water, and the siphon stops.**

> **So a siphon may run perfectly for hours and then fail, with no change in conditions at all — simply because enough air has gathered at the top.**

> **That is why a working siphon needs an air-release arrangement at its summit, or must be periodically primed.**

**The altitude effect, which reduces the limit further in the hills:**

| Location | Atmospheric head | Practical siphon limit |
|---|---|---|
| **Sea level** | **10.3 m** | **7 to 8 m** ← |
| **Kathmandu, 1,400 m** | **About 8.8 m** ← | **About 6 m** ← |
| **3,000 m** | **About 7.3 m** | **About 4.5 m** ← |

> **A SIPHON DESIGNED AT SEA LEVEL AND BUILT IN THE HILLS WILL NOT WORK, which is the same trap met with pump suction lift and turbine setting — and for exactly the same reason.**

> **All three depend on the atmospheric pressure available to push water up, and all three shrink together as altitude rises.**

> **Recognising them as one problem rather than three is worth doing: whenever a design relies on atmospheric pressure to lift or hold water, the site's altitude must be substituted for the textbook 10.3 m.**

**Where siphons are used, and how they behave:**

| Use | Note |
|---|---|
| **Drawing water over an embankment or a canal bank without a cutting** ← | **The classic irrigation application** ← |
| **Emptying a tank or reservoir with no bottom outlet** | ← |
| **SIPHON SPILLWAYS on dams** ← | **Which have a remarkable property: they PRIME automatically as the water rises and then discharge at full capacity almost immediately** ← |
| **In water treatment, transferring between tanks** | ← |

> **THE SIPHON SPILLWAY IN THE THIRD ROW IS WORTH KNOWING BECAUSE ITS BEHAVIOUR IS SO UNLIKE AN ORDINARY SPILLWAY: an overflow spillway's discharge rises gradually with the head above its crest, following Q ∝ H^1.5.**

> **A siphon spillway does nothing at all until the water reaches its priming level, at which point it primes and discharges at very nearly its FULL capacity within seconds.**

> **The advantage is that it passes a large discharge with a very small rise in reservoir level, which is valuable where freeboard is scarce.**

> **The disadvantage is that it is ALL OR NOTHING, and the sudden onset and cessation send surges downstream. It can also "hunt" — priming, drawing the level down below the priming point, breaking, refilling, and repeating — which produces a pulsating discharge and vibration.**

> **For that reason siphon spillways are used sparingly, and usually as an auxiliary to a conventional overflow rather than as the main spillway.**

examTip.trick: **Theoretical limit ≈ 10.3 − 0.24 ≈ 10 m; practical limit 7-8 m** after velocity head, friction and air release are allowed for.
examTip.trap: **DISSOLVED AIR comes out of solution long before the water boils**, collects at the summit, and breaks the column — so a siphon can run for hours and then stop with no change in conditions.
examTip.mnemonic: **Siphon height, pump suction lift and turbine setting are ONE problem** — all limited by the atmospheric head available, all shrinking with altitude. About 6 m in Kathmandu, not 8.

questions.stem: In the classical THREE-RESERVOIR problem, three pipes from reservoirs at different levels meet at a junction. The solution proceeds by:
options: Assuming the flow in all three pipes is equal
Assuming the friction factor is the same in all three pipes
Ignoring the middle reservoir entirely
ASSUMING a piezometric HEAD at the junction, computing the flow in each pipe, and adjusting that head by trial until CONTINUITY is satisfied at the junction
questions.solution:
**By assuming a piezometric HEAD at the junction**, computing the flow in each pipe from the head difference, and adjusting the assumed head by trial until the flows balance — that is, until continuity is satisfied.

**The procedure:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **1. ASSUME a piezometric head H_J at the junction** ← | **A sensible first guess is the level of the MIDDLE reservoir** ← |
| **2. For each pipe, the head difference is (reservoir level − H_J)** ← | **POSITIVE means flow INTO the junction; negative means flow OUT of it** ← |
| **3. Compute each flow from the Darcy or Hazen-Williams equation** | ← |
| **4. Check CONTINUITY: Σ(inflow) must equal Σ(outflow)** ← | **The junction stores nothing** ← |
| **5. If they do not balance, ADJUST H_J and repeat** ← | **Too much inflow means H_J was too low; raise it** ← |
| **6. Converge** | **Usually in three or four trials, or graphically by plotting the imbalance against H_J** ← |

> **THE KEY QUESTION THE PROBLEM TURNS ON, AND WHY THE FIRST GUESS IS THE MIDDLE RESERVOIR'S LEVEL:**

| If H_J is... | Then the middle reservoir |
|---|---|
| **BELOW the middle reservoir's level** | **SUPPLIES water to the junction — flow is OUT of it** ← |
| **ABOVE the middle reservoir's level** | **RECEIVES water from the junction — flow is INTO it** ← |
| **EXACTLY at its level** | **NO FLOW in that pipe at all** ← |

> **THE DIRECTION OF FLOW IN THE MIDDLE PIPE IS THEREFORE NOT KNOWN IN ADVANCE, and that is the whole difficulty of the problem — it must emerge from the solution rather than being assumed at the start.**

> **The highest reservoir always supplies and the lowest always receives; the middle one may do either.**

> **Starting the trial AT the middle reservoir's level is efficient precisely because it immediately settles the question: compute the other two flows at that head, and if the higher reservoir's inflow exceeds the lower one's outflow, H_J must rise and the middle reservoir must be receiving.**

**What makes the problem instructive rather than merely tedious:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Two governing conditions** | **CONTINUITY at the junction, and a consistent piezometric head at the junction shared by all three pipes** ← |
| **These are exactly the conditions of any pipe NETWORK** ← | **Junction continuity, and a single head at each junction** ← |
| **So the three-reservoir problem is the smallest possible pipe network** ← | **And its trial-and-error solution is the germ of the Hardy Cross method and of every modern network solver** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS WHY THE PROBLEM IS STILL TAUGHT: it contains, in a form small enough to solve by hand, exactly the structure of a real distribution network analysis.**

> **Hardy Cross's method applies the same two conditions to a network of loops, correcting the assumed flows iteratively instead of a single assumed head.**

> **And a modern solver does the same thing with a matrix and hundreds of junctions.**

> **Understanding why the three-reservoir problem cannot be solved directly — because the flow direction in one pipe is unknown until the head is known, and the head is unknown until the flows are known — is understanding why network analysis is iterative in principle rather than merely in practice.**

**And a practical note on where the arrangement arises:**

| Situation | Note |
|---|---|
| **A service reservoir connected into a transmission main between two others** ← | **Filling at night when demand is low and the head is high; supplying by day when it falls** ← |
| **A break-pressure tank on a gravity main with branches** | ← |
| **A pumped supply into a network with elevated storage** ← | **The tank floats on the system, absorbing and releasing according to the pressure** ← |

> **THE FIRST AND THIRD ROWS DESCRIBE THE NORMAL OPERATION OF AN ELEVATED SERVICE RESERVOIR AND IT IS EXACTLY THE THREE-RESERVOIR PROBLEM IN PRACTICE: the tank's flow reverses twice a day as the network's piezometric head rises above and falls below the tank's water level.**

> **That is what a balancing reservoir is FOR — it absorbs the mismatch between a steady supply and a varying demand, and it does so automatically, with no valve and no operator, simply because the junction head moves relative to its own level.**

examTip.trick: **Assume the junction head, compute each flow, check continuity, adjust and repeat.** Start the trial at the MIDDLE reservoir's level — it settles the flow direction immediately.
examTip.trap: **The flow direction in the middle pipe is UNKNOWN in advance** — it supplies if H_J is below its level and receives if above. That is why the problem cannot be solved directly.
examTip.mnemonic: **It is the smallest possible pipe NETWORK** — junction continuity plus one head per junction, which is exactly Hardy Cross and every modern solver. And it is how a balancing reservoir works, twice a day.

questions.stem: In a rectangular channel, a hydraulic jump occurs where the upstream depth is 0.5 m and the upstream Froude number is 3.0. The depth after the jump (the conjugate depth) is approximately:
questions.solution:
**About 1.89 m.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **The conjugate (sequent) depth relation** | **y₂/y₁ = ½ [√(1 + 8 Fr₁²) − 1]** ← |
| **Fr₁² = 9, so 8 Fr₁² = 72** | ← |
| **√(1 + 72)** | **= √73 = 8.544** |
| **y₂/y₁ = ½ (8.544 − 1)** | **= ½ × 7.544 = 3.772** ← |
| **y₂ = 3.772 × 0.5** | **= 1.886 ≈ 1.89 m** ← |

> **Option (a) 1.50 m is y₁ × Fr₁, a plausible-looking but meaningless product; option (d) 3.00 m mistakes the Froude number for the depth ratio.**

**Where the relation comes from, since it is worth knowing it is exact:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The jump is analysed by the MOMENTUM equation, not energy** ← | **Because an unknown and substantial amount of energy is DISSIPATED in the turbulence** ← |
| **The quantity conserved across the jump is the SPECIFIC FORCE (momentum function)** ← | **M = A ȳ + Q²/(gA)** ← |
| **Equating the specific force before and after, for a rectangular channel, yields the conjugate depth relation** | **Which is therefore EXACT, not empirical** ← |
| **The two depths having the same specific force are called CONJUGATE (or sequent) depths** ← | **Distinct from ALTERNATE depths, which share the same specific ENERGY** ← |

> **THE DISTINCTION IN THE LAST ROW IS EXAMINED OFTEN AND IS WORTH KEEPING CLEAR:**

> **ALTERNATE depths — same specific ENERGY, different depths, one subcritical and one supercritical. They occur where the flow changes smoothly, with no loss.**

> **CONJUGATE depths — same specific FORCE. They are the depths either side of a hydraulic JUMP, where energy IS lost.**

> **Using the energy equation across a jump, or the momentum equation across a smooth transition, is the standard error, and it produces answers that are wrong by a large margin.**

**The energy loss, which is the jump's purpose:**

| Quantity | Value here |
|---|---|
| **Energy loss E_L = (y₂ − y₁)³ / (4 y₁ y₂)** ← | **= (1.386)³ / (4 × 0.5 × 1.886) = 2.663/3.772 = 0.706 m** ← |
| **Upstream specific energy E₁ = y₁ + V₁²/2g** | **V₁ = Fr₁√(g y₁) = 3 × 2.215 = 6.64 m/s, so E₁ = 0.5 + 2.25 = 2.75 m** ← |
| **Efficiency of dissipation** | **0.706 / 2.75 = 26 per cent of the incoming energy destroyed** ← |

> **A QUARTER OF THE ENERGY DESTROYED IN A FEW METRES OF CHANNEL, and that is what a stilling basin is built to achieve.**

**The classification of jumps by Froude number, which determines the basin design:**

| Fr₁ | Type | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **1.0 to 1.7** | **UNDULAR jump** | **A series of standing waves; very little energy lost** ← |
| **1.7 to 2.5** | **WEAK jump** | **Smooth surface; 5 to 15 % loss** |
| **2.5 to 4.5** | **OSCILLATING jump** ← | **AWKWARD — an unstable oscillating jet generates waves that travel far downstream and can erode banks** ← |
| **4.5 to 9.0** | **STEADY jump** ← | **The BEST — stable, well-balanced, 45 to 70 % energy loss, insensitive to tailwater** ← |
| **Above 9.0** | **STRONG (choppy) jump** | **Very effective (up to 85 %) but rough, and hard on the structure** ← |

> **THE OSCILLATING RANGE IN THE MIDDLE ROW IS THE ONE TO AVOID IN DESIGN, and this jump at Fr₁ = 3.0 falls squarely in it.**

> **The jet oscillates irregularly between the bed and the surface, generating waves that persist for a long way downstream and attack the channel banks.**

> **Where the Froude number cannot be moved out of this range by adjusting the geometry, the remedy is a stilling basin with BAFFLE BLOCKS and a stepped end sill, which force the jump to stabilise in position and break up the oscillation — which is precisely what the standard basin designs for this range are shaped to do.**

examTip.trap: **CONJUGATE depths share specific FORCE (across a jump, where energy is lost); ALTERNATE depths share specific ENERGY (across a smooth transition).** Using the wrong equation is the standard error.
examTip.mnemonic: **Fr₁ = 2.5-4.5 is the OSCILLATING jump — the one to avoid**, throwing waves far downstream. 4.5-9.0 is the steady, well-behaved jump. Baffle blocks tame the oscillating range.

questions.stem: Water flowing SUBCRITICALLY in a rectangular channel passes over a smooth HUMP in the bed. Provided the flow does not choke, the water surface over the hump will:
options: Rise, because the bed has risen
Remain at the same level
DROP, because the specific energy is reduced by the hump's height and a subcritical flow responds to a loss of specific energy by DECREASING its depth
Become supercritical immediately
questions.solution:
**The water surface DROPS** over the hump — a result that surprises most people the first time they meet it.

**The reasoning:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Neglecting losses, the total energy line is HORIZONTAL across the hump** ← | ← |
| **The specific energy E is measured from the BED** ← | **So raising the bed by Δz REDUCES the specific energy available: E₂ = E₁ − Δz** ← |
| **On the specific energy curve, a SUBCRITICAL flow sits on the UPPER limb** ← | **Where depth INCREASES with specific energy** ← |
| **So reducing E moves the point DOWN the upper limb — the depth DECREASES** ← | ← |
| **The SURFACE level is bed level + depth, and here the depth falls by MORE than the bed rises** ← | **So the water surface DROPS over the hump** ← |

> **THE RESULT STATED PLAINLY: over a hump, a SUBCRITICAL flow speeds up and its surface DROPS. A SUPERCRITICAL flow slows down and its surface RISES.**

> **The two regimes respond in OPPOSITE directions to the same obstruction, which is the single most useful thing to know about channel transitions.**

**The specific energy curve, which makes it visible:**

| Limb | Flow | Behaviour as E decreases |
|---|---|---|
| **UPPER limb (depth above critical)** | **SUBCRITICAL** ← | **Depth DECREASES toward critical** ← |
| **LOWER limb (depth below critical)** | **SUPERCRITICAL** ← | **Depth INCREASES toward critical** ← |
| **The NOSE of the curve** | **CRITICAL flow** | **The MINIMUM specific energy for that discharge, E_min = 1.5 y_c** ← |

> **BOTH LIMBS MOVE TOWARD THE CRITICAL DEPTH AS THE SPECIFIC ENERGY IS REDUCED, and that is the underlying principle: any obstruction that reduces the specific energy pushes the flow, from either side, toward critical.**

**CHOKING, which is what happens when the hump is too high:**

| Situation | What happens |
|---|---|
| **Hump height Δz < E₁ − E_min** | **The flow passes over, depth adjusts, upstream is unaffected** ← |
| **Δz EXACTLY equals E₁ − E_min** ← | **CRITICAL flow occurs at the crest — the limiting case** ← |
| **Δz GREATER than that** ← | **The flow CHOKES — the given discharge cannot pass with the available energy** ← |
| **The consequence of choking** | **The UPSTREAM depth must RISE, increasing the specific energy until the flow can pass — a BACKWATER effect propagating upstream** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE PRACTICALLY IMPORTANT ONE AND IT HAS REAL CONSEQUENCES: a channel obstruction that is too large does not simply cause a local disturbance.**

> **It raises the water level for a considerable distance UPSTREAM, because the flow must accumulate enough energy to get past — and in subcritical flow, disturbances travel upstream freely.**

> **That is the mechanism of AFFLUX at a bridge, a weir, or a culvert: the structure constricts the flow, the flow chokes, and the level rises upstream until the discharge can pass.**

> **Land that floods upstream of a new bridge or a new road embankment is flooding for exactly this reason, and it is why the afflux calculation is a required part of any structure across a watercourse — and why the land affected by it must be identified and accounted for.**

**And the critical crest as a MEASURING device, which is the useful application:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **When critical flow occurs at the crest, there is a UNIQUE relation between the head upstream and the discharge** ← | **q = √(g y_c³), and y_c = (2/3) E** ← |
| **So measuring one depth gives the discharge** ← | **With no need to measure velocity at all** ← |
| **This is the principle of the BROAD-CRESTED WEIR and the critical-depth FLUME** ← | ← |
| **And of the PARSHALL and VENTURI flumes** ← | **Which force critical flow by contracting the width instead of raising the bed** ← |

> **THE CRITICAL SECTION IS THEREFORE THE MOST USEFUL THING IN OPEN CHANNEL MEASUREMENT: it is a CONTROL, at which depth and discharge are uniquely related and independent of what happens downstream.**

> **Every open channel flow measuring structure works by deliberately creating one — by a hump, a contraction, or a drop — and then measuring a single depth upstream of it.**

examTip.trick: **A hump reduces the specific energy (E₂ = E₁ − Δz), and a SUBCRITICAL flow on the upper limb responds by getting SHALLOWER** — so the surface drops.
examTip.trap: **Subcritical and supercritical respond in OPPOSITE directions** — over a hump, subcritical drops and supercritical rises. Both move TOWARD critical as E falls.
examTip.mnemonic: **Too high a hump CHOKES the flow and raises the level far UPSTREAM** — that is exactly the afflux at a bridge or culvert. And a deliberately created critical section is the basis of every flume and broad-crested weir.

questions.stem: The UNIT HYDROGRAPH method rests on two fundamental assumptions, namely:
options: That rainfall is uniform in intensity and that the catchment is circular
That the catchment is impermeable and that base flow is zero
That the storm duration equals the time of concentration and that the runoff coefficient is 1.0
LINEARITY (the ordinates are proportional to the rainfall excess) and TIME INVARIANCE (the same catchment gives the same unit hydrograph shape for storms of the same duration)
questions.solution:
**LINEARITY** — the direct runoff ordinates are proportional to the depth of rainfall excess — and **TIME INVARIANCE**, that the same catchment always produces the same unit hydrograph shape for a storm of the same duration.

**The definition, first:**

> **A D-hour UNIT HYDROGRAPH is the direct runoff hydrograph resulting from ONE UNIT (1 cm, or 1 inch) of rainfall EXCESS falling UNIFORMLY over the whole catchment in D hours.**

| Element of the definition | Note |
|---|---|
| **One UNIT of rainfall EXCESS** ← | **Excess, not total rainfall — the losses have already been deducted** ← |
| **DIRECT runoff** ← | **Base flow has been separated out and is NOT part of the unit hydrograph** ← |
| **UNIFORMLY over the whole catchment** | **Both in space and, within the duration D, in time** ← |
| **In D hours** | **The duration is part of the definition — a 6-hour UH differs from a 2-hour UH for the same catchment** ← |

> **THE FIRST TWO ROWS CONTAIN THE TWO THINGS MOST OFTEN GOT WRONG: the unit hydrograph relates EXCESS rainfall to DIRECT runoff.**

> **Total rainfall and total streamflow do not enter into it, and forgetting to deduct losses or to separate base flow makes every subsequent calculation wrong.**

**The two assumptions and what they permit:**

| Assumption | Meaning | What it permits |
|---|---|---|
| **LINEARITY (proportionality)** ← | **3 cm of excess produces ordinates 3 times those for 1 cm** ← | **SCALING the unit hydrograph to any rainfall depth** ← |
| **SUPERPOSITION (a consequence of linearity)** ← | **The runoff from successive rainfall blocks can be ADDED, each lagged by its own start time** ← | **Building the hydrograph for a complex, multi-block storm** ← |
| **TIME INVARIANCE** ← | **The catchment's response does not change from storm to storm** ← | **Using a UH derived from one storm to predict another** ← |

> **SUPERPOSITION IS WHAT MAKES THE METHOD USEFUL RATHER THAN MERELY DESCRIPTIVE, and it is worth seeing clearly: a real storm is not one uniform block of rain.**

> **It is a sequence of blocks of differing intensity. Linearity lets each block's contribution be computed by scaling the unit hydrograph, and superposition lets them be added with the appropriate lags.**

> **So a single unit hydrograph, derived once, can generate the flood hydrograph for any storm pattern whatever — which is the whole point of the technique.**

**Where the assumptions fail, stated honestly:**

| Failure | Note |
|---|---|
| **Catchments are NOT truly linear** ← | **A large flood travels faster and its peak is proportionately higher than linearity predicts — the response is genuinely non-linear** ← |
| **Rainfall is never uniform over a large catchment** ← | **Which is why the method is limited to catchments below about 5,000 km², and preferably much smaller** ← |
| **Storm MOVEMENT matters** | **A storm travelling downstream produces a sharper peak than one travelling upstream — and the UH cannot distinguish them** ← |
| **The catchment CHANGES over time** | **Urbanisation, deforestation, reservoirs — so an old unit hydrograph may no longer apply** ← |
| **Antecedent conditions vary** | **Affecting the losses, which the UH does not address at all** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE ONE MOST RELEVANT TO NEPAL AND SOUTH ASIA AND IT UNDERMINES TIME INVARIANCE DIRECTLY: a unit hydrograph derived from records of the 1970s describes a catchment that no longer exists.**

> **Deforestation, terracing, road building and urban expansion all make a catchment respond FASTER — a higher, earlier peak from the same rainfall.**

> **So an old unit hydrograph systematically UNDERESTIMATES the flood peak of a developed catchment, and a design based on it is unsafe in exactly the direction that matters.**

> **Checking whether the catchment has changed materially since the record was gathered is therefore part of using the method properly, and it is routinely skipped because the records are what they are and re-deriving is expensive.**

> **Despite all of this, the unit hydrograph remains the most widely used flood estimation tool for gauged catchments, because it is simple, it uses data that actually exist, and its errors are understood — which is a fair summary of why approximate methods survive in engineering long after their limitations are known.**

examTip.trick: **LINEARITY (ordinates scale with rainfall excess) and TIME INVARIANCE (the same catchment gives the same response).** Linearity gives SUPERPOSITION, which is what makes the method useful.
examTip.trap: **It relates EXCESS rainfall to DIRECT runoff** — losses deducted, base flow separated. Using total rainfall or total streamflow invalidates everything downstream of it.
examTip.mnemonic: **Deforestation and urbanisation make a catchment respond FASTER**, so an old unit hydrograph UNDERESTIMATES the peak — unsafe in exactly the wrong direction. Check whether the catchment still exists as recorded.

questions.stem: A cantilever 4 m long carries a uniformly distributed load of 10 kN/m over the OUTER 2 m of its length (that is, from 2 m to 4 m from the fixed end). The bending moment at the fixed end is:
options: 40 kNm
60 kNm
80 kNm
120 kNm
questions.solution:
**60 kNm.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Total load on the loaded length** | **W = 10 kN/m × 2 m = 20 kN** ← |
| **Its RESULTANT acts at the CENTROID of the loaded length** ← | **The midpoint of the outer 2 m, which is 3 m from the fixed end** ← |
| **Bending moment at the fixed end** | **M = W × distance = 20 × 3** |
| **M** | **= 60 kNm** ← |

> **Option (a) 40 kNm uses the distance to the NEAR end of the load (2 m); option (c) 80 kNm uses the distance to the FAR end (4 m).**

> **Both are the right method with the wrong lever arm, and getting the lever arm right — to the CENTROID of the load, not to either of its ends — is the whole of this question.**

**The bending moment diagram, which the numbers alone do not show:**

| Region | Shear force | Bending moment |
|---|---|---|
| **0 to 2 m from the fixed end (UNLOADED)** | **CONSTANT at 20 kN** ← | **LINEAR — rising from 20 kNm at 2 m to 60 kNm at the support** ← |
| **2 to 4 m (LOADED)** | **Varies LINEARLY from 0 at the tip to 20 kN at 2 m** ← | **PARABOLIC — from 0 at the tip to 20 kNm at 2 m** ← |

> **THE DIAGRAM IS THEREFORE PART PARABOLA AND PART STRAIGHT LINE, meeting smoothly at the 2 m point, and that is a good check on the reasoning:**

> **Over an UNLOADED length, dV/dx = 0 so the shear is constant, and dM/dx = V so the moment is LINEAR.**

> **Over a UDL, the shear is linear and the moment is PARABOLIC.**

> **Each integration raises the degree by one, and the transition between the two must be smooth in slope because the shear is continuous at that point.**

**A useful check: computing the moment the long way**

| Method | Working |
|---|---|
| **Take moments of the whole distributed load about the support** | **∫ from 2 to 4 of (10 × x) dx = 10 × [x²/2] from 2 to 4** ← |
| **= 10 × (8 − 2)** | **= 60 kNm ✓** ← |

> **The integral gives the same answer, which confirms that replacing a distributed load by its resultant at its centroid is exact for computing a moment about any point — not an approximation.**

> **That equivalence is worth being confident about, because it is what allows almost every distributed load problem to be turned into a point load problem.**

**And the general principle for a cantilever, which makes such problems quick:**

| Principle | Note |
|---|---|
| **Work from the FREE END toward the support** ← | **No reactions are needed — the free end has none** ← |
| **The moment at any section is the sum of (each load beyond it) × (its distance to that section)** ← | ← |
| **The maximum moment is always AT THE FIXED END** ← | **For any downward loading on a cantilever** ← |
| **The maximum shear is also at the fixed end** | **Equal to the total load** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE PRACTICAL ADVANTAGE OF A CANTILEVER IN ANALYSIS AND IT IS WORTH EXPLOITING: because the free end carries no reaction, the internal forces at any section can be found directly from the loads beyond it.**

> **There is no need to compute reactions at all, and no simultaneous equations — which is why a cantilever is the one beam whose diagrams can be sketched with almost no calculation.**

> **It is also the reason a cantilever is statically DETERMINATE with a single fixed support: three reaction components, three equilibrium equations, no redundancy.**

examTip.trick: **W = 10 × 2 = 20 kN acting at the CENTROID of the loaded length, 3 m from the support: M = 60 kNm.**
examTip.trap: **Options (a) and (c) use the distance to the near end (2 m) and the far end (4 m).** The lever arm goes to the load's CENTROID — right method, wrong arm.
examTip.mnemonic: **Work a cantilever from the FREE END** — no reactions needed, no simultaneous equations. The unloaded length gives a LINEAR moment, the loaded length a PARABOLIC one, meeting smoothly.

questions.stem: An INTERNAL HINGE introduced within the span of a continuous beam is useful in analysis because it:
options: Increases the beam's bending capacity at that point
Prevents the beam from deflecting
Transfers no shear force across the section
Provides ONE ADDITIONAL EQUATION of condition — that the bending moment there is ZERO — which can make an otherwise indeterminate beam statically determinate
questions.solution:
**It provides one additional EQUATION OF CONDITION** — that the bending moment at the hinge is ZERO — which reduces the degree of static indeterminacy by one.

**What a hinge does and does not transmit:**

| Action | Transmitted across an internal hinge? |
|---|---|
| **SHEAR force** | **YES** ← (so option (c) is false) |
| **AXIAL force** | **YES** ← |
| **BENDING MOMENT** | **NO — it is zero by definition** ← |
| **Rotation** | **The two sides rotate INDEPENDENTLY** ← |

> **THE COMBINATION IN THE FIRST AND THIRD ROWS IS THE POINT: a hinge is a connection that carries FORCE but not MOMENT.**

> **It is not a break in the beam — the two parts stay connected and shear passes freely — but the beam can kink there, so no bending moment can develop.**

**How the equation of condition works:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Static indeterminacy D_s = (number of unknown reactions) − (equilibrium equations available)** ← | **Three equations in a plane** ← |
| **Each internal hinge ADDS one equation: ΣM = 0 for all forces on one side of it** ← | ← |
| **So D_s = r − 3 − (number of equations of condition)** ← | ← |

| Example | Reactions | Hinges | D_s |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A two-span continuous beam on 4 simple supports** | **4** | **0** | **4 − 3 = 1, INDETERMINATE** ← |
| **The same beam with ONE internal hinge** | **4** | **1** | **4 − 3 − 1 = 0, DETERMINATE** ← |
| **A propped cantilever (fixed + roller)** | **4** | **0** | **1** |
| **The same with a hinge** | **4** | **1** | **0 — determinate** ← |

> **THAT IS THE ANALYTICAL VALUE OF A HINGE, and it is why the three-hinged arch is so much easier to analyse than a two-hinged one: three hinges provide the extra condition that makes it determinate, so it can be solved by statics alone.**

**Why hinges are provided in REAL structures, which is the more important question:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **To make the structure INSENSITIVE to support SETTLEMENT** ← | **A determinate structure develops NO stress from a settlement — it simply moves. An indeterminate one develops large forces** ← |
| **To eliminate stresses from TEMPERATURE change** ← | **The same argument** ← |
| **To allow for shrinkage and creep** | ← |
| **The GERBER (cantilever) BEAM** ← | **A continuous beam with hinges placed so it is determinate — used in bridges precisely to avoid settlement stresses on poor foundations** ← |
| **To simplify construction and erection** | **Each determinate segment can be erected independently** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE ENGINEERING REASON THAT MATTERS MOST AND IT IS A GENUINE DESIGN CHOICE WITH A REAL TRADE-OFF:**

> **An INDETERMINATE structure is more efficient — it redistributes load, has redundancy against local failure, and generally uses less material.**

> **But it is also SENSITIVE: a support that settles 20 mm, or a temperature change of 30 °C, induces forces that were never part of the applied loading and can be large.**

> **A DETERMINATE structure is less efficient and completely indifferent to both. Settle its support and it rotates; heat it and it expands; no stress arises in either case.**

> **So on poor, variable or unpredictable foundations, a determinate structure is often the right answer despite using more material — which is why the Gerber beam was invented and why three-hinged arches were used where two-hinged ones would have been lighter.**

> **THE REDUNDANCY POINT DESERVES THE COUNTER-ARGUMENT THOUGH: a determinate structure has NO alternative load path.**

> **Remove one member and it collapses, because there is by definition nothing spare. An indeterminate structure can lose a member and redistribute, which is the whole basis of ROBUSTNESS and of resistance to progressive collapse.**

> **Modern practice therefore tends to prefer indeterminacy and to deal with settlement and temperature by analysis, rather than to design them away by releases — but the older reasoning remains valid where the foundations genuinely cannot be predicted.**

examTip.trick: **A hinge transmits SHEAR and AXIAL force but NO moment** — giving one extra equation, ΣM = 0 about the hinge for one side. D_s = r − 3 − (number of conditions).
examTip.trap: **Option (c) is false** — shear passes freely across an internal hinge. The beam is not broken there; it can only kink.
examTip.mnemonic: **A determinate structure is INDIFFERENT to settlement and temperature** — that is why Gerber beams and three-hinged arches exist. The price is no alternative load path and no robustness.

questions.stem: A load applied SUDDENLY to an elastic bar (placed on it with zero initial velocity and released) produces a maximum stress that is:
options: TWICE that produced by the same load applied GRADUALLY
Equal to that produced by a gradually applied load
Half that of a gradually applied load
Four times that of a gradually applied load
questions.solution:
