**TWICE the stress produced by the same load applied gradually.**

**The proof, by ENERGY, which takes three lines:**

| Step | Reasoning |
|---|---|
| **A suddenly applied load P descends through the full extension δ while its magnitude stays constant at P** ← | **It is not applied progressively; it is at full value from the first instant** ← |
| **Work done by the load** | **W = P δ** ← |
| **Strain energy stored in the bar at extension δ** | **U = ½ P′ δ, where P′ is the internal resisting force at that extension** ← |
| **Equating work and energy: P δ = ½ P′ δ** | **So P′ = 2P** ← |
| **Hence the maximum stress and deflection are DOUBLE** ← | ← |

> **THE ESSENTIAL DIFFERENCE IS IN THE FIRST ROW AND IT IS WORTH STATING CLEARLY: a GRADUALLY applied load builds from zero to P as the bar extends, so the average force doing work is P/2.**

> **A SUDDENLY applied load is at its full value P throughout the extension, so the average force doing work is P.**

> **Twice the work is done, so twice the strain energy must be stored, and since U goes as the square of the deflection... the deflection doubles and the force at maximum deflection doubles with it.**

> **The bar then oscillates about the static position, overshooting to twice the static deflection and returning, until damping settles it at the static value.**

> **So the factor of 2 is a TRANSIENT peak, not a permanent condition — but the peak is what the material must survive.**

**The general IMPACT case, of which this is a special instance:**

| Case | Impact factor |
|---|---|
| **GRADUAL (static) application** | **1** ← |
| **SUDDEN application, zero drop height** | **2** ← (this question) |
| **Load dropped from height h** | **1 + √(1 + 2h/δ_st), where δ_st is the static deflection** ← |
| **Check: putting h = 0 in that expression** | **1 + √1 = 2 ✓ — the sudden case falls out of the general one** ← |

> **THE CONSISTENCY CHECK IN THE LAST ROW IS WORTH DOING BECAUSE IT CONFIRMS BOTH RESULTS AT ONCE: the general impact formula must reduce to the sudden-loading factor of 2 when the drop height is zero, and it does.**

> **The general formula also shows how severe impact becomes: for a drop of even a few times the static deflection, the factor rises quickly. With h = 100 δ_st the factor is about 15.**

**Why this matters in practice:**

| Situation | Note |
|---|---|
| **A load DROPPED into a hopper, a skip or a truck body** ← | **Designed with an impact allowance, not for the static weight** ← |
| **CRANE loads — lifting and snatching** ← | **Codes specify an impact factor of 25 % or more on the hook load** ← |
| **BRIDGE loading from moving vehicles** ← | **An impact allowance is added to the live load, decreasing with span** ← |
| **PILE driving** | **The extreme case** ← |
| **A load suddenly TRANSFERRED when a prop or a temporary support is removed** ← | **Which is precisely why props should be released GRADUALLY, not knocked away** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE SITE PRACTICE THAT FOLLOWS DIRECTLY FROM THIS RESULT AND IT IS OFTEN NOT UNDERSTOOD BY THOSE DOING IT: striking a prop by knocking it out applies its load SUDDENLY to the structure below, doubling the stress momentarily.**

> **Releasing it gradually — by lowering a wedge, a screw jack or a sand box — applies the load statically, and the structure sees half as much.**

> **On a marginal or young structure that factor of two is the difference between a satisfactory transfer and a failure, and it costs nothing but a few minutes and the right equipment.**

> **It is also why heavy falsework is designed with jacks or sand boxes at the props rather than folding wedges: controlled release is a structural requirement, not a convenience.**

examTip.trick: **A gradual load averages P/2 while extending; a sudden load is at full P throughout.** Twice the work, twice the deflection, twice the stress.
examTip.trap: **The factor of 2 is a TRANSIENT peak** — the bar oscillates and settles at the static deflection. But the peak is what the material must survive.
examTip.mnemonic: **General impact factor 1 + √(1 + 2h/δ_st), which gives exactly 2 at h = 0.** Hence: release props with jacks or sand boxes, never knock them out — the sudden transfer doubles the stress.

questions.stem: A steel bar is subjected to a uniaxial tensile stress of 150 MPa. Taking E = 200 GPa and Poisson's ratio 0.30, the VOLUMETRIC STRAIN of the bar is:
questions.solution:
**3.00 × 10⁻⁴.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Longitudinal strain** | **ε_x = σ/E = 150/200,000 = 7.5 × 10⁻⁴** ← |
| **Lateral strains** | **ε_y = ε_z = −ν ε_x = −0.30 × 7.5 × 10⁻⁴ = −2.25 × 10⁻⁴ each** ← |
| **Volumetric strain** | **e_v = ε_x + ε_y + ε_z** ← |
| **= 7.5 − 2.25 − 2.25, all × 10⁻⁴** | **= 3.00 × 10⁻⁴** ← |
| **Or directly** | **e_v = (σ/E)(1 − 2ν) = 7.5 × 10⁻⁴ × 0.4 = 3.00 × 10⁻⁴** ← |

> **Option (d) 7.5 × 10⁻⁴ is the LONGITUDINAL strain alone, forgetting that the bar contracts laterally; option (b) is the lateral strain.**

**The general relation, and what it tells you:**

| Relation | Note |
|---|---|
| **e_v = ε_x + ε_y + ε_z — the sum of the three direct strains** ← | **For small strains, the volumetric strain is simply their sum** ← |
| **For UNIAXIAL stress: e_v = (σ/E)(1 − 2ν)** ← | ← |
| **For a general three-dimensional stress state** | **e_v = (σ_x + σ_y + σ_z)(1 − 2ν)/E** ← |
| **For HYDROSTATIC pressure p** | **e_v = −3p(1 − 2ν)/E = −p/K, which DEFINES the bulk modulus** ← |

> **THE (1 − 2ν) FACTOR APPEARS IN EVERY ONE OF THEM, and it is the single most informative grouping in elasticity:**

| ν | (1 − 2ν) | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **0** | **1** | **No lateral contraction at all — the volume change equals the axial strain (cork)** ← |
| **0.3 (steel)** | **0.4** | **Only 40 % of the axial strain appears as volume change; the rest is cancelled by lateral contraction** ← |
| **0.5 (rubber, undrained clay)** | **ZERO** ← | **NO VOLUME CHANGE WHATEVER — the material is INCOMPRESSIBLE** ← |

> **THE ν = 0.5 ROW IS THE PHYSICALLY IMPORTANT LIMIT AND IT MAKES THE WHOLE EXPRESSION MEMORABLE: at ν = 0.5 the lateral contractions exactly cancel the axial extension, so a bar stretched in one direction thins in the other two by precisely enough to keep its volume constant.**

> **That is why ν cannot exceed 0.5: a larger value would mean the volume DECREASED under tension, which is impossible for a stable material.**

> **And it is why undrained saturated clay is analysed with ν = 0.5 — the water cannot escape, so no volume change can occur, and the material must obey that value exactly.**

**A useful practical consequence, worth noting:**

| Observation | Note |
|---|---|
| **Steel's volumetric strain in tension is only 40 % of its axial strain** ← | **So a steel bar stretched by 1 mm per metre increases in volume by only 0.4 parts in 10,000** ← |
| **Metals change volume very little under stress** ← | **Which is why PLASTIC deformation is assumed to occur at CONSTANT VOLUME** ← |
| **Plastic flow involves ν_effective = 0.5** ← | **Dislocations slide; atoms rearrange without the material becoming denser or less dense** ← |

> **THE CONSTANT-VOLUME ASSUMPTION IN PLASTICITY IS NOT AN APPROXIMATION MADE FOR CONVENIENCE — it reflects the physical mechanism, and it has a direct practical use: it means the reduction in cross-sectional area during a tensile test can be computed from the elongation, and the TRUE stress obtained without measuring the neck.**

> **It is also why metal forming operations — rolling, drawing, extrusion — conserve volume, so that the output length can be computed exactly from the input volume and the final cross-section.**

examTip.trick: **e_v = (σ/E)(1 − 2ν) = 7.5 × 10⁻⁴ × 0.4 = 3.0 × 10⁻⁴.** Option (d) is the axial strain alone, forgetting the lateral contraction.
examTip.trap: **Volumetric strain is the SUM of the three direct strains**, and the two lateral ones are NEGATIVE — which is where the (1 − 2ν) comes from.
examTip.mnemonic: **At ν = 0.5, (1 − 2ν) = 0 and the volume cannot change** — which is why ν can never exceed 0.5, why undrained clay uses exactly 0.5, and why plastic flow conserves volume.

questions.stem: The SHEAR CENTRE of a thin-walled open section such as a CHANNEL is:
options: Always coincident with the centroid
The point through which a transverse load must pass if the member is to bend WITHOUT TWISTING
The point of maximum shear stress in the section
The centroid of the web only
questions.solution:
**The point through which a transverse load must pass if the member is to bend WITHOUT TWISTING.**

**Why it exists:**

| Step | Reasoning |
|---|---|
| **A transverse load produces SHEAR STRESSES distributed over the cross-section** ← | **Which flow along the walls of a thin-walled section — the SHEAR FLOW** ← |
| **Those stresses have a RESULTANT force, and also a resultant MOMENT about any chosen point** ← | ← |
| **For an unsymmetrical section such as a channel, the shear flow in the FLANGES produces a TORQUE** ← | **Because the two flange forces form a couple** ← |
| **If the applied load does not produce an equal and opposite torque, the member TWISTS** ← | ← |
| **The SHEAR CENTRE is the point about which the shear flow's moment is ZERO** ← | **Load applied there produces bending only** ← |

> **OPTION (A) IS TRUE FOR A DOUBLY SYMMETRIC SECTION AND FALSE IN GENERAL, which is the point of the question:**

| Section | Shear centre location |
|---|---|
| **DOUBLY SYMMETRIC (I-section, rectangle, circle)** | **COINCIDES with the centroid** ← |
| **Section with ONE axis of symmetry (channel, tee)** | **Lies ON that axis, but NOT at the centroid** ← |
| **CHANNEL** | **OUTSIDE the section altogether, on the opposite side of the web from the flanges** ← |
| **ANGLE (two intersecting legs)** | **At the INTERSECTION of the two legs' centrelines** ← |
| **Tee section** | **At the intersection of the flange and web centrelines** ← |

> **THE CHANNEL'S SHEAR CENTRE LYING OUTSIDE THE SECTION IS THE STRIKING RESULT AND IT HAS A REAL CONSEQUENCE: the load must be applied at a point where there is no material at all.**

> **In practice that means the load must be applied through a bracket that reaches out to that point, or the section must be restrained against twisting, or the twisting must be accepted and designed for.**

> **A channel used as a purlin with the load applied at its web will twist, and its actual stresses will be substantially higher than a simple bending calculation predicts.**

**THE ANGLE AND TEE RESULTS IN THE LAST TWO ROWS HAVE A SATISFYING EXPLANATION worth knowing:**

> **In an angle or a tee, each leg's shear flow resultant passes through that leg's own centreline. Two forces both passing through the point where the centrelines intersect can produce no moment about that point.**

> **So the shear centre of any section made of two intersecting rectangles is simply their intersection — which can be written down by inspection, with no calculation at all.**

**Why it matters, and why it matters less than it might:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **OPEN sections have very low torsional stiffness** ← | **So even a small unintended torque produces a large twist** ← |
| **The twist adds WARPING stresses to the bending stresses** | **Which a bending-only calculation misses entirely** ← |
| **CLOSED sections are enormously stiffer in torsion** ← | **So the shear centre matters far less for a tube or a box** ← |
| **A section restrained against twisting by the structure** | **The problem largely disappears — a channel bolted flat against a wall cannot twist** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW EXPLAINS WHY THE SHEAR CENTRE IS AN ISSUE FOR CHANNELS, ANGLES AND ZEDS AND HARDLY EVER FOR TUBES: torsional stiffness differs between open and closed sections by two or three orders of magnitude.**

> **An open section twists readily under a small torque, so the eccentricity matters. A closed section resists it easily, so a modest eccentricity produces a negligible twist.**

> **The practical rules that follow are simple: where an open section must carry load eccentric to its shear centre, either restrain it against twisting at intervals, use a closed section, or pair two channels back to back so that the combined section is symmetric and its shear centre returns to the centroid.**

> **The last of these is why channels are so often used in pairs, and it is the cheapest of the three answers.**

examTip.trick: **The point through which a load must pass to bend the member WITHOUT twisting** — where the shear flow's resultant moment is zero.
examTip.trap: **It coincides with the centroid only for DOUBLY SYMMETRIC sections.** For a channel it lies OUTSIDE the section entirely, on the far side of the web.
examTip.mnemonic: **For an ANGLE or TEE it is simply the intersection of the two legs' centrelines** — both shear resultants pass through it, so no moment. Write it down by inspection. And pairing two channels restores symmetry.

questions.stem: A short column of rectangular section 200 mm × 300 mm carries an axial compressive load of 100 kN applied with an eccentricity of 50 mm along the 300 mm dimension. The extreme fibre stresses are:
options: 1.67 MPa compressive on both faces
3.33 MPa compressive and 3.33 MPa tensile
2.50 and 0.83 MPa, both compressive
3.33 MPa compressive and ZERO on the opposite face
questions.solution:
**3.33 MPa compressive on one face and exactly ZERO on the other.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Area** | **A = 200 × 300 = 60,000 mm²** |
| **Section modulus about the bending axis** | **Z = b d²/6 = 200 × 300²/6 = 3.0 × 10⁶ mm³** ← |
| **DIRECT stress** | **P/A = 100,000/60,000 = 1.667 N/mm²** ← |
| **BENDING stress** | **P e / Z = 100,000 × 50 / 3.0 × 10⁶ = 1.667 N/mm²** ← |
| **Maximum** | **1.667 + 1.667 = 3.33 MPa compressive** ← |
| **Minimum** | **1.667 − 1.667 = ZERO** ← |

> **THE TWO COMPONENTS COME OUT EXACTLY EQUAL, WHICH IS NOT A COINCIDENCE: the eccentricity of 50 mm is precisely d/6 for a 300 mm depth.**

> **That is the boundary of the MIDDLE THIRD, and it is the eccentricity at which the stress on the far face falls exactly to zero.**

**The MIDDLE THIRD RULE, which this question illustrates:**

| Eccentricity | Stress distribution |
|---|---|
| **e = 0** | **Uniform compression P/A across the whole section** ← |
| **0 < e < d/6** | **Compression everywhere, but varying — trapezoidal** ← |
| **e = d/6 EXACTLY** ← | **Compression varying linearly from 2P/A at one face to ZERO at the other — this question** ← |
| **e > d/6** | **TENSION develops on the far face** ← |

> **The condition for no tension is therefore that the load lie within the MIDDLE THIRD of the depth — that is, within d/6 either side of the centre.**

> **For bending about both axes, the load must lie within the KERN (core) of the section, which for a rectangle is a rhombus with diagonals d/3 and b/3.**

**Why the rule matters, and where:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **MASONRY and plain concrete, which cannot take tension** ← | **A tensile stress means a crack opens — so the resultant must stay within the middle third** ← |
| **GRAVITY DAMS** ← | **The resultant of all forces must stay within the middle third of the base, for no tension at the heel** ← |
| **Retaining wall bases** | **Same requirement** ← |
| **Chimneys, piers and pedestals in masonry** | ← |
| **NOT a constraint for reinforced concrete or steel** ← | **Which can carry tension — the rule applies to materials that cannot** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE QUALIFICATION THAT KEEPS THE RULE IN PROPORTION: the middle third rule is not a general principle of structural mechanics.**

> **It is a consequence of using a material with no tensile strength, and it disappears entirely for a reinforced section.**

> **Applying it to a reinforced concrete column would be pointlessly restrictive, and forgetting it for a masonry pier is a genuine error.**

**And the kern's shape for other sections, worth knowing:**

| Section | Kern |
|---|---|
| **RECTANGLE b × d** | **A rhombus with diagonals d/3 and b/3 — the "middle third"** ← |
| **SOLID CIRCLE of diameter D** | **A concentric circle of diameter D/4 — so e must be less than D/8** ← |
| **HOLLOW circular section** | **A circle of diameter (D² + d²)/(4D)** ← |

> **THE CIRCLE'S RESULT IS WORTH NOTING BECAUSE IT IS OFTEN MISQUOTED: for a solid circle the limiting eccentricity is D/8, not D/6.**

> **The kern is the "middle QUARTER" in diameter terms, which is a tighter limit than the rectangle's middle third — because a circle has proportionately less material at its extremes to resist the bending.**

> **Which is a small illustration of a general point: the kern is a property of the section's SHAPE, expressed as Z/A, and each shape has its own.**

examTip.trick: **P/A = 1.667 and Pe/Z = 1.667, so 3.33 MPa and ZERO.** They are equal because e = 50 mm is exactly d/6 — the middle-third boundary.
examTip.trap: **e > d/6 puts TENSION on the far face** — which is fatal in masonry, plain concrete, a gravity dam base or a retaining wall, and irrelevant for reinforced concrete.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rectangle: middle THIRD (e ≤ d/6). Solid circle: middle QUARTER in diameter (e ≤ D/8)** — a tighter limit, because a circle has less material at its extremes.

questions.stem: A THREE-HINGED PARABOLIC arch carrying a uniformly distributed load over its entire horizontal span develops:
options: ZERO bending moment at every section — the arch is in pure axial compression throughout
A maximum bending moment at the crown
A maximum bending moment at the quarter points
Uniform bending moment along its whole length
questions.solution:
**ZERO bending moment at every section** — the arch carries the load in pure axial compression.

**Why:**

| Step | Reasoning |
|---|---|
| **For a UDL over the whole horizontal span, the "free" bending moment diagram of an equivalent simply supported beam is a PARABOLA** ← | **M_beam = wx(L−x)/2** ← |
| **The arch's horizontal thrust H produces a relieving moment of H × y at every section** ← | **Where y is the rise of the arch axis at that point** ← |
| **Net bending moment M = M_beam − H y** ← | ← |
| **If the arch's SHAPE y(x) is itself a PARABOLA of the same form, the two are proportional at every point** ← | **And with H = wL²/(8h), they are exactly EQUAL** ← |
| **So M = 0 everywhere** ← | ← |

> **THE PRINCIPLE, STATED GENERALLY: an arch whose SHAPE matches the shape of the free bending moment diagram of its loading carries that loading with NO bending at all.**

> **Such a shape is called the FUNICULAR (or line of thrust) for that loading, and it is the ideal arch form for it.**

**The funicular shapes for the standard loadings:**

| Loading | Funicular shape |
|---|---|
| **UDL over the horizontal SPAN** | **PARABOLA** ← |
| **Load uniform along the arch's own LENGTH (its self-weight)** | **CATENARY** ← |
| **A single point load** | **Two straight segments meeting under the load** ← |
| **A general set of point loads** | **A polygon — the FUNICULAR POLYGON** ← |

> **THE PARABOLA-CATENARY PAIR IS THE SAME DISTINCTION MET WITH CABLES, AND IT IS NOT A COINCIDENCE: an arch is a cable turned upside down.**

> **A hanging cable under a given load takes a shape in which it carries that load in pure TENSION.**

> **Invert that shape and build it as a rigid arch, and it carries the same load in pure COMPRESSION.**

> **This is exactly how Gaudí and Heinrich Hübsch designed arch and vault forms — by hanging weighted strings, photographing the result, and inverting the photograph. The hanging model finds the funicular shape automatically, by physics rather than by calculation.**

**Why real arches nevertheless have bending moments:**

| Cause | Note |
|---|---|
| **The loading is not the one the shape was chosen for** ← | **A parabolic arch under a PARTIAL or a moving load has substantial bending — and this governs bridge arch design** ← |
| **Temperature change** | **Which alters the thrust in a two-hinged or fixed arch — though NOT in a three-hinged one** ← |
| **Support movement (rib shortening, yielding abutments)** | **Same** ← |
| **The arch's own self-weight follows a catenary, not a parabola** | **A small discrepancy in a shallow arch** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE DECISIVE PRACTICAL POINT FOR BRIDGES AND IT IS WHY ARCH RIBS ARE NOT INFINITELY SLENDER: an arch shaped for a full-span UDL is not funicular for a load on half the span.**

> **A vehicle on one half of an arch bridge produces a bending moment that the full-span analysis does not show at all, and the PARTIAL loading case usually governs the rib's design.**

> **So the classic examination result — zero moment under full UDL — is true, elegant, and precisely not the case that sizes the member.**

**AND THE THREE-HINGED ARCH'S OWN ADVANTAGE, worth recording:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Three hinges make it statically DETERMINATE** ← | **Solvable by statics alone** ← |
| **It is INSENSITIVE to temperature change, support settlement and rib shortening** ← | **Because a determinate structure develops no stress from imposed deformations** ← |
| **Against: the hinges are expensive, need maintenance, and the crown hinge is a weakness** ← | ← |
| **And it has no redundancy** | ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE SAME ARGUMENT MET WITH THE GERBER BEAM, and it is why three-hinged arches were favoured on doubtful foundations: an abutment that spreads by 20 mm produces enormous forces in a fixed arch and none at all in a three-hinged one.**

examTip.trick: **An arch whose SHAPE matches the free bending moment diagram of its loading carries it with ZERO bending** — a parabolic arch under a full-span UDL is exactly that case.
examTip.trap: **A PARTIAL or moving load produces substantial bending** — and that case, not the full UDL, is what sizes an arch bridge rib.
examTip.mnemonic: **An arch is a cable upside down** — UDL over the span gives a parabola, self-weight a catenary. Gaudí found his forms by hanging weighted strings and inverting the photograph.

questions.stem: For a SPACE (three-dimensional) pin-jointed truss with m members, j joints and r reaction components, the condition for STATIC DETERMINACY is:
options: m + r = 2j
m + r = j + 3
m + r = 3j
questions.solution:
**m + r = 3j.**

**Why 3j:**

| Step | Reasoning |
|---|---|
| **At each joint of a SPACE truss, three equilibrium equations are available** ← | **ΣF_x = 0, ΣF_y = 0, ΣF_z = 0 — there are no moment equations at a pin joint** ← |
| **With j joints, the total number of equations is 3j** ← | ← |
| **The unknowns are the m member forces plus the r reaction components** ← | ← |
| **Determinate when unknowns = equations** | **m + r = 3j** ← |
| **m + r < 3j** | **UNSTABLE — a mechanism** ← |
| **m + r > 3j** | **INDETERMINATE, to degree (m + r − 3j)** ← |

> **The PLANE truss condition, m + r = 2j, follows from exactly the same reasoning with two equations per joint — which is option (a), and is the well-known case that makes it the natural distractor.**

**The two conditions side by side:**

| Truss | Equations per joint | Determinacy condition | Minimum reactions |
|---|---|---|---|
| **PLANE** | **2** ← | **m + r = 2j** ← | **3** ← |
| **SPACE** | **3** ← | **m + r = 3j** ← | **6** ← |

> **THE MINIMUM REACTION COUNT IN THE LAST COLUMN FOLLOWS FROM THE RIGID BODY'S DEGREES OF FREEDOM: a body in a plane has three (two translations and one rotation), so three restraints are the minimum for stability.**

> **A body in space has six (three translations and three rotations), so six restraints are the minimum.**

> **With r = 3 for a plane truss the condition reduces to the familiar m = 2j − 3, which is option (d) — correct for a plane truss with the minimum reactions, and not the general condition, and certainly not the space truss condition.**

**The essential caveat, which the equation cannot express:**

| Warning | Note |
|---|---|
| **Satisfying the count is NECESSARY but NOT SUFFICIENT** ← | **The arrangement must also be geometrically STABLE** ← |
| **A truss can satisfy m + r = 2j and still be a MECHANISM** ← | **If members are badly arranged — one part over-braced and another part not braced at all** ← |
| **Three reactions can be improperly arranged** | **All PARALLEL, or all CONCURRENT at a point — the truss can then translate or rotate** ← |
| **So a visual check for stability must accompany the count** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW GIVES THE TWO CLASSIC IMPROPER ARRANGEMENTS AND THEY ARE WORTH BEING ABLE TO SPOT: three PARALLEL reactions cannot resist a force perpendicular to them, and three CONCURRENT reactions cannot resist a moment about their common point.**

> **In both cases the count is satisfied and the structure moves — which is why the count is called a NECESSARY condition and never a sufficient one.**

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE MORE INSIDIOUS CASE because it can be hidden in a large truss: adding an extra member in one panel and omitting one in another leaves the total unchanged.**

> **The count still balances, one region is redundantly braced and the other is a mechanism, and the truss collapses in the unbraced region.**

> **This is precisely the kind of error a purely numerical check cannot detect, and it is why the panel-by-panel inspection of a truss's bracing is worth doing before any analysis is begun.**

**And where space trusses are actually used:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **Space-frame ROOFS over large column-free areas** ← | **Sports halls, terminals, exhibition buildings — highly efficient and very stiff** ← |
| **Transmission line TOWERS** ← | **Which are space trusses, though usually analysed as two intersecting plane trusses** ← |
| **Offshore platform jackets, crane booms, masts** | ← |
| **Geodesic domes** | ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW DESCRIBES A COMMON AND LEGITIMATE SIMPLIFICATION: a transmission tower is genuinely three-dimensional, and it is usually analysed as two plane trusses at right angles, each taking the loads in its own plane.**

> **The approximation works because the bracing is arranged so that the two planes act largely independently — and it is a good illustration of how a difficult analysis is made tractable by choosing a structural arrangement that justifies a simplification, rather than by computing the difficult case.**

examTip.trick: **Three equations per joint in space, so m + r = 3j** (against 2j in a plane). Minimum reactions 6 in space, 3 in a plane.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) m = 2j − 3 is the PLANE condition with r = 3** — a special case of a special case, and not the general rule.
examTip.mnemonic: **The count is NECESSARY, never SUFFICIENT** — three parallel or three concurrent reactions satisfy it and still move, and an over-braced panel can hide an unbraced one. Inspect the bracing panel by panel.

questions.stem: MOHR'S SECOND moment-area theorem states that the vertical DEVIATION of a point A on the elastic curve from the TANGENT drawn at another point B is equal to:
options: The area of the M/EI diagram between A and B
The MOMENT of the area of the M/EI diagram between A and B, taken ABOUT the point A
The slope of the M/EI diagram at A
The area of the bending moment diagram divided by the span
questions.solution:
**The MOMENT of the area of the M/EI diagram between A and B, taken about the point A** — the point at which the deviation is being measured.

**The two theorems together:**

| Theorem | Statement | Gives |
|---|---|---|
| **FIRST (slope) theorem** | **The change in SLOPE between two points equals the AREA of the M/EI diagram between them** ← | **A rotation** ← |
| **SECOND (deflection) theorem** | **The DEVIATION of one point from the tangent at another equals the FIRST MOMENT of that M/EI area, taken about the point where the deviation is measured** ← | **A distance** ← |

> **THE PARALLEL WITH AREA PROPERTIES IS EXACT AND MAKES THE PAIR EASY TO REMEMBER: the first theorem uses the AREA of the M/EI diagram, the second uses its FIRST MOMENT of area.**

> **It is the same relationship as between a force and its moment, or between an area and its centroid — and in fact the second theorem is most easily applied as (area) × (distance from its CENTROID to the point A).**

**THE CRITICAL DETAIL — ABOUT WHICH POINT:**

| Rule | Note |
|---|---|
| **The moment is taken about the point where the DEVIATION is being measured** ← | **NOT about the point where the tangent is drawn** ← |
| **The deviation of A from the tangent at B uses moments about A** ← | ← |
| **The deviation of B from the tangent at A uses moments about B** ← | **A DIFFERENT quantity, with a different value** ← |

> **THE TWO DEVIATIONS IN THE LAST TWO ROWS ARE NOT EQUAL, and confusing them is the standard error in this method.**

> **The deviation of A from the tangent at B and the deviation of B from the tangent at A involve the same M/EI area but moments about different points, so their values differ.**

> **A quick check: the notation t_{A/B} means "the deviation of A measured from the tangent at B", and the FIRST subscript is the point about which moments are taken.**

**Why the method is used, and where it excels:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **Very efficient for CANTILEVERS** ← | **The tangent at the fixed end is HORIZONTAL and does not move, so the deviation from it IS the deflection** ← |
| **Efficient for SYMMETRIC simply supported beams** ← | **The tangent at midspan is horizontal, so the deviation of a support from it gives the midspan deflection directly** ← |
| **Excellent for beams of VARYING EI** ← | **Stepped or tapered members — the M/EI diagram simply changes shape, and the method is unaffected** ← |
| **Gives the answer at ONE chosen point** | **Efficient when only one value is wanted** ← |
| **Graphical and intuitive** | ← |

> **THE FIRST TWO ROWS DESCRIBE THE TRICK ON WHICH THE METHOD DEPENDS IN PRACTICE, and it is worth stating explicitly: the theorems give DEVIATIONS from a tangent, not deflections.**

> **They become useful only when a tangent whose position is KNOWN can be found — and there are exactly two such situations.**

> **At a FIXED support, the tangent is horizontal and passes through a point that does not move, so deviations from it are true deflections.**

> **At the MIDSPAN of a symmetrically loaded simply supported beam, the tangent is horizontal by symmetry, and the deviation of a support from it equals the midspan deflection.**

> **For an unsymmetrically loaded simply supported beam neither applies, and the method needs an extra step — find the deviation of one support from the tangent at the other, use it to locate that tangent, and then work from it. That is doable but no longer elegant, and the conjugate beam or unit load method is usually quicker.**

**The THIRD ROW IS WHERE THE METHOD GENUINELY OUTPERFORMS THE ALTERNATIVES, though, and it is worth ending on:**

> **For a beam whose section changes along its length — a haunched beam, a stepped shaft, a tapered cantilever — integrating the differential equation is awkward because EI is a function of x.**

> **The moment-area method absorbs the variation into the M/EI DIAGRAM, which is simply drawn with different scales over different regions, and then treated as an ordinary area.**

> **The varying stiffness ceases to be an analytical difficulty and becomes a matter of drawing the diagram correctly, which is a genuine advantage and the reason the method survives alongside more general ones.**

examTip.trick: **First theorem: AREA of the M/EI diagram gives the change in SLOPE. Second theorem: its FIRST MOMENT gives the DEVIATION.** Same relationship as area to centroid.
examTip.trap: **Moments are taken about the point where the DEVIATION is measured, not where the tangent is drawn** — t_{A/B} and t_{B/A} are different quantities.
examTip.mnemonic: **The theorems give deviations from a TANGENT, not deflections** — useful only where a known tangent exists: a fixed support, or the midspan of a symmetric beam. And it handles VARYING EI beautifully.

questions.stem: A SUPPORT SETTLEMENT of a few millimetres in a statically INDETERMINATE continuous beam:
options: Produces no stress, since the beam simply follows the support down
Reduces the bending moments everywhere
Affects only the settled support
Induces ADDITIONAL BENDING MOMENTS and reactions throughout the beam, whose magnitude is proportional to EI and can be substantial
questions.solution:
**It induces ADDITIONAL bending moments and reactions throughout the beam**, whose magnitude is proportional to EI and can be substantial.

**Why an indeterminate structure is affected and a determinate one is not:**

| Structure | Effect of a support settlement |
|---|---|
| **DETERMINATE (e.g. a simply supported beam)** | **NO STRESS — the beam simply rotates and follows the support down, with the reactions unchanged** ← |
| **INDETERMINATE (e.g. a continuous beam)** | **The beam is FORCED to bend to accommodate the movement, because the other supports hold it — and bending means moment** ← |

> **THE ESSENTIAL IDEA: in a determinate structure there are just enough restraints to hold it, so any imposed movement is accommodated by rigid-body motion.**

> **In an indeterminate structure the extra restraints FIGHT the movement, and the resulting internal forces are the price of that resistance.**

**The magnitude, which is where the danger lies:**

| Case | Induced moment |
|---|---|
| **A propped cantilever of span L with the prop settling by Δ** | **M = 3 E I Δ / L²** ← |
| **A fixed-ended beam of span L with one support settling by Δ** | **M = 6 E I Δ / L²** ← |

> **THE FORM OF THESE EXPRESSIONS CARRIES THE WHOLE LESSON AND EACH TERM MATTERS:**

| Term | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Proportional to EI** ← | **A STIFFER beam attracts MORE moment from the same settlement — stiffness is a LIABILITY here, not an asset** ← |
| **Proportional to Δ** | **Directly — a settlement twice as large gives twice the moment** ← |
| **INVERSELY proportional to L²** ← | **SHORT spans are far worse than long ones — halving the span QUADRUPLES the induced moment** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS COUNTER-INTUITIVE AND IMPORTANT: in every other context a stiffer member is better, and here it is worse.**

> **A settlement imposes a DEFORMATION, not a force. The structure must accommodate that deformation, and the force required to bend a stiff member into the required shape is larger than for a flexible one.**

> **So a heavy, stiff continuous beam on poor foundations is more vulnerable to settlement than a light flexible one — which reverses the usual instinct entirely.**

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE ONE WITH THE MOST PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE: a short-span continuous structure on settling foundations is in serious trouble.**

> **A 30 mm settlement under a 20 m span is a rotation of 1.5 in 1,000 and is easily absorbed. The same 30 mm under a 4 m span is 7.5 in 1,000 and induces 25 times the moment.**

> **This is why short, stiff, continuous structures on poor ground crack, and why the same settlement causes visible damage in a small building and none in a long-span bridge.**

**What is done about it:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **Design the FOUNDATIONS to limit differential settlement** | **The first and best answer** ← |
| **Make the structure DETERMINATE where settlement cannot be predicted** ← | **Gerber beams, three-hinged arches, simply supported spans** ← |
| **Use a stiff RAFT so the whole structure settles together** | **Converting differential settlement into uniform settlement** ← |
| **INCLUDE the estimated settlement in the analysis as a load case** ← | **Which is standard for bridges on compressible ground** ← |
| **Provide for JACKING at the bearings** ← | **So the settlement can be corrected during the structure's life** ← |
| **Rely on CREEP and cracking to relieve the moments** ← | **Real in concrete — sustained settlement moments relax substantially over time, which is why the effect is less damaging than the elastic calculation suggests** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS A GENUINE AND IMPORTANT MITIGATION IN CONCRETE STRUCTURES AND IT IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING RATHER THAN RELYING ON BLINDLY: the elastic formula assumes the settlement is applied instantly to a linear elastic beam.**

> **In reality settlement occurs slowly, over months or years, and concrete CREEPS under sustained stress.**

> **The induced moments therefore RELAX — often to half the elastic value or less — because the beam gradually deforms to accommodate the movement instead of resisting it.**

> **This is why continuous concrete structures survive settlements that an elastic calculation says should have cracked them severely, and it is why codes permit a reduced effective E for the settlement load case.**

> **It also carries a warning: a settlement that occurs SUDDENLY — a foundation failure, a washout, a seismic event — gets none of that relief, and the full elastic moments do develop.**

examTip.trick: **M = 6EIΔ/L² for a fixed-ended beam, 3EIΔ/L² for a propped cantilever.** A DETERMINATE structure develops no stress at all — it just follows the support down.
examTip.trap: **Moment is proportional to EI — a STIFFER beam attracts MORE**, reversing the usual instinct. A settlement imposes a deformation, and bending a stiff member into shape takes more force.
examTip.mnemonic: **Inversely proportional to L², so SHORT spans suffer most** — the same 30 mm is trivial over 20 m and 25 times worse over 4 m. And concrete CREEP relaxes the moments, unless the settlement is sudden.

questions.stem: The design philosophy underlying modern seismic codes is that a structure should:
options: Resist MINOR shaking without damage, resist MODERATE shaking with repairable non-structural damage, and resist SEVERE shaking without COLLAPSE — although it may be damaged beyond repair
Remain entirely undamaged under the strongest possible earthquake
Be designed for the largest recorded ground acceleration with a factor of safety of 3
Be made as stiff as possible so that it does not move
questions.solution:
**Minor shaking without damage; moderate shaking with repairable damage; severe shaking WITHOUT COLLAPSE, though the structure may be damaged beyond economic repair.**

**The three-level philosophy:**

| Level of shaking | Performance required | Objective |
|---|---|---|
| **MINOR, frequent** | **NO damage at all — the structure remains fully serviceable** ← | **Serviceability** ← |
| **MODERATE, occasional** | **No STRUCTURAL damage; some non-structural damage that can be REPAIRED** ← | **Damage control** ← |
| **SEVERE, rare (the design earthquake)** | **The structure may be SEVERELY damaged, but must NOT COLLAPSE** ← | **LIFE SAFETY** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE ONE THAT MUST BE UNDERSTOOD AND IS MOST OFTEN MISREPRESENTED TO CLIENTS: the code's objective under the design earthquake is to save LIVES, not to save the building.**

> **A code-compliant building that survives a severe earthquake standing but cracked, leaning and fit only for demolition has PERFORMED EXACTLY AS INTENDED.**

> **Its occupants got out. That is what the design was for.**

> **Option (b) describes what most building owners assume they are buying, and it is neither what the code offers nor economically achievable — designing every ordinary building to remain elastic through the strongest credible shaking would cost several times as much.**

**Why elastic design for the full earthquake force is not attempted:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **The elastic force from a severe earthquake is ENORMOUS** ← | **Several times what any economic structure could carry without yielding** ← |
| **An earthquake imposes a DISPLACEMENT, not a force** ← | **The ground moves, and the building must follow — a stronger building simply attracts MORE force** ← |
| **So DUCTILITY is used instead of strength** ← | **The structure is allowed to yield, absorbing energy through inelastic deformation** ← |
| **The RESPONSE REDUCTION FACTOR R embodies this** ← | **The elastic force is DIVIDED by R — 5 for a special moment resisting frame, 3 for an ordinary one** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW CONTAINS THE INSIGHT THAT MAKES SEISMIC DESIGN DIFFERENT FROM ALL OTHER LOADING, and option (d) is the intuition it corrects:**

> **Wind applies a FORCE, so a stronger building resists it better.**

> **An earthquake applies a ground DISPLACEMENT. A stiffer, stronger building has a shorter period, attracts a HIGHER spectral acceleration, and therefore a LARGER force — so making it stiffer can make matters worse, not better.**

> **What survives an earthquake is not the strongest structure but the one that can DEFORM the most without losing its ability to carry gravity load.**

> **That reorientation — from strength to ductility — is the central idea of modern seismic design, and everything else follows from it.**

**THE R FACTOR IN THE LAST ROW CARRIES AN OBLIGATION THAT IS ROUTINELY IGNORED, and it is worth stating firmly:**

> **Dividing the elastic force by R = 5 is a promise that the structure WILL behave ductilely — that it will yield in a controlled way, at chosen locations, through many cycles, without losing strength.**

> **That promise is kept only by DETAILING: close stirrups at the beam and column ends, 135° hooks anchored into the core, strong-column weak-beam proportioning, adequate anchorage and lap lengths, and confinement of the joint.**

> **A structure designed with R = 5 and detailed as though R = 1 has been designed for one fifth of the elastic force and given none of the ductility that justified the reduction.**

> **That is the single most dangerous error in seismic design, it is invisible on the drawings unless the detailing is examined, and it is exactly what was found in the buildings that collapsed in 2015.**

> **The calculation is the easy part. The detailing is where the safety actually resides.**

**And the CAPACITY DESIGN principle that follows:**

| Principle | Note |
|---|---|
| **CHOOSE where the structure will yield** ← | **At beam ends, away from the joints — not at column ends** ← |
| **Make those locations DUCTILE by detailing** | ← |
| **Make everything else STRONGER than the chosen fuses** ← | **So the yielding occurs where you designed it to, and nowhere else** ← |
| **STRONG COLUMN, WEAK BEAM** ← | **Because a beam hinge is local and repairable; a column hinge produces a storey mechanism and collapse** ← |

> **The analogy is with an electrical fuse: you do not hope the weakest point is somewhere harmless, you DESIGN it to be, and you make everything else stronger so that it is.**

examTip.trick: **Minor — no damage. Moderate — repairable damage. Severe — no COLLAPSE, though possibly beyond repair.** The design earthquake objective is LIFE SAFETY, not saving the building.
examTip.trap: **An earthquake imposes a DISPLACEMENT, not a force** — so a stiffer, stronger building attracts MORE force. Ductility, not strength, is what survives.
examTip.mnemonic: **R = 5 is a PROMISE of ductility, kept only by DETAILING** — close stirrups, 135° hooks into the core, strong column weak beam. Design with R = 5 and detail as if R = 1 and you have a fifth of the force and none of the ductility.

questions.stem: For a reinforced concrete moment-resisting frame building WITHOUT infill walls, of total height 15 m, the approximate fundamental natural period given by IS 1893 as T = 0.075 h^0.75 is:
questions.solution:
**About 0.57 seconds.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **T = 0.075 h^0.75, with h in metres** | ← |
| **15^0.75** | **= 7.622** ← |
| **T = 0.075 × 7.622** | **= 0.5716 s** |
| **T** | **≈ 0.57 s** ← |

> **A useful rough check: for a regular RC frame the period is often quoted as roughly 0.1 seconds per STOREY, and a 15 m building is about five storeys — giving 0.5 s, which brackets the computed value nicely.**

**The empirical period formulae:**

| Structure | Formula |
|---|---|
| **RC moment-resisting frame WITHOUT infill** | **T = 0.075 h^0.75** ← |
| **STEEL moment-resisting frame without infill** | **T = 0.085 h^0.75 — LONGER, because steel frames are more flexible** ← |
| **Any building WITH brick INFILL panels** ← | **T = 0.09 h / √d, where d is the base dimension in the direction considered** ← |

> **THE INFILL FORMULA IN THE LAST ROW GIVES A MUCH SHORTER PERIOD, and the difference matters a great deal:**

> **Brick infill panels are usually treated as non-structural and are not modelled — but they are stiff, and they stiffen the frame enormously in their own plane.**

> **A stiffer building has a SHORTER period; a shorter period usually means a HIGHER spectral acceleration; and a higher acceleration means a LARGER seismic force.**

> **So a frame designed as a bare frame, on a long period, and then filled with brick panels, attracts substantially more force than it was designed for.**

> **The infill that was ignored as "non-structural" has changed the structure's dynamic properties fundamentally, and this is one of the most consequential simplifications in ordinary building design.**

**Why the natural period matters at all:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **The design seismic coefficient depends on Sa/g, read from the RESPONSE SPECTRUM at the period T** ← | **So T determines the force** ← |
| **The spectrum PEAKS at short periods — roughly 0.1 to 0.55 s for medium soil** ← | **Where Sa/g reaches 2.5** ← |
| **Beyond the plateau, Sa/g FALLS as 1/T** ← | **So tall, flexible buildings attract proportionately LESS acceleration** ← |
| **This building at 0.57 s** | **Sits right at the edge of the plateau — near the MAXIMUM of the spectrum** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE UNCOMFORTABLE POSITION FOR A FOUR-TO-SIX STOREY BUILDING AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING: buildings of that height have periods in the range where the response spectrum is at its peak.**

> **They attract the highest spectral acceleration of any building type, and they are also the commonest form of construction in Nepali towns.**

> **Very tall buildings, with periods of two or three seconds, attract far less acceleration — which is part of why well-engineered high-rises often perform better in earthquakes than mid-rise ones, contrary to intuition.**

**And RESONANCE, which is the reason the spectrum has a peak in the first place:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **The ground shakes with its own predominant period, governed by the SOIL** ← | **Rock shakes at short periods; deep soft soil at longer ones** ← |
| **If the BUILDING's period matches the GROUND's, resonance amplifies the response enormously** ← | ← |
| **Deep soft deposits amplify LONG-period motion** | **Endangering TALL buildings** ← |
| **Rock and stiff sites transmit SHORT-period motion** | **Endangering SHORT, stiff buildings** ← |

> **THE MEXICO CITY EARTHQUAKE OF 1985 IS THE CLASSIC ILLUSTRATION AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING: the city sits on a deep, soft former lake bed with a natural period of about 2 seconds.**

> **Buildings of 6 to 20 storeys have periods close to that, and they were devastated. Buildings shorter and taller than that range, in the same streets, largely survived.**

> **The lesson is that the soil's period must be considered alongside the building's, and it is why the response spectrum in every code is given separately for hard, medium and soft soil.**

> **For the Kathmandu valley — a deep, soft lacustrine basin — this is not an academic point: the basin amplifies long-period motion, and it is why site-specific spectra are increasingly required for significant structures there.**

examTip.trick: **T = 0.075 × 15^0.75 = 0.075 × 7.622 = 0.57 s.** Rough check: about 0.1 s per storey, and 15 m is roughly five storeys.
examTip.trap: **With brick INFILL, T = 0.09h/√d gives a much SHORTER period and a LARGER force** — the "non-structural" panels stiffen the frame and change its dynamics fundamentally.
examTip.mnemonic: **The spectrum PEAKS around 0.1-0.55 s, exactly where 4-6 storey buildings sit** — the commonest form in Nepali towns attracts the highest acceleration. Mexico City 1985: soft soil at 2 s destroyed the 6-20 storey range.

questions.stem: The principal difficulty in HOT WEATHER concreting is that a high ambient temperature:
options: ACCELERATES setting and increases the rate of evaporation, causing rapid slump loss, plastic shrinkage cracking, and a LOWER ultimate strength even though the early strength is higher
Prevents the cement from hydrating at all
Reduces the water demand of the mix
Has no effect provided the concrete is covered
questions.solution:
**It accelerates the setting and increases evaporation** — causing rapid slump loss, plastic shrinkage cracking, and a LOWER ultimate strength despite a higher early strength.

**The effects, and the mechanism of each:**

| Effect | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Rapid SLUMP LOSS** ← | **Faster hydration and evaporation stiffen the mix before it can be placed** ← |
| **Shorter setting time; risk of a COLD JOINT** ← | **The previous layer sets before the next arrives** ← |
| **PLASTIC SHRINKAGE cracking** ← | **Water evaporates from the surface faster than bleed water rises to replace it, and the drying surface cracks while the concrete is still plastic** ← |
| **HIGHER early strength, LOWER ultimate strength** ← | **The counter-intuitive one, explained below** ← |
| **Greater water demand for the same slump** | **Which itself lowers the strength** ← (so option (c) is backwards) |
| **Higher risk of thermal cracking in thick sections** | **The peak temperature and the gradient are both greater** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE MOST IMPORTANT AND THE LEAST OBVIOUS, and the reason is worth understanding:**

> **Rapid hydration produces a HYDRATION PRODUCT that is poorly distributed. The gel forms quickly around each cement grain, creating a dense shell that impedes further hydration and leaving a more porous structure between the grains.**

> **Slow hydration allows the gel to distribute uniformly through the paste, producing a denser, more homogeneous microstructure.**

> **So concrete cured warm reaches 7-day strengths quickly and then plateaus, while the same concrete cured cool is slower initially and OVERTAKES it — ending 10 to 15 per cent stronger at 28 days and beyond.**

> **This is a general rule worth carrying: in cement hydration, FAST is not better. Speed is bought at the cost of the final quality.**

**PLASTIC SHRINKAGE CRACKING deserves its own note, since it is the most visible hot-weather defect:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **It occurs within HOURS of placing, while the concrete is still plastic** ← | **Long before any drying shrinkage** ← |
| **The cracks are shallow, roughly parallel, and often randomly oriented** | **Sometimes described as "map" or "crazing" cracks** ← |
| **It happens when the EVAPORATION RATE exceeds the BLEEDING rate** ← | **Above about 1.0 kg/m² per hour is the accepted danger threshold** ← |
| **Driven by high temperature, LOW HUMIDITY, and above all WIND** ← | **Wind is the factor most often underestimated** ← |
| **Remedy: prevent the evaporation** | **Windbreaks, fog spraying, evaporation retardant, and covering IMMEDIATELY after finishing** ← |

> **THE WIND FACTOR IN THE FOURTH ROW IS WORTH SINGLING OUT: on the standard evaporation nomograph, wind has a larger effect than either temperature or humidity.**

> **A moderate breeze can triple the evaporation rate, and a slab poured on a windy 30 °C day with low humidity is at far greater risk than one poured on a still 38 °C day.**

> **Site staff watch the thermometer and rarely the wind, which is why the cracks often appear on days that did not feel especially hot.**

**The measures for hot weather concreting:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **COOL the ingredients** ← | **Shade and spray the aggregate stockpiles; use chilled mixing water or ICE replacing part of it** ← |
| **Use a RETARDING admixture** | **To restore the working time** ← |
| **Place at NIGHT or in the early morning** ← | **The simplest and most effective measure of all** ← |
| **Shade the formwork and reinforcement, and cool it before placing** | **Steel bars in the sun can exceed 60 °C** ← |
| **Minimise the time between mixing and placing** | ← |
| **Begin CURING immediately and keep it continuous** ← | **Any interruption in hot weather is far more damaging than in cool** ← |
| **Use a lower initial concrete temperature; codes commonly cap it at 30 to 32 °C** | ← |

> **THE NIGHT PLACING IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE MEASURE THAT SOLVES EVERY PROBLEM AT ONCE AND COSTS THE LEAST: the ambient temperature is lower, the humidity higher, the wind usually calmer, and there is no solar radiation on the formwork or the fresh surface.**

> **It is standard practice for large pours in hot climates and it requires nothing but lighting and a willingness to reorganise the shift — which is a good deal cheaper than ice, admixtures and repairs.**

> **The COOLING OF REINFORCEMENT in the fourth row is a related detail that is almost always forgotten: bars lying in direct sun all morning are hot enough to flash-set the concrete against them, producing a weak, cracked interface exactly where the bond matters most.**

examTip.trick: **Faster setting, more evaporation, slump loss, plastic shrinkage cracks, and HIGHER early but LOWER ultimate strength.** Option (c) is backwards — water demand rises.
examTip.trap: **Fast hydration gives a poorly distributed gel** — a dense shell round each grain and porous space between. Warm-cured concrete plateaus; cool-cured overtakes it by 10-15 % at 28 days.
examTip.mnemonic: **WIND matters more than temperature for plastic shrinkage** — a breezy 30 °C day is worse than a still 38 °C one. And NIGHT placing fixes everything at once for almost no cost.

questions.stem: CREEP of concrete differs from SHRINKAGE in that creep is:
options: A volume change caused by loss of moisture, occurring whether or not the concrete is loaded
The continuing INCREASE IN STRAIN with time under a SUSTAINED STRESS, occurring only while the concrete is loaded
An instantaneous elastic deformation on loading
A change in volume caused by a change in temperature
questions.solution:
**Creep is the continuing increase in strain with time under a SUSTAINED STRESS**, and it occurs only while the concrete is loaded.

**The two compared:**

| Aspect | CREEP | SHRINKAGE |
|---|---|---|
| **Requires a LOAD?** | **YES — no stress, no creep** ← | **NO — it happens in unloaded concrete** ← (option a) |
| **Cause** | **Sustained stress; the gel water migrates and the C-S-H structure rearranges** ← | **LOSS OF MOISTURE to the atmosphere (drying shrinkage), plus autogenous and carbonation shrinkage** ← |
| **Direction** | **In the direction of the applied stress** ← | **In ALL directions, uniformly** ← |
| **Magnitude** | **1 to 3 times the initial elastic strain** ← | **200 to 600 microstrain typically** ← |
| **Time course** | **Rapid at first; roughly half in 3 months, 75 % in a year, continuing for years** ← | **Similar time course** ← |
| **Recoverable?** | **PARTIALLY — some creep recovers when the load is removed** ← | **Partially — shrinkage reverses on re-wetting, though not fully** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE DEFINING TEST AND THE CLEANEST WAY TO SEPARATE THEM: an unloaded concrete specimen SHRINKS but does not creep.**

> **In practice the two occur together and are hard to separate experimentally — which is why creep is usually measured as the difference between a loaded and an identical unloaded specimen kept in the same conditions.**

**What increases creep:**

| Factor | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Higher applied STRESS** | **Creep is roughly PROPORTIONAL to stress, up to about 0.4 f_ck** ← |
| **Loading at an EARLY AGE** ← | **Much greater creep — young concrete creeps far more** ← |
| **Higher water-cement ratio; more cement paste** | **The paste creeps; the aggregate does not** ← |
| **LOW humidity** | **Drying creep adds to basic creep** ← |
| **Higher temperature** | ← |
| **SMALLER member (higher surface-to-volume ratio)** | **Dries faster, so more drying creep** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW HAS A DIRECT SITE CONSEQUENCE AND CONNECTS TO THE FORMWORK STRIKING QUESTION: concrete loaded at 7 days creeps substantially more than the same concrete loaded at 28 days.**

> **So early striking of props does not merely cause an immediate deflection — it commits the member to a much larger long-term creep deflection as well, permanently.**

**Where creep matters, and where it helps:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **Long-term DEFLECTION of beams and slabs** ← | **Two to three times the immediate deflection — which is why the span/depth rules are calibrated as they are** ← |
| **LOSS OF PRESTRESS** ← | **The concrete shortens, the tendon shortens with it, and its tension falls — one of the principal prestress losses** ← |
| **Increased deflection and second-order effects in slender columns** | ← |
| **BENEFICIAL: it RELIEVES stresses caused by imposed deformations** ← | **Support settlement, temperature, shrinkage restraint — the moments relax over time** ← |
| **BENEFICIAL: it redistributes stress between concrete and steel** ← | **In a reinforced column, sustained load transfers gradually from the creeping concrete onto the non-creeping steel** ← |
| **BENEFICIAL: it relieves stress concentrations** | ← |

> **THE LAST THREE ROWS ARE WORTH EMPHASISING BECAUSE CREEP IS USUALLY PRESENTED AS PURELY A NUISANCE, and it is not:**

> **Creep is what allows concrete structures to survive the settlements, temperature changes and restrained shrinkage that an elastic calculation says should crack them severely.**

> **A stress caused by an imposed DEFORMATION relaxes as the material creeps to accommodate it, whereas a stress caused by an applied LOAD does not.**

> **That distinction is the key: creep relieves deformation-induced stress and does nothing to relieve load-induced stress, which is exactly the behaviour one would choose if given the option.**

> **THE COLUMN CASE IN THE FIFTH ROW IS QUANTITATIVELY SIGNIFICANT AND OFTEN OVERLOOKED: in a heavily loaded reinforced concrete column under sustained load, the concrete creeps and the steel does not.**

> **Over years, a substantial share of the load transfers from the concrete to the reinforcement — the steel stress can rise by 50 per cent or more above its short-term value.**

> **The column does not fail, because the total is unchanged and the steel has the capacity, but it means the steel in an old column is working harder than its original design calculation suggests — which matters when assessing an existing structure for additional load.**

examTip.trick: **Creep needs a sustained LOAD; shrinkage happens in unloaded concrete.** Creep acts in the direction of stress; shrinkage in all directions.
examTip.trap: **Loading at an EARLY AGE greatly increases creep** — so striking props early commits the member to a permanently larger long-term deflection, not just an immediate one.
examTip.mnemonic: **Creep RELIEVES stress from imposed deformations (settlement, temperature) and not from applied loads** — exactly the behaviour you would choose. And it transfers load from concrete onto the steel over years.

questions.stem: Reinforced concrete beams are deliberately designed as UNDER-REINFORCED rather than over-reinforced because in an under-reinforced section:
options: Less steel is required, so the beam is cheaper
The concrete reaches its full strength before the steel
The STEEL YIELDS FIRST, so the beam deflects and cracks visibly, giving ample WARNING before the concrete crushes and the failure is DUCTILE
The neutral axis lies below the centroid
questions.solution:
**Because the STEEL YIELDS FIRST**, so the beam deflects and cracks visibly, giving ample warning before the concrete crushes — a DUCTILE failure.

**The three cases:**

| Section | Steel area | Failure sequence | Character |
|---|---|---|---|
| **UNDER-reinforced** | **LESS than the balanced amount** ← | **Steel YIELDS first; the neutral axis rises; deflection and cracking increase greatly; eventually the concrete crushes** ← | **DUCTILE, with warning** ← |
| **BALANCED** | **Exactly the balanced amount** | **Steel yields and concrete crushes SIMULTANEOUSLY** ← | **The theoretical boundary — not used in design** ← |
| **OVER-reinforced** | **MORE than the balanced amount** ← | **The CONCRETE crushes while the steel is still ELASTIC** ← | **BRITTLE, SUDDEN, no warning** ← |

> **THE OVER-REINFORCED CASE IS PROHIBITED FOR ONE REASON ONLY, AND IT IS NOT STRENGTH: an over-reinforced beam is actually STRONGER than an under-reinforced one of the same size.**

> **It is prohibited because it fails WITHOUT WARNING.**

> **The concrete crushes suddenly in compression while the steel is still elastic, the beam has shown almost no deflection and no wide cracks beforehand, and everyone beneath it is still there when it goes.**

> **Option (a) is therefore a true statement about cost that is entirely beside the point — the reason is safety, not economy.**

**How the code enforces it:**

| Mechanism | Note |
|---|---|
| **A limit on the NEUTRAL AXIS DEPTH x_u** ← | **x_u,max/d = 0.53 for Fe 250, 0.48 for Fe 415, 0.46 for Fe 500** ← |
| **Why the limit works** | **A deep neutral axis means a lot of concrete in compression, which means a lot of steel in tension — that is, an over-reinforced section** ← |
| **A limit on the MOMENT of resistance, M_u,lim** | **The moment at x_u,max — beyond it, compression steel must be added** ← |
| **A MAXIMUM steel percentage of 4 % of the gross area** | **A separate practical limit** ← |
| **The limits TIGHTEN as the steel grade rises** ← | **0.53 → 0.48 → 0.46** ← |

> **THE TIGHTENING WITH STEEL GRADE IN THE LAST ROW HAS A GOOD REASON AND IS WORTH KNOWING: higher-grade steel yields at a higher strain.**

> **For the beam to be ductile, the steel must reach its yield strain before the concrete reaches its crushing strain of 0.0035.**

> **A Fe 500 bar needs more strain to yield than a Fe 250 bar, so the neutral axis must be higher — that is, the section must have proportionately less steel — for the same guarantee.**

> **The limit is therefore not an arbitrary tabulated number but a direct consequence of the strain compatibility that defines the balanced condition.**

**What ductility actually buys, which is the wider point:**

| Benefit | Note |
|---|---|
| **WARNING before collapse** ← | **Large deflections and wide cracks — the building tells you** ← |
| **MOMENT REDISTRIBUTION in continuous beams** ← | **A yielded section stops attracting moment and passes it to less-stressed sections — which is only possible if the section can rotate without failing** ← |
| **Energy absorption under EARTHQUAKE loading** ← | **The whole basis of seismic design, as the response reduction factor assumes** ← |
| **Tolerance of settlement, temperature and construction inaccuracy** | ← |
| **Robustness against local overload** | ← |

> **THE SECOND AND THIRD ROWS SHOW THAT THE UNDER-REINFORCED REQUIREMENT IS NOT MERELY A SAFETY PRECAUTION BUT AN ENABLING CONDITION: several of the most valuable properties of reinforced concrete structures depend on sections being able to yield and rotate.**

> **Moment redistribution, plastic analysis and seismic energy dissipation are all unavailable to a structure whose members fail in a brittle manner.**

> **So designing under-reinforced does not merely avoid a hazard — it purchases capabilities that are then relied on elsewhere in the design, including in the response reduction factor that reduced the seismic force in the first place.**

examTip.trick: **Under-reinforced: steel yields FIRST, so the beam deflects and cracks visibly — DUCTILE, with warning.** Over-reinforced: concrete crushes while the steel is elastic — sudden and brittle.
examTip.trap: **An over-reinforced beam is actually STRONGER** — it is prohibited for lack of WARNING, not for lack of capacity.
examTip.mnemonic: **x_u,max/d = 0.53, 0.48, 0.46 for Fe 250, 415, 500 — tightening as the grade rises**, because higher-grade steel needs more strain to yield before concrete crushes at 0.0035.

questions.stem: Where the full development length of a reinforcing bar cannot be provided in a straight run, ANCHORAGE may be obtained by bending the bar. As per IS 456, the anchorage value of a standard 90° BEND is taken as:
options: 4 times the bar diameter
16 times the bar diameter, subject to a maximum of 20 times
The full development length
8 TIMES the bar diameter for each 45° of bend, subject to a maximum of 16 times the diameter
questions.solution:
**8 times the bar diameter for each 45° of bend, subject to a maximum of 16 times the diameter** — so a standard 90° bend is worth 16φ.

**The anchorage values:**

| Detail | Anchorage value |
|---|---|
| **Each 45° of BEND** | **8φ** ← |
| **A 90° bend** | **2 × 8φ = 16φ** ← |
| **Maximum for any bend, however sharp** | **16φ** ← |
| **A standard U-HOOK (180° turn)** | **16φ** ← |
| **The straight length beyond the bend** | **ADDED to the above, at its actual length** ← |

> **THE MAXIMUM IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE DETAIL THAT MAKES THE ANSWER COMPLETE AND IS OFTEN OMITTED: bending the bar further than 90° gains nothing.**

> **A 135° or 180° bend is still worth only 16φ, because beyond a right angle the additional turn contributes little extra bearing against the concrete and mainly increases the risk of splitting.**

> **So a U-hook is not worth twice a 90° bend, and the extra steel is spent on convenience of fixing rather than on anchorage.**

**How bends provide anchorage at all:**

| Mechanism | Note |
|---|---|
| **A straight bar anchors by BOND along its surface** ← | **Requiring the full development length L_d** ← |
| **A BENT bar adds MECHANICAL bearing** ← | **The concrete inside the bend is compressed, and it resists the bar being pulled through** ← |
| **The bend radius must be adequate** ← | **Too tight and the concrete inside the bend is crushed and split — minimum 4φ internal radius for mild steel, more for high yield** ← |
| **Bends are ineffective in COMPRESSION bars** ← | **A hook does nothing for a bar in compression — it simply straightens under load — so compression anchorage must be by straight length alone** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS AN IMPORTANT RESTRICTION THAT IS FREQUENTLY BREACHED: hooks and bends count for anchorage in TENSION only.**

> **A compression bar hooked at its end gains nothing from the hook, and providing one gives a false sense that the anchorage is adequate. Compression bars need their full straight development length.**

**DEVELOPMENT LENGTH itself, for context:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **L_d = φ σ_s / (4 τ_bd)** ← | **The bar's force divided by the bond capacity of its surface** ← |
| **For deformed bars, τ_bd is increased by 60 per cent** ← | **The ribs provide mechanical interlock, not just adhesion** ← |
| **In COMPRESSION, τ_bd is increased by a further 25 per cent** | **Because the bar's end bears on the concrete, and there is no splitting from tension** ← |
| **Typical value for Fe 415 in M20** | **About 47φ in tension — some 750 mm for a 16 mm bar** ← |
| **L_d is proportional to φ** ← | **So LARGER bars need proportionately longer anchorage** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW HAS A DESIGN CONSEQUENCE WORTH KNOWING: since L_d ∝ φ while a bar's AREA goes as φ², using several small bars instead of a few large ones gives the same steel area with a much shorter anchorage requirement.**

> **In a congested joint, or where the available anchorage length is short, switching from 25 mm bars to 16 mm bars can solve an anchorage problem entirely — at the cost of more bars to fix.**

> **That is one of the standard ways out of a detailing difficulty, and it is worth reaching for before resorting to mechanical anchors or couplers.**

**And a closing practical caution:**

> **Anchorage and lap failures are among the commonest causes of structural failure in reinforced concrete, and they are almost always DETAILING failures rather than design ones — a bar stopped short, a lap in the wrong place, a hook that could not be fitted and was quietly omitted.**

> **The calculation is straightforward; the difficulty is that the bar must physically FIT, be fixable by hand, and allow the concrete to pass around it.**

> **A detail that cannot be built as drawn will be built as something else, and nobody will record what.**

examTip.trick: **8φ per 45° of bend, capped at 16φ** — so a 90° bend and a 180° U-hook are both worth 16φ. Straight length beyond the bend is added on top.
examTip.trap: **Hooks and bends count in TENSION only** — a compression bar's hook does nothing and simply straightens. Compression anchorage must be by straight length.
examTip.mnemonic: **L_d ∝ φ while area ∝ φ²** — so several small bars need much shorter anchorage than a few large ones for the same area. The standard escape from a congested joint.

questions.stem: In a FLAT SLAB construction, a DROP PANEL is provided principally to:
options: INCREASE the slab's thickness locally around the column, so as to resist the high PUNCHING SHEAR and the large negative bending moment there
Improve the appearance of the soffit
Reduce the slab's span
Carry the services below the slab
questions.solution:
**To increase the slab's thickness locally around the column**, resisting the high punching shear and the large negative moment that concentrate there.

**What a flat slab is, and its difficulty:**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **A slab supported DIRECTLY on columns, with NO BEAMS** ← | **That is the definition** ← |
| **Advantages** | **A flat soffit, so simpler formwork, easier services, and a REDUCED STOREY HEIGHT — which over many floors saves a great deal** ← |
| **The difficulty** | **Everything the beams would have done must be done by the slab — and the load must funnel into a small column area** ← |
| **The consequence** | **Very high PUNCHING SHEAR and a large NEGATIVE MOMENT concentrated at the column** ← |

> **THE STOREY HEIGHT SAVING IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE COMMERCIAL DRIVER AND IT IS SUBSTANTIAL: removing 500 mm of beam depth from each floor of a twenty-storey building saves 10 m of height — a whole extra floor within the same envelope, or a large saving in cladding, services risers, columns and lifts.**

> **That is why flat slabs are used for offices, car parks and apartments despite their structural awkwardness.**

**The two thickening devices:**

| Device | What it is | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| **DROP PANEL** | **A thickened area of SLAB around the column, typically extending L/6 to L/3 each way and adding 25 to 50 % to the depth** ← | **Increases the shear perimeter's effective depth, and provides depth for the large negative moment steel** ← |
| **COLUMN HEAD (capital)** | **A FLARED enlargement at the TOP OF THE COLUMN** ← | **Increases the PERIMETER over which punching shear is resisted** ← |
| **Both together** | The classic arrangement | ← |
| **Neither** | **A "flat plate" — used for light loads and short spans** ← | **Simplest formwork of all** ← |

> **THE TWO WORK ON THE TWO DIFFERENT TERMS OF THE PUNCHING SHEAR CAPACITY, which is a neat way to remember which does what:**

> **Punching resistance = (shear stress capacity) × (critical PERIMETER) × (effective DEPTH).**

> **A COLUMN HEAD increases the PERIMETER. A DROP PANEL increases the DEPTH. Using both attacks both terms, which is why they are traditionally used together.**

**PUNCHING SHEAR, which is what makes flat slabs dangerous:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **The column tries to punch a truncated CONE through the slab** ← | **Checked on a perimeter at d/2 from the column face** ← |
| **The failure is SUDDEN and BRITTLE** ← | **With no warning deflection — quite unlike a flexural failure** ← |
| **And it can trigger PROGRESSIVE COLLAPSE** ← | **The slab drops off one column onto the floor below, which then carries an impact load it was never designed for, and punches in turn** ← |
| **The whole building can unzip floor by floor** ← | **Which has happened, repeatedly** ← |

> **THE PROGRESSIVE COLLAPSE MECHANISM IN THE THIRD AND FOURTH ROWS IS THE REASON FLAT SLABS DEMAND PARTICULAR CARE, and it is the most serious failure mode in the whole of building structures:**

> **A beam-and-slab floor that fails locally usually sheds load to adjacent members and stops. A flat slab that punches at one column loses its support entirely at that point and falls.**

> **The essential safeguard is INTEGRITY REINFORCEMENT — bottom bars running continuously THROUGH the column cage in both directions, properly anchored.**

> **These bars are not required by the flexural calculation and contribute nothing under normal loading. Their purpose is that after a punching failure has occurred, they act as a CATENARY and hold the slab hanging from the column instead of letting it fall.**

> **They convert a catastrophic collapse into a severe but localised failure, they cost almost nothing, and their omission has been identified in the investigation of more than one flat-slab collapse.**

> **It is a good example of a detail whose entire value lies in what happens AFTER the structure has already failed — which is precisely the kind of provision that gets deleted as unnecessary by someone reading the calculations alone.**

**And a note on seismic behaviour, which matters in Nepal:**

> **A flat slab frame has poor lateral resistance: the slab-column connection is weak in transferring moment, and the connection is precisely where punching failure occurs.**

> **Under seismic drift, the moment transferred at the connection adds to the gravity shear, and the punching capacity is reduced just when the demand rises.**

> **So flat slab buildings in seismic regions must be provided with a separate lateral system — SHEAR WALLS or a core — to carry the earthquake forces and limit the drift, rather than relying on the slab-column frame.**

examTip.trick: **A DROP PANEL thickens the slab (more DEPTH); a COLUMN HEAD flares the column (more PERIMETER).** Punching resistance = stress × perimeter × depth, so the two attack different terms.
examTip.trap: **Punching failure is sudden and brittle, and it triggers PROGRESSIVE COLLAPSE** — the slab falls onto the floor below, which punches in turn, and the building unzips.
examTip.mnemonic: **INTEGRITY bottom bars through the column cage do nothing under normal load** — they catch the slab as a catenary AFTER a punch. Cost almost nothing; deleted by whoever reads only the calculations.

questions.stem: In the design of a reinforced concrete DOG-LEGGED staircase spanning between landing beams, the loading on the inclined WAIST SLAB is computed by:
options: Applying the load per square metre of the SLOPING surface directly
Converting the self-weight of the waist and steps to a load per square metre of the HORIZONTAL PLAN area, and adding the live load, which already acts per unit plan area
Ignoring the weight of the steps
Using half the live load, since only half the tread is occupied
questions.solution:
**By converting the self-weight of the waist and the steps to a load per square metre of HORIZONTAL PLAN area**, and adding the live load, which already acts per unit plan area.

**Why the conversion is necessary:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **The waist slab's SELF-WEIGHT acts on its SLOPING area** ← | **Which is LONGER than its horizontal projection** ← |
| **The LIVE load acts on the PLAN area** ← | **People and furniture occupy horizontal space, not sloping space** ← |
| **The two are therefore expressed in DIFFERENT bases and cannot simply be added** ← | ← |
| **The span is measured HORIZONTALLY** ← | **So everything must be converted to a load per metre of HORIZONTAL span** ← |
| **Conversion factor** | **Multiply the waist's weight per m² of slope by √(R² + T²)/T, where R is the rise and T the tread** ← |

> **THE FACTOR IN THE LAST ROW IS SIMPLY THE RATIO OF THE SLOPING LENGTH TO THE HORIZONTAL LENGTH, and for a typical stair with R = 150 mm and T = 300 mm it is √(150² + 300²)/300 = 335/300 = 1.118.**

> **So the waist's self-weight is increased by about 12 per cent when expressed per unit of plan area — a modest but real correction, and one that is often forgotten.**

**The complete load build-up for a waist slab:**

| Component | Note |
|---|---|
| **Self-weight of the WAIST slab** | **Thickness × 25 kN/m³, MULTIPLIED by the slope factor** ← |
| **Weight of the STEPS (the triangular treads and risers)** ← | **Equivalent to a slab of thickness R/2 over the plan area — a neat and exact result** ← |
| **Finishes on the tread and riser** | **Per unit plan area, or converted** ← |
| **LIVE load** | **3 to 5 kN/m² per PLAN area, depending on the building's use** ← |

> **THE STEP-WEIGHT RESULT IN THE SECOND ROW IS WORTH KNOWING BECAUSE IT SAVES A CALCULATION EVERY TIME: a triangular step of rise R and tread T has an area of RT/2 per step, spread over a plan length T.**

> **So its equivalent uniform thickness over the plan area is exactly R/2 — regardless of the tread.**

> **A 150 mm rise therefore adds the weight of a 75 mm slab, whatever the going, which is easy to remember and quick to apply.**

**The EFFECTIVE SPAN, which is the other part of staircase design and is frequently got wrong:**

| Arrangement | Effective span |
|---|---|
| **Stair spanning between LANDING BEAMS at each end** | **The clear horizontal distance between the beams, plus the effective depth or the bearing** ← |
| **Landings spanning in the SAME direction as the stair** ← | **The whole flight PLUS both landings spans together — a long span, and the one that governs** ← |
| **Landings spanning at RIGHT ANGLES to the stair, onto side walls** ← | **The stair spans only between the landings — a much SHORTER span, and a much thinner waist** ← |

> **THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THE LAST TWO ROWS IS LARGE AND IS THE MOST CONSEQUENTIAL DECISION IN STAIRCASE DESIGN: whether the landings are supported on side walls or not can double the effective span, and therefore multiply the required waist thickness substantially.**

> **A designer who assumes the landings are supported at their sides, when in fact no wall exists there, will produce a stair that is far too thin — and the error is invisible on the structural drawing because it lies in an assumption about the ARCHITECTURE rather than in the calculation.**

> **Checking what actually supports the landings, on the architectural plan and not on the structural one, is therefore the first step in designing any staircase.**

**And a practical note on the geometry, which links back to building technology:**

> **The rise and tread must satisfy the comfort rule — commonly 2R + T between 550 and 700 mm, or R × T of about 40,000 to 45,000 mm² — and the treads must be uniform throughout a flight.**

> **A single step of different height in a flight is a serious trip hazard, because people climb stairs by rhythm rather than by looking, and it is a recurring cause of falls where a screed thickness has changed between the bottom step and the rest.**

examTip.trick: **Self-weight acts on the SLOPING area, live load on the PLAN area** — convert the first by √(R²+T²)/T (about 1.12 for a typical stair) so both are per unit of plan.
examTip.trap: **The steps' weight equals a slab of thickness R/2 over the plan area** — exactly, and independent of the tread. A 150 mm rise adds 75 mm of slab.
examTip.mnemonic: **Whether the LANDINGS are supported on side walls can double the effective span** — and the error lies in an architectural assumption, invisible on the structural drawing. Check what holds the landings up.
