questions.stem: A HIGH STRENGTH FRICTION GRIP (HSFG) bolted connection differs from an ordinary bearing-type bolted connection in that in an HSFG connection the load is transferred:
options: By the bolts bearing against the sides of their holes
By welding in addition to the bolts
By FRICTION between the clamped plate surfaces, generated by a controlled high PRE-TENSION in the bolts, so that no slip occurs and the bolt shanks are not loaded in shear at working load
Only in tension along the bolt axis
questions.solution:
**By FRICTION between the clamped plate surfaces**, generated by a controlled high pre-tension in the bolts — so no slip occurs and the bolt shanks carry no shear at working load.

**The two mechanisms compared:**

| Aspect | BEARING type (ordinary bolts) | HSFG (friction grip) |
|---|---|---|
| **Load transferred by** | **SHEAR in the bolt and BEARING on the plate** ← (option a) | **FRICTION between the plate faces** ← |
| **Bolt pre-tension** | **Nominal — just enough to hold the parts together** | **HIGH and CONTROLLED — about 70 % of the bolt's proof load** ← |
| **SLIP under load** | **Occurs, as the bolts take up the hole clearance** ← | **NONE at working load — the joint is a SLIP-CRITICAL connection** ← |
| **Bolt material** | **Grade 4.6 mild steel typically** | **Grade 8.8, 10.9 — high tensile** ← |
| **Faying surface preparation** | **Not critical** | **CRITICAL — must be clean, unpainted, free of oil, mill scale and loose rust** ← |
| **Behaviour under FATIGUE and load reversal** | **POOR — the slip works back and forth, and the holes elongate** ← | **EXCELLENT — nothing moves at all** ← |
| **Cost** | Low | **Higher: the bolts, the tightening equipment, and the surface preparation** ← |

> **THE THIRD AND SIXTH ROWS TOGETHER GIVE THE REASON HSFG BOLTS ARE SPECIFIED, and it is usually not raw strength:**

> **A bearing-type connection must SLIP before it can take load, because the holes are 2 mm larger than the bolts and the bolt must travel across that clearance before it bears.**

> **In a static structure that slip happens once, harmlessly, and the joint then behaves properly.**

> **Under REVERSING or FATIGUE loading — a bridge, a crane girder, a machine support, a structure subject to wind or earthquake — the joint slips back and forth with every cycle. The holes elongate, the bolts loosen, the joint becomes progressively sloppier, and fatigue cracks initiate at the hole edges.**

> **An HSFG joint never slips, so none of that occurs. That is what is being bought.**

**The importance of the FAYING SURFACE, which is the whole basis of the mechanism:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **The slip resistance is μ × (bolt pre-tension) × (number of interfaces)** ← | **Where μ is the SLIP FACTOR of the contact surfaces** ← |
| **μ = 0.45 for grit-blasted steel; 0.20 or less for painted or oily surfaces** ← | **A factor of more than two** ← |
| **So PAINT on the faying surface HALVES the connection's capacity or worse** ← | ← |
| **Which is why HSFG faying surfaces are masked off before painting** ← | **And why painting them by mistake is a real and expensive site error** ← |

> **THE PAINTING ERROR IN THE LAST ROW IS COMMON ENOUGH TO BE WORTH NAMING: a fabricator who paints the whole member, including the contact faces, has destroyed the connection's design capacity while apparently doing a careful job.**

> **The joint looks perfect, the bolts are correctly tightened, and it will slip at half its design load.**

> **Detection requires either inspection before assembly or a slip test — neither of which happens routinely — so the specification must be explicit that faying surfaces are to be masked, and the inspection must occur before the plates are brought together.**

**How the pre-tension is achieved and verified:**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **TORQUE control with a calibrated wrench** ← | **Simple, and the LEAST reliable — the torque-tension relation depends heavily on friction in the threads and under the nut, so it varies by ±30 %** ← |
| **TURN-OF-NUT method** ← | **Tighten to snug, then a specified further rotation — measures the bolt's EXTENSION rather than the torque, so it is far more reliable** ← |
| **DIRECT TENSION INDICATOR washers** ← | **Washers with protrusions that flatten to a measurable gap at the correct tension — visual and inspectable** ← |
| **Load-indicating bolts** | **Which shear off a spline at the correct tension** ← |

> **THE PROGRESSION FROM THE FIRST TO THE LATER METHODS ILLUSTRATES A GENERAL PRINCIPLE IN CONSTRUCTION QUALITY CONTROL: measure the thing you actually care about, not something correlated with it.**

> **What matters is the bolt's TENSION. Torque is only a proxy, and a poor one, because most of the applied torque is consumed by friction that varies with the thread condition, the lubrication and the weather.**

> **Turn-of-nut and direct tension indicators measure the extension or the clamping force itself, which is why they have displaced torque control for critical work — and why a direct tension indicator's flattened washer can be checked by an inspector with a feeler gauge, long after the crew has left.**

examTip.trick: **Load transferred by FRICTION between clamped faces, from a controlled pre-tension of about 70 % of proof load** — the bolt shank carries no shear at working load.
examTip.trap: **The reason is usually SLIP and FATIGUE, not strength** — a bearing joint must slip 2 mm to take load, and under reversal it works back and forth, elongating holes and cracking.
examTip.mnemonic: **PAINT on the faying surface halves the slip factor (0.45 blasted, 0.20 painted)** — a careful fabricator who paints the whole member destroys the joint. Mask the contact faces and inspect before assembly.

questions.stem: The FIBRE SATURATION POINT of timber is the moisture content at which:
options: The timber begins to decay
The timber is completely saturated with water
Timber is safe to use structurally
The CELL CAVITIES are free of water but the CELL WALLS are still fully saturated — about 25 to 30 per cent — BELOW which the timber begins to SHRINK and to GAIN strength
questions.solution:
**The moisture content at which the cell CAVITIES are empty of free water but the cell WALLS remain saturated** — about 25 to 30 per cent — and below which timber begins to shrink and to gain strength.

**The two kinds of water in timber:**

| Water | Where | Effect of removing it |
|---|---|---|
| **FREE water** | **In the CELL CAVITIES (the lumens)** ← | **NO shrinkage and NO change in strength — it is simply drained away** ← |
| **BOUND water** | **Held within the CELL WALLS** ← | **SHRINKAGE occurs, and the STRENGTH RISES markedly** ← |

> **THE FIBRE SATURATION POINT IS THE BOUNDARY BETWEEN THE TWO — the moment when all the free water has gone and the removal of bound water is about to begin.**

> **That is why it is such an important threshold: ABOVE it, drying changes nothing but the weight; BELOW it, every property changes.**

**What happens below the fibre saturation point:**

| Property | Change |
|---|---|
| **SHRINKAGE** | **Begins, and continues in proportion as the moisture falls** ← |
| **STRENGTH** | **RISES substantially — roughly 4 to 6 per cent for each 1 per cent reduction in moisture content** ← |
| **Stiffness** | **Rises** |
| **Weight** | **Continues to fall** |
| **Susceptibility to FUNGAL DECAY** | **FALLS — fungi need above about 20 per cent moisture to grow** ← |

> **THE STRENGTH FIGURE IN THE SECOND ROW IS STRIKING AND IS WHY SEASONING MATTERS SO MUCH: drying timber from 30 per cent down to 12 per cent can nearly DOUBLE its strength.**

> **Green timber is not merely heavy and unstable — it is genuinely weak, and using it structurally means using perhaps half the material's capacity.**

> **Which is why permissible stresses in timber codes are specified for a stated moisture condition, and why using them for green timber without correction is unsafe.**

**SHRINKAGE, which is the other consequence and is markedly ANISOTROPIC:**

| Direction | Shrinkage from green to oven dry |
|---|---|
| **LONGITUDINAL (along the grain)** | **0.1 to 0.3 % — negligible** ← |
| **RADIAL (toward the pith)** | **About 4 %** ← |
| **TANGENTIAL (around the growth rings)** | **About 8 % — roughly TWICE the radial** ← |

> **THE TANGENTIAL-TO-RADIAL RATIO OF ABOUT 2:1 IS THE CAUSE OF ALMOST EVERY DRYING DEFECT IN TIMBER, and it makes them predictable:**

> **Because a board shrinks twice as much around the rings as across them, it distorts as it dries, and the way it distorts depends on where in the log it was cut.**

| Defect | Cause |
|---|---|
| **CUPPING — a flat board curving across its width** ← | **The face nearer the bark shrinks more tangentially than the face nearer the pith, so the board curls AWAY from the heart** ← |
| **CHECKS and SPLITS at the ends** ← | **The ends dry faster than the middle, and the tangential shrinkage tears them open** ← |
| **A log drying whole develops radial splits** | **The circumference must shrink more than the radius, and the only way is to crack** ← |

> **QUARTER-SAWN timber — cut so the growth rings run roughly perpendicular to the face — is far more stable in width than plain-sawn, precisely because its width shrinks RADIALLY rather than tangentially.**

> **It wastes more of the log and costs more, and it is worth it for flooring, joinery and anything where dimensional stability matters.**

**And the EQUILIBRIUM moisture content, which is the practical target:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Timber continually exchanges moisture with the air until it reaches EQUILIBRIUM with the ambient humidity** ← | **It never stops responding** ← |
| **Typical EMC: 12 to 16 % outdoors in a temperate climate; 8 to 10 % in a heated interior** ← | **Higher in a humid monsoon climate** ← |
| **Timber must be SEASONED to approximately its service EMC before installation** ← | **Or it will move afterwards** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE PRACTICAL RULE AND ITS VIOLATION IS THE COMMONEST CAUSE OF JOINERY FAILURE: a door or a floor installed at 20 per cent moisture in a building that will settle at 10 per cent will shrink after installation.**

> **Gaps open between floorboards, panels split, joints pull apart, and doors that fitted perfectly develop gaps.**

> **The reverse also happens — timber seasoned too dry and installed in a humid environment swells, and doors jam and floors buckle.**

> **Neither is a defect in the timber. Both are a failure to match the moisture content to the environment it will live in, and the remedy is simply to condition the material on site before fixing it — which takes a week and costs nothing.**

examTip.trick: **Cell cavities empty, cell walls still saturated — about 25-30 %.** Above it, drying changes nothing but weight; below it, shrinkage begins and strength rises.
examTip.trap: **Strength rises roughly 4-6 % per 1 % reduction in moisture below FSP** — drying from 30 % to 12 % nearly DOUBLES it. Green timber is genuinely weak, not merely heavy.
examTip.mnemonic: **Tangential shrinkage is about TWICE radial (8 % vs 4 %), and longitudinal is negligible** — which explains cupping, end checks and radial log splits, and why quarter-sawn timber is stable.

questions.stem: FLUORIDE in drinking water is unusual among the quality parameters in that:
options: It has no effect on health at any concentration
TOO LITTLE causes dental CARIES while TOO MUCH causes dental and skeletal FLUOROSIS — so there is both a minimum desirable and a maximum permissible limit
It is removed completely by ordinary sand filtration
It is only present in surface water, never in groundwater
questions.solution:
**Too LITTLE causes dental caries, and too MUCH causes fluorosis** — so fluoride has both a minimum desirable and a maximum permissible concentration.

**The dose-response, which is the point of the question:**

| Concentration | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Below about 0.5 mg/L** | **Increased incidence of dental CARIES (tooth decay)** ← |
| **About 0.8 to 1.0 mg/L** | **OPTIMUM — maximum protection against caries with minimal risk** ← |
| **1.5 mg/L** | **The permissible limit in most standards, including Nepal's and WHO's** ← |
| **Above 1.5 to 3 mg/L** | **DENTAL FLUOROSIS — mottling, brown staining and pitting of tooth enamel** ← |
| **Above about 4 to 10 mg/L, over years** | **SKELETAL FLUOROSIS — bone and joint pain, stiffness, and in severe cases crippling deformity** ← |

> **ALMOST EVERY OTHER DRINKING WATER PARAMETER HAS ONLY AN UPPER LIMIT — less is always better for turbidity, coliforms, arsenic, lead and nitrate.**

> **Fluoride is the notable exception, and it is why some countries deliberately ADD fluoride to water supplies that are naturally deficient, while others must remove it from supplies that have too much.**

> **The same substance is therefore dosed in one place and treated out in another, which makes it a good illustration of the fact that a water quality standard describes a RANGE of acceptability, not merely a ceiling.**

**Where excess fluoride comes from:**

| Source | Note |
|---|---|
| **NATURAL, from fluoride-bearing rocks and minerals** ← | **Fluorite, apatite, micas — dissolved by groundwater over long residence times** ← |
| **GROUNDWATER is the usual problem source** ← | **Which disposes of option (d) — deep groundwater is far more likely to be high in fluoride than surface water** ← |
| **Deep wells and long residence times give higher concentrations** ← | **More contact time with the rock** ← |
| **Industrial sources** | **Aluminium smelting, phosphate fertiliser, brick kilns — locally significant** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW MAKES THIS PROBLEM STRUCTURALLY SIMILAR TO ARSENIC, and the similarity is worth noting: both are natural, both are in groundwater, both are invisible and tasteless, and both cause chronic disease over years.**

> **And both were introduced into communities by the same well-meaning intervention — sinking tube wells to escape bacteriologically contaminated surface water.**

> **The general lesson is the same one: a new source must be tested for the FULL suite of parameters, not merely for the hazard that prompted the change.**

**Defluoridation, which is genuinely difficult:**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **NALGONDA technique — lime plus alum, then settle and filter** ← | **Developed in India specifically for this; cheap, uses familiar chemicals, but produces sludge and needs careful dosing** ← |
| **ACTIVATED ALUMINA adsorption** | **Effective; the medium must be regenerated periodically** ← |
| **BONE CHAR** | **Traditional and effective; culturally unacceptable in some communities** ← |
| **Reverse osmosis** | **Highly effective and expensive; wastes water; removes everything else too** ← |
| **BLENDING with a low-fluoride source** ← | **Often the cheapest and simplest answer where one exists** ← |
| **Switching source entirely** | ← |

> **THE BLENDING OPTION IN THE FIFTH ROW IS FREQUENTLY THE PRACTICAL ANSWER AND IS OFTEN OVERLOOKED IN FAVOUR OF A TREATMENT PLANT: fluoride is a simple dissolved substance, and mixing a high-fluoride source with a low-fluoride one in the right proportion produces water within the limit, with no chemicals, no operator and no ongoing cost.**

> **A source at 3 mg/L blended equally with one at 0.2 mg/L gives 1.6 mg/L; blended one part in three gives 1.13 mg/L, comfortably within the standard.**

> **Where two sources exist, that arithmetic should be done before any treatment process is considered — and the same applies to arsenic, to hardness and to salinity.**

> **It is the cheapest form of water treatment there is, and its only requirement is that the two sources can be brought together, which is an engineering problem rather than a chemical one.**

examTip.trick: **Optimum about 0.8-1.0 mg/L; permissible limit 1.5 mg/L.** Below 0.5 gives caries; above 1.5 gives dental fluorosis and above ~4, skeletal fluorosis.
examTip.trap: **Almost every other parameter has only an UPPER limit** — fluoride is the exception, dosed into deficient supplies and removed from excessive ones.
examTip.mnemonic: **Like arsenic: natural, in GROUNDWATER, invisible, chronic** — and introduced by the same tube-well programmes. Test a new source for the FULL suite. And BLENDING two sources is the cheapest fix of all.

questions.stem: The INCREMENTAL INCREASE method of population forecasting differs from the arithmetical increase method in that it:
options: Assumes a constant percentage rate of growth
Uses the population of similar neighbouring towns
Fits an S-shaped curve to the recorded data
Adds to the average increase a further allowance for the average INCREMENT of that increase — that is, it allows for the rate of growth itself CHANGING
questions.solution:
**It adds, to the average increase per decade, a further allowance for the average INCREMENT of that increase** — allowing for the growth rate itself to change.

**The three simple methods compared:**

| Method | Assumption | Formula | Suits |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ARITHMETICAL increase** | **Constant ABSOLUTE increase per decade** ← | **P_n = P + n x̄, with x̄ the average increase** ← | **Large, OLD, saturated cities** ← |
| **GEOMETRICAL increase** | **Constant PERCENTAGE rate of growth** ← (option a) | **P_n = P (1 + r/100)ⁿ** ← | **YOUNG, rapidly expanding towns** ← |
| **INCREMENTAL increase** | **The increase itself changes by a constant amount** ← | **P_n = P + n x̄ + [n(n+1)/2] ȳ, with ȳ the average increment** ← | **A COMPROMISE — the most generally useful of the three** ← |

> **THE INCREMENTAL METHOD SITS BETWEEN THE OTHER TWO AND THAT IS ITS VIRTUE: the arithmetical method assumes growth never accelerates, and the geometrical method assumes it accelerates forever.**

> **Neither is true of a real town over several decades. The incremental method allows the growth to accelerate or decelerate at a steady rate, which is closer to what actually happens.**

> **Note that ȳ can be NEGATIVE — for a town whose growth is slowing, the increments are negative and the forecast bends downward, which the geometrical method can never do.**

**The comparison of the results, which is worth knowing:**

| Method | Tends to give |
|---|---|
| **Arithmetical** | **The LOWEST forecast** ← |
| **Incremental increase** | **Intermediate** ← |
| **Geometrical** | **The HIGHEST forecast — and it grows without limit** ← |

> **THE GEOMETRICAL METHOD'S UNBOUNDED GROWTH IS ITS FUNDAMENTAL WEAKNESS AND IT SHOWS UP CLEARLY OVER LONG PERIODS: at 3 per cent per annum a town doubles every 23 years, so over a 50-year design period it grows by a factor of four and a half.**

> **Extended far enough it exceeds any conceivable population, which no real town does.**

> **Real settlements grow slowly at first, then rapidly, then slowly again as they saturate — which is an S-shaped curve.**

**THE LOGISTIC CURVE, which is option (c) and is the honest description:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **An S-shaped (sigmoid) curve with an upper SATURATION population** ← | **P_s, the maximum the area can support** ← |
| **Growth is slow, then rapid, then slows again as P approaches P_s** ← | **Which matches observed urban growth well** ← |
| **Its difficulty** | **P_s must be ESTIMATED, and it is not observable from the data — so the method's realism comes with a substantial guess built in** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS WHY THE SIMPLER METHODS SURVIVE: the logistic curve is the most realistic model and it requires the one parameter nobody can determine.**

> **An estimate of the saturation population is a judgement about land availability, planning policy, economic prospects and migration over fifty years, and getting it wrong makes the curve worse than a simple straight-line extrapolation.**

**And the caution that applies to every one of these methods:**

| Caution | Note |
|---|---|
| **All of them EXTRAPOLATE the past** ← | **And assume the future resembles it** ← |
| **A single event can invalidate every one** ← | **A new highway, an industrial estate, a university, an administrative reorganisation, a disaster, or a change in migration policy** ← |
| **Kathmandu's growth was driven by factors no demographic method would have forecast** ← | **The conflict of the 1996-2006 period drove rural-to-urban migration that no trend line contained** ← |
| **So the forecast should be a RANGE, and the design STAGEABLE** ← | **Rather than a single number treated as a prediction** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE PRACTICAL CONCLUSION AND IT CONNECTS BACK TO THE DESIGN PERIOD QUESTION: since the forecast cannot be reliable over 30 years, the sensible response is not a better forecast but a design that can be extended.**

> **Reserve the land, size the trunk mains generously because they cannot be duplicated cheaply, and stage the treatment works and pumps that can.**

> **A scheme that can grow with its town is worth more than one sized precisely for a population that was guessed.**

examTip.trick: **P_n = P + n x̄ + [n(n+1)/2] ȳ** — the average increase PLUS the average increment of that increase. Option (a) is the geometrical method, (c) the logistic curve.
examTip.trap: **Arithmetical gives the lowest forecast, geometrical the highest and unbounded, incremental sits between.** And ȳ can be NEGATIVE for a town whose growth is slowing.
examTip.mnemonic: **The logistic curve is the most realistic and needs the one parameter nobody can determine** — the saturation population. Hence: forecast a RANGE, and make the design STAGEABLE.

questions.stem: THRUST BLOCKS are provided at bends, tees and reducers in a buried pressure pipeline in order to:
options: Resist the UNBALANCED HYDRAULIC FORCE that arises where the flow changes direction or the pipe's section changes, and transfer it into the surrounding soil
Support the weight of the pipe
Protect the pipe from traffic loading
Prevent the pipe from floating when the trench is flooded
questions.solution:
**To resist the UNBALANCED HYDRAULIC FORCE** that arises where the flow changes direction or the pipe's section changes, and to transfer it into the surrounding soil.

**Where the force comes from:**

| Location | Unbalanced force |
|---|---|
| **A BEND** | **The pressure and momentum forces on the two legs do not cancel — a resultant acts OUTWARD along the bisector of the bend** ← |
| **A TEE or a branch** | **The branch's pressure force is unopposed** ← |
| **A REDUCER (change of diameter)** | **The pressure acts on the difference in area** ← |
| **A DEAD END or a closed valve** | **The full pressure acts on the end area — the largest force of all** ← |
| **On a straight, uniform pipe** | **NO unbalanced force — the pressure acts equally in all directions** ← |

> **THE MAGNITUDE OF THESE FORCES IS ROUTINELY UNDERESTIMATED, and one number makes the point:**

> **A 90° bend on a 600 mm pipe at 10 bar (1 MPa) generates a resultant thrust of about 2 P A sin(θ/2) = 2 × 1,000 kPa × 0.283 m² × sin 45° = 400 kN.**

> **That is 40 tonnes, acting continuously, on a bend buried in soft ground.**

> **Without a thrust block the bend moves, the joints pull apart, and the pipeline separates — usually at the flexible joint immediately behind the bend, which is the weakest point.**

**Design considerations for a thrust block:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **The block must bear against UNDISTURBED soil** ← | **NOT against backfill, which has a fraction of the strength — so the trench must be cut back to firm ground behind the block** ← |
| **Sized on the soil's PASSIVE resistance or safe bearing pressure** ← | **With the cautions about passive pressure noted elsewhere — the movement required to mobilise it is large** ← |
| **The thrust is proportional to the TEST pressure, not the working pressure** ← | **The pipeline is tested at 1.5 times working pressure, and that is when it is most likely to move** ← |
| **Concrete poured against the trench face, not in formwork** | **So it bears directly** ← |
| **The block must not encase the JOINT** ← | **Or the joint cannot be dismantled for repair, and the pipe cannot flex** ← |
| **Anchor blocks for VERTICAL bends must resist uplift** | **Where the bend turns upward, the thrust is upward and the block's WEIGHT resists it** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE ONE MOST OFTEN VIOLATED IN PRACTICE AND IT DEFEATS THE WHOLE PROVISION: a thrust block cast against loose backfill has almost no resistance, because the backfill simply compresses and the block moves with it.**

> **The trench behind the bend must be cut back to undisturbed material and the concrete poured directly against that face.**

> **A block that looks substantial and bears on nothing is worse than no block at all, because it gives the appearance of provision.**

> **THE TEST PRESSURE POINT IN THE THIRD ROW EXPLAINS WHY PIPELINES SO OFTEN MOVE DURING TESTING: the hydrostatic test applies the highest pressure the line will ever see, often before the backfill is complete and before the thrust blocks have gained full strength.**

> **The standard precaution is to complete and cure the thrust blocks BEFORE pressure testing, and to backfill sufficiently to provide restraint — which conflicts with the desire to leave the joints exposed for inspection during the test, and has to be resolved deliberately rather than by default.**

**The alternative to thrust blocks, which is increasingly used:**

| Alternative | Note |
|---|---|
| **RESTRAINED (self-anchoring) JOINTS** ← | **Joints that transmit longitudinal tension, so the pipeline resists the thrust by FRICTION along its own length** ← |
| **Welded or fused joints** | **Steel and HDPE pipelines are inherently restrained — which is one of HDPE's real advantages** ← |
| **Advantages** | **No excavation for blocks, no curing time, works in poor soil where passive resistance is unreliable** ← |
| **The restrained length must be calculated** | **Enough pipe either side of the bend for friction to develop the required force** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS A GENUINE PRACTICAL ADVANTAGE OF FUSION-WELDED HDPE IN DIFFICULT GROUND, and it is relevant to Nepali hill schemes: a butt-fused HDPE main is a continuous pipe with no joints to pull apart, so bends need no thrust blocks at all.**

> **In steep, unstable or inaccessible terrain, where casting concrete blocks means carrying cement and water to every bend, that is a substantial saving — and it removes the failure mode entirely rather than resisting it.**

examTip.trick: **Unbalanced thrust at bends, tees, reducers and dead ends** — 2PA sin(θ/2) for a bend. A 600 mm pipe at 10 bar on a 90° bend gives about 40 tonnes.
examTip.trap: **The block must bear on UNDISTURBED soil, not backfill** — and it is sized on the TEST pressure (1.5 × working), which is when pipelines usually move.
examTip.mnemonic: **Fusion-welded HDPE and steel need NO thrust blocks** — the pipe restrains itself by friction along its length. A real advantage where carrying cement to every bend is the alternative.

questions.stem: In a municipal water distribution system, the minimum RESIDUAL PRESSURE that should be maintained at the consumer's connection during peak demand is typically:
options: About 2 to 3 m of water
About 60 to 70 m of water
About 7 to 17 m of water (roughly 0.7 to 1.7 bar), rising to a higher figure at a fire hydrant during firefighting
Any pressure above zero is acceptable
questions.solution:
**About 7 to 17 m of water (roughly 0.7 to 1.7 bar)** at the consumer's connection during peak demand, with a higher figure required at a hydrant during firefighting.

**The requirements:**

| Situation | Minimum residual head |
|---|---|
| **Single-storey buildings** | **About 7 m** ← |
| **Two-storey buildings** | **About 12 m** ← |
| **Three-storey buildings** | **About 17 m** ← |
| **At a FIRE HYDRANT during firefighting** | **Higher — commonly 10 to 15 m minimum at the hydrant with the fire flow being drawn, and more where direct hydrant pressure is relied on** ← |
| **MAXIMUM pressure in the system** | **Typically limited to about 70 m — above that, fittings leak and burst** ← |

> **THE UPPER LIMIT IN THE LAST ROW IS AS IMPORTANT AS THE LOWER ONE AND IS OFTEN NEGLECTED, and option (b) is the trap it addresses: too much pressure is a real problem, not merely a waste.**

| Consequence of excessive pressure | Note |
|---|---|
| **LEAKAGE rises steeply** ← | **Leakage from a given defect increases with pressure, so a high-pressure zone loses far more water** ← |
| **More frequent BURSTS** | **And each burst creates a new leak path** ← |
| **Household fittings, taps and float valves fail** | **They are rated for a limited pressure** ← |
| **Water is WASTED at every tap** | **A tap at 70 m delivers far more than one at 20 m for the same opening** ← |
| **Pumping ENERGY is wasted** | ← |

> **THAT IS WHY PRESSURE MANAGEMENT — dividing a network into ZONES, each with its own pressure-reducing valve — is among the most cost-effective interventions available to a water utility, and it was noted earlier as the first measure to take against non-revenue water.**

**Why pressure zones are essential in hilly terrain, which is Nepal's situation:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **In a gravity system the pressure at any point is the elevation difference from the reservoir** ← | **So a 100 m fall gives 100 m of pressure, whatever the pipe** ← |
| **In hill towns, elevation differences of 100 m or more within one settlement are ordinary** ← | ← |
| **The lower parts of the network would be at 10 bar and the upper parts at nothing** ← | **Both unacceptable** ← |
| **The answer is BREAK PRESSURE TANKS and pressure zones** ← | **Each tank resets the hydraulic grade line to its own level, capping the pressure below it** ← |
| **Each zone is then designed to keep its pressures within the 7 to 70 m window** ← | ← |

> **THE BREAK PRESSURE TANK IS THEREFORE NOT AN OPTIONAL REFINEMENT IN A HILL SCHEME BUT A NECESSITY, and it does two jobs at once: it limits the static pressure on the pipe below it, allowing a lighter and cheaper pipe class to be used, and it provides a point at which the flow can be controlled and measured.**

> **Without them, the pipe class for the whole descent would be governed by the total static head, which on a long Nepali gravity main can be several hundred metres — requiring a pipe far heavier and more expensive than the flow requires.**

**And the distinction between STATIC and RESIDUAL pressure, which the question turns on:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **STATIC pressure** | **With NO FLOW — simply the elevation difference to the water surface** ← |
| **RESIDUAL (dynamic) pressure** ← | **DURING flow — the static pressure MINUS all the friction and minor losses to that point** ← |
| **The design condition** | **The residual pressure at the most unfavourable point during PEAK HOUR demand** ← |
| **And separately, during FIRE FLOW** | **Peak demand PLUS the fire draw — a more severe condition** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW DESCRIBES THE CASE THAT USUALLY GOVERNS THE PIPE SIZES IN AN URBAN NETWORK: the fire flow is drawn at one hydrant, in addition to the peak domestic demand everywhere else.**

> **It is a large concentrated draw at an arbitrary point, and the network must still deliver an adequate pressure at that hydrant and at every consumer.**

> **Since the fire could be anywhere, the check must be made at several critical locations — and it is why urban distribution mains are commonly larger than the domestic demand alone would require.**

examTip.trick: **About 7 m (single storey), 12 m (two), 17 m (three) at peak demand**, with more at a hydrant during firefighting. Maximum pressure capped at about 70 m.
examTip.trap: **The UPPER limit matters too** — excess pressure multiplies leakage, bursts fittings and wastes water and energy. Pressure zoning is among the best-value interventions available.
examTip.mnemonic: **RESIDUAL pressure is static MINUS the friction losses at peak flow** — and the FIRE FLOW case (fire draw plus peak demand) usually governs the pipe sizes in an urban network.

questions.stem: FLOCCULATION, as distinct from coagulation, is the process in which:
options: A coagulant chemical is rapidly dispersed through the raw water
GENTLE, prolonged STIRRING brings the destabilised particles into CONTACT with one another so that they AGGREGATE into larger, settleable FLOCS
The pH of the water is adjusted before treatment
Chlorine is added to oxidise organic matter
questions.solution:
**Gentle, prolonged stirring that brings the destabilised particles into CONTACT so they aggregate into larger, settleable FLOCS.**

**The two stages, which are consecutive and quite different:**

| Stage | What happens | Mixing | Time |
|---|---|---|---|
| **COAGULATION** | **The coagulant is dispersed and DESTABILISES the colloidal particles, neutralising their surface charge** ← | **RAPID, violent mixing — a flash mixer** ← | **Seconds — 30 to 60 s** ← (option a) |
| **FLOCCULATION** | **The destabilised particles COLLIDE and stick together, growing into visible flocs** ← | **GENTLE, slow stirring** ← | **MINUTES — 20 to 40 min** ← |

> **THE CONTRAST IN THE MIXING REQUIREMENTS IS THE HEART OF THE MATTER AND IT IS THE OPPOSITE OF WHAT INTUITION SUGGESTS:**

> **COAGULATION needs violent mixing, because the coagulant must reach every particle before it hydrolyses — which takes less than a second — so the dispersion must be essentially instantaneous.**

> **FLOCCULATION needs GENTLE mixing, because the growing flocs are fragile. Stir too vigorously and they are torn apart faster than they form, and the process never produces a settleable floc at all.**

> **Yet some stirring is essential, because without motion the particles never meet. Too little and no collisions occur; too much and the flocs break.**

**The VELOCITY GRADIENT G, which quantifies exactly that balance:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **G = √(P / μ V)** ← | **P the power input, μ the viscosity, V the tank volume — units of s⁻¹** ← |
| **G for RAPID mixing** | **300 to 1,000 s⁻¹** ← |
| **G for FLOCCULATION** | **20 to 75 s⁻¹ — an order of magnitude less** ← |
| **The design parameter is G × t** ← | **The product of velocity gradient and detention time — typically 30,000 to 150,000 for flocculation** ← |

> **THE G × t PRODUCT IN THE LAST ROW IS THE USEFUL DESIGN QUANTITY BECAUSE IT MEASURES THE TOTAL NUMBER OF PARTICLE COLLISIONS: a high G for a short time and a low G for a long time can produce the same total contact opportunity.**

> **Since a high G breaks flocs, the sensible choice is a LOW G maintained for a LONG time — which is why flocculation basins are large and their paddles turn slowly.**

**TAPERED FLOCCULATION, which is the refinement worth knowing:**

| Stage | G value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **First compartment** | **HIGHEST — perhaps 60 s⁻¹** ← | **The particles are still small and tough; vigorous stirring maximises collisions and they cannot yet be broken** ← |
| **Middle compartment** | **Intermediate — 40 s⁻¹** | ← |
| **Last compartment** | **LOWEST — 20 s⁻¹** ← | **The flocs are now large and fragile, so the stirring must be gentle enough not to destroy what has been built** ← |

> **TAPERING THE VELOCITY GRADIENT DOWN THE LENGTH OF THE BASIN IS AN ELEGANT PIECE OF PROCESS DESIGN: it matches the mixing intensity to the fragility of the floc at each stage, giving fast growth at the start and preservation at the end.**

> **A basin with uniform stirring must compromise — either too gentle at the start, wasting time, or too vigorous at the end, breaking the flocs it has just made.**

**And the practical points that decide whether it works:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **SHORT-CIRCUITING must be prevented** ← | **Baffles between compartments, so the water actually spends the design detention time in the basin** ← |
| **The transfer to the SEDIMENTATION tank must be gentle** ← | **A floc destroyed in the connecting channel or by a pump is a floc that will not settle — so flocculated water is NEVER pumped** ← |
| **The optimum coagulant dose is found by JAR TEST** | **Not by calculation — it depends on the raw water's character that day** ← |
| **pH matters greatly** | **Alum works best around pH 6.5 to 7.5** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS A RULE WORTH REMEMBERING BECAUSE IT CONSTRAINS THE WHOLE PLANT LAYOUT: everything achieved in twenty minutes of careful flocculation can be undone in five seconds by a pump impeller or a sharp drop.**

> **So the flocculator must sit immediately upstream of the clarifier, connected by a wide, slow, gently curved channel, and the hydraulic profile must be arranged so the flow reaches the clarifier by gravity.**

> **That single requirement is why treatment plants are laid out as a descending sequence of units, with all the pumping done at the beginning — a layout decision driven by the fragility of a floc.**

examTip.trick: **Coagulation = RAPID mixing for SECONDS, to destabilise. Flocculation = GENTLE mixing for MINUTES, to aggregate.** Option (a) describes coagulation.
examTip.trap: **Too little stirring and particles never meet; too much and the flocs tear apart.** G = 300-1,000 s⁻¹ for rapid mixing, only 20-75 for flocculation.
examTip.mnemonic: **TAPER G down the basin — high where flocs are small and tough, low where they are large and fragile.** And never PUMP flocculated water: five seconds in an impeller undoes twenty minutes of work.

questions.stem: ACTIVATED CARBON is used in water treatment principally to remove:
options: Bacteria and viruses
Suspended solids and turbidity
Dissolved calcium and magnesium hardness
TASTE, ODOUR, colour and dissolved ORGANIC compounds, including pesticides and disinfection by-product precursors, by ADSORPTION
questions.solution:
**Taste, odour, colour and dissolved ORGANIC compounds** — including pesticides, industrial chemicals and the natural organic matter that forms disinfection by-products — by ADSORPTION.

**How adsorption differs from the other removal mechanisms:**

| Mechanism | Removes | Example process |
|---|---|---|
| **STRAINING / filtration** | **SUSPENDED particles too large to pass** ← | **Sand filters, screens** ← (option b) |
| **SEDIMENTATION** | **Particles denser than water, given time** | Settling tanks |
| **COAGULATION** | **Colloids, by destabilising them** | ← |
| **DISINFECTION** | **Living organisms, by killing them** ← | Chlorine, UV, ozone ← (option a) |
| **PRECIPITATION / ion exchange** | **DISSOLVED ions such as hardness** ← | Lime-soda softening ← (option c) |
| **ADSORPTION** ← | **DISSOLVED MOLECULES, which ADHERE to a solid surface** ← | **Activated carbon** ← |

> **THE DISTINCTION THAT MATTERS IS BETWEEN PARTICLES AND DISSOLVED MOLECULES: filtration and sedimentation remove things suspended IN the water; adsorption removes things dissolved in it.**

> **A dissolved organic molecule causing an earthy taste will pass through any filter, however fine, because it is not a particle at all — it is part of the solution.**

> **Only a process that acts at the molecular level can remove it, and adsorption onto a very large surface is the practical one.**

**Why activated carbon works so well:**

| Property | Note |
|---|---|
| **An ENORMOUS internal surface area** ← | **500 to 1,500 m² per GRAM — a handful has the surface area of several football fields** ← |
| **Created by ACTIVATION** ← | **Charring a carbon source (coconut shell, coal, wood) and then partially oxidising it with steam to open a vast network of micropores** ← |
| **Organic molecules are HYDROPHOBIC and prefer the carbon surface to the water** ← | **Which is why adsorption is spontaneous** ← |
| **The pore SIZE distribution must suit the molecule** | **Micropores for small molecules, mesopores for larger ones** ← |

> **THE SURFACE AREA FIGURE IN THE FIRST ROW IS THE WHOLE REASON THE MATERIAL IS USED AND IT IS WORTH APPRECIATING: adsorption capacity is proportional to available surface, and no other cheap material comes close.**

> **Coconut shell carbon, which is abundant in South Asia, produces a particularly fine micropore structure and is widely used.**

**The two forms and their applications:**

| Form | Use |
|---|---|
| **POWDERED activated carbon (PAC)** ← | **Dosed into the water intermittently, when a taste or odour episode occurs, and removed with the sludge — cheap, flexible, no capital plant** ← |
| **GRANULAR activated carbon (GAC)** ← | **A permanent bed the water passes through, like a filter — continuous treatment, but it must be REGENERATED or replaced when exhausted** ← |

> **THE PAC OPTION IS THE PRACTICAL ONE FOR AN OCCASIONAL PROBLEM AND IS UNDERUSED: an algal bloom in a reservoir produces an earthy-musty taste for a few weeks a year, and dosing powdered carbon during those weeks costs a fraction of installing a permanent GAC contactor.**

> **The carbon is simply added to the raw water, adsorbs the offending compounds, and is removed in the clarifier sludge along with the coagulant floc.**

> **A permanent GAC bed is justified where the contamination is continuous — an industrial catchment, high natural organic matter, or a requirement to control disinfection by-products year-round.**

**THE BREAKTHROUGH PROBLEM, which governs GAC operation:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **A carbon bed has a FINITE capacity** ← | **Unlike a sand filter, which is cleaned and restored by backwashing** ← |
| **As it saturates, an ADSORPTION WAVE moves down the bed** ← | **The upper layers exhaust first** ← |
| **When the wave reaches the outlet, BREAKTHROUGH occurs** ← | **And the contaminant appears in the treated water, without warning** ← |
| **Backwashing does NOT restore capacity** ← | **It only removes trapped particles; the adsorbed molecules remain** ← |
| **Regeneration requires thermal treatment at high temperature** | **Usually done off-site, and some carbon is lost each cycle** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE MISCONCEPTION MOST WORTH CORRECTING: a GAC bed looks like a sand filter, is backwashed like a sand filter, and is not restored by it.**

> **An operator who treats a carbon bed as a filter will backwash it faithfully and be surprised when the taste returns — because the carbon has been full for months and the backwashing did nothing about it.**

> **Carbon exhaustion must be tracked by monitoring the OUTLET water quality, not by the headloss across the bed, and the replacement interval is a consumable cost that must be budgeted from the outset.**

examTip.trick: **Adsorption removes DISSOLVED MOLECULES — taste, odour, colour, pesticides, organics.** Filtration removes particles, disinfection kills organisms, softening removes ions.
examTip.trap: **A dissolved molecule passes through ANY filter** — it is part of the solution, not a particle. Only a molecular-level process removes it.
examTip.mnemonic: **BACKWASHING does not restore a carbon bed** — it removes trapped particles and leaves the adsorbed molecules. Track exhaustion by OUTLET quality, not headloss, and budget the replacement.

questions.stem: A COMBINED SEWER OVERFLOW (CSO) is:
options: A structure that allows the DILUTED excess flow in a combined sewer to spill to a watercourse during heavy rain, so that the interceptor and the treatment works are not overwhelmed
A tank storing sewage during power failures
The overflow from a septic tank
A device that separates grit from sewage
questions.solution:
**A structure that allows the diluted excess flow in a COMBINED sewer to spill to a watercourse during heavy rain**, so that the interceptor sewer and the treatment works are not overwhelmed.

**Why it is necessary:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **A COMBINED sewer carries both sanitary sewage and STORM water in one pipe** ← | ← |
| **The storm flow can be 50 to 100 times the dry weather flow** ← | **The disparity noted earlier: 200 litres per second of sewage against several thousand of runoff** ← |
| **Carrying all of it to the treatment works is impossible** ← | **The works would have to be sized for the storm flow and would then run at 1 per cent of capacity most of the time — hydraulically and biologically unworkable** ← |
| **So the excess is SPILLED, once it has been diluted** ← | **The overflow operates only when the flow exceeds a set multiple of the dry weather flow — commonly 6 DWF** ← |

> **THE DILUTION IN THE LAST ROW IS THE JUSTIFICATION, AND IT IS A GENUINE ONE ALTHOUGH UNCOMFORTABLE: the spilled flow is mostly rainwater, and the sewage in it has been diluted five or six times over.**

> **The receiving watercourse is also in flood at that moment, and dilutes it further.**

> **So the argument is that the pollution load reaching the river during a storm is acceptable in exchange for not building a treatment works ten times larger than needed for 99 per cent of the year.**

**The problems with CSOs, stated honestly:**

| Problem | Note |
|---|---|
| **Untreated sewage DOES reach the watercourse** ← | **Diluted, but with pathogens, gross solids and floating material** ← |
| **The FIRST FLUSH is the worst of it** ← | **The first runoff of a storm scours out the solids and grease that have settled in the sewers during dry weather — so the earliest and dirtiest flow is exactly what spills** ← |
| **AESTHETIC pollution** | **Sanitary items, plastics and grease left on the banks — highly visible and deeply unpopular** ← |
| **They operate far more often than the public expects** | **Dozens of times a year in many systems** ← |
| **Climate change is increasing storm intensity** | **So they operate more often still** ← |

> **THE FIRST FLUSH EFFECT IN THE SECOND ROW UNDERMINES THE DILUTION ARGUMENT SUBSTANTIALLY AND IS THE STRONGEST TECHNICAL CRITICISM OF CSOs: the theory assumes the spill is dilute, and the first spill of each storm is the most concentrated flow the sewer ever carries.**

> **Solids and grease deposited during days of low dry-weather flow are resuspended in the first few minutes of a storm, and they go straight over the weir.**

> **The engineering response is a STORAGE TANK at the overflow: the first flush is captured and held, and returned to the works for treatment after the storm; only the genuinely diluted later flow spills.**

> **That is the standard modern retrofit, and it is expensive because the tanks must be large and are usually built in constrained urban ground.**

**The design features of a CSO chamber:**

| Feature | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **A weir set at a level corresponding to the design flow (e.g. 6 DWF)** ← | **So it spills only above that** ← |
| **A SCREEN on the overflow** ← | **Retaining gross solids and sanitary items — the single most valuable improvement, and cheap** ← |
| **A stilling arrangement to avoid scouring the outfall** | ← |
| **A flap valve at the outfall** | **Preventing river water backing up into the sewer during a flood** ← |
| **Monitoring of spill frequency and duration** ← | **Increasingly required, and it is what turned CSOs into a public issue once the data became visible** ← |

> **THE SCREEN IN THE SECOND ROW DESERVES EMPHASIS BECAUSE IT ADDRESSES THE MOST VISIBLE HARM AT THE LOWEST COST: most public objection to CSOs concerns the gross solids left on riverbanks rather than the invisible bacteriological load.**

> **A screen on the overflow removes essentially all of it for a fraction of the cost of a storage tank, and it makes an enormous difference to how the discharge is perceived — and to the actual amenity of the watercourse.**

**And the strategic answer:**

> **The long-term remedy is to stop combining the two flows: SEPARATE systems for all new development, progressive separation of existing systems where practicable, and SUSTAINABLE DRAINAGE — soakaways, permeable paving, green roofs, detention ponds — to keep the rainwater out of the sewer altogether.**

> **The last of these is the most promising, because it addresses the volume at source rather than conveying it and then dealing with it: rain that never enters the sewer needs no overflow, no storage and no treatment.**

examTip.trick: **It spills diluted excess flow (above about 6 DWF) to a watercourse** so the interceptor and works are not overwhelmed by a storm flow 50-100 times the dry weather flow.
examTip.trap: **The FIRST FLUSH undermines the dilution argument** — the first minutes of a storm scour out solids and grease deposited during dry weather, so the dirtiest flow is exactly what spills.
examTip.mnemonic: **A SCREEN on the overflow removes the visible harm for a fraction of a storage tank's cost.** And the real answer is keeping rain out of the sewer: separate systems and sustainable drainage.

questions.stem: A LAMP HOLE in a sewerage system is:
options: An opening in a manhole cover for ventilation
A chamber where a street gully discharges into the sewer
A small vertical SHAFT from ground level down to the sewer, through which a light could be lowered so that the sewer could be inspected from the manholes on either side
A pit for collecting grit
questions.solution:
**A small vertical shaft from ground level down to the sewer**, through which a lamp could be lowered so that an inspector at a manhole on either side could see whether the length between them was clear.

**Its purpose and its obsolescence:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Provided where a MANHOLE could not be built** ← | **Where the sewer is very deep, or the ground above is obstructed** ← |
| **Typically a 150 to 300 mm pipe with a cover at the surface** | **Far cheaper than a manhole** ← |
| **A light was lowered and observed from the manholes each side** ← | **If the light could be seen from both, the sewer was clear** ← |
| **It also served as a rodding and flushing point** | ← |
| **Now largely OBSOLETE** ← | **CCTV inspection does the job far better, and the lamp hole gives no access for cleaning** ← |

> **The technique is charmingly simple and it worked: a blockage or a collapse anywhere between the lamp hole and the manhole would interrupt the line of sight, and the inspector would know both that there was a problem and roughly where.**

> **CCTV has displaced it because a camera not only detects a blockage but shows its nature, its extent and the condition of the pipe — and can be pushed through from a manhole without any additional shaft at all.**

**The sewer appurtenances, gathered, since the terminology is examined:**

| Appurtenance | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **MANHOLE** | **Access for inspection, cleaning and rodding; at every change of direction, gradient or size, and at intervals along straight lengths** ← |
| **DROP MANHOLE** | **Where an incoming sewer is much higher, bringing the flow down a vertical pipe rather than cascading into the chamber** ← |
| **LAMP HOLE** | **This question** ← |
| **CATCH BASIN (gully)** ← | **A chamber at a road inlet with a SUMP that traps grit and a water seal that traps odour, before the water enters the sewer** ← (option b is close, but a catch basin is the chamber, not a lamp hole) |
| **FLUSHING TANK** ← | **An automatic siphonic tank at the HEAD of a sewer, discharging periodically to flush a reach where the flow is too small to be self-cleansing** ← |
| **INVERTED SIPHON (depressed sewer)** | **Carrying the sewer beneath an obstruction, running full under pressure** ← |
| **GREASE and OIL trap** | **At commercial kitchens and garages** ← |
| **VENTILATING column** | **Keeping the sewer's atmosphere moving** ← |
| **STORM water overflow** | **On a combined system** ← |

> **THE FLUSHING TANK IN THE FIFTH ROW SOLVES A REAL AND AWKWARD PROBLEM AND IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING: at the very head of a sewerage system, only a few houses contribute, so the flow is tiny and intermittent.**

> **No gradient steep enough to achieve the self-cleansing velocity at that flow is practicable — it would drive the sewer far too deep within a few hundred metres.**

> **So the sewer inevitably silts up in its uppermost reach.**

> **A flushing tank fills slowly from a water supply or from the sewage itself, and when full it discharges its whole contents at once through an automatic siphon — a sudden surge that scours the reach clean and needs no operator, no power and no moving parts beyond the siphon itself.**

> **It is another instance of the recurring principle in these systems: for a function that must happen reliably and unattended, a device with no controls beats one with them.**

**And the CATCH BASIN in the fourth row is worth a closing note because it is often got wrong:**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **A SUMP below the outlet** ← | **Grit and road detritus settle in it instead of entering the sewer** ← |
| **A water SEAL** | **Excluding sewer odour from the street — in a combined system especially** ← |
| **It requires REGULAR CLEANING** ← | **Or the sump fills, and it then passes everything straight through — worse than useless, because it is assumed to be working** ← |

> **The last row is the practical failure: catch basins are effective only while they are emptied, and a city that installs thousands of them and cleans none has installed thousands of odour traps that pass grit freely into its sewers.**

> **The maintenance obligation is created at the moment of installation, and it is permanent.**

examTip.trick: **A small vertical shaft for lowering a LIGHT, so the sewer could be sighted from the manholes either side** — used where a manhole could not be built, and now displaced by CCTV.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) describes a CATCH BASIN** — a gully chamber with a grit sump and a water seal. Both are appurtenances, and they do quite different things.
examTip.mnemonic: **A FLUSHING TANK siphons automatically to scour the sewer's head reach**, where the flow is too small for self-cleansing at any practicable gradient. No power, no operator, no controls.

questions.stem: SLUDGE DRYING BEDS dewater digested sewage sludge principally by:
options: Mechanical pressing between filter cloths
DRAINAGE of water downward through a sand and gravel bed, followed by EVAPORATION from the exposed surface
Centrifugal separation
Chemical precipitation of the water
questions.solution:
**By DRAINAGE of water downward through a sand and gravel bed, followed by EVAPORATION from the exposed surface.**

**How they work:**

| Stage | Note |
|---|---|
| **Digested sludge is run onto the bed to a depth of 200 to 300 mm** ← | ← |
| **DRAINAGE — water passes down through the sand into underdrains within a day or two** ← | **This removes most of the water and is the faster of the two mechanisms** ← |
| **EVAPORATION — the remaining water leaves the exposed surface over the following weeks** ← | **Slower, and entirely weather-dependent** ← |
| **The sludge cracks as it dries, exposing more surface and accelerating the evaporation** ← | **A helpful self-reinforcing effect** ← |
| **The dried cake, at 40 to 60 % solids, is lifted off by hand or by a small loader** | ← |
| **The whole cycle takes 2 to 6 weeks in good weather** ← | **And much longer, or indefinitely, in the monsoon** ← |

> **THE MONSOON DEPENDENCE IN THE LAST ROW IS THE DECISIVE LIMITATION IN NEPAL AND SOUTH ASIA, and it is not a detail: for three or four months of the year, evaporation essentially stops and the beds fill with rainwater.**

> **A works relying on open drying beds must therefore either provide enough bed area to store the whole monsoon's sludge production, or provide COVERED beds, or accept that sludge accumulates and the digesters back up.**

> **The area required is large — roughly 0.1 to 0.2 m² per person served — and it is one of the reasons drying beds, though cheap to build and operate, are often the constraint on a plant's site.**

**The dewatering methods compared:**

| Method | Solids achieved | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Gravity THICKENING** | **4 to 8 %** | **A preliminary step, not full dewatering** ← |
| **DRYING BEDS** | **40 to 60 %** ← | **Cheapest; no power, no chemicals, no skilled operation; large area; weather-dependent** ← |
| **BELT FILTER PRESS** | **18 to 25 %** ← | **Continuous, moderate cost, needs polymer conditioning** ← |
| **PLATE-AND-FRAME FILTER PRESS** | **30 to 45 %** ← | **The highest cake solids of the mechanical methods; batch operation** ← |
| **CENTRIFUGE** | **20 to 30 %** ← | **Compact and fully enclosed, so no odour; high power and maintenance** ← |
| **Drying LAGOONS** | Variable | Simplest of all; very large area |

> **THE COMPARISON IN THE SECOND AND THIRD ROWS IS WORTH NOTING BECAUSE IT SURPRISES PEOPLE: a simple drying bed produces a DRIER cake than an expensive belt press.**

> **Sun and time achieve what mechanical pressure cannot, because evaporation removes water that is physically bound within the sludge flocs and no press can squeeze out.**

> **What the mechanical methods buy is not dryness but SPEED, RELIABILITY, small AREA and independence from the weather — which is exactly what a large urban works needs and a small rural one does not.**

> **So the technology choice follows the same logic met with slow and rapid sand filters: the low-technology option often performs BETTER, and the high-technology one is chosen for area, consistency and operability rather than for results.**

**Why the sludge is DIGESTED before drying, which matters:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **Digestion destroys 40 to 50 % of the volatile solids** ← | **So there is less to handle** ← |
| **It makes the sludge far LESS ODOROUS** ← | **Raw sludge on an open bed is intolerable near any settlement** ← |
| **It greatly improves the DRAINABILITY** | **Digested sludge releases its water much more readily** ← |
| **It reduces pathogens substantially** | **Though not to a safe level for unrestricted use** ← |
| **It produces BIOGAS** | **Which can run the works** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE ONE THAT DECIDES WHETHER OPEN DRYING BEDS ARE ACCEPTABLE AT ALL, and it should be stated plainly: raw, undigested sludge spread on open beds beside a town produces an odour nuisance that will close the works.**

> **Digestion is therefore not merely a solids-reduction step but the precondition for the cheapest dewatering method — and a plant designed with open beds and a digester that does not work will find itself unable to use either.**

**And the final disposal, which is where the value lies:**

> **Dried digested sludge is a genuine soil conditioner, rich in organic matter and nutrients, and using it on agricultural land closes a nutrient loop that would otherwise send phosphorus and nitrogen to the river.**

> **The constraints are pathogens, heavy metals from industrial discharges, and public acceptance — and of these, the HEAVY METALS are the one that engineering can address, by controlling industrial discharges to the sewer at source rather than trying to remove metals from the sludge afterwards.**

> **A works receiving uncontrolled industrial effluent produces sludge that cannot be used on land and must be landfilled, which converts a resource into a liability — and the decision that determines which happens is made in the trade effluent consents, not at the treatment works.**

examTip.trick: **DRAINAGE through sand into underdrains (days), then EVAPORATION from the surface (weeks)** — giving 40-60 % solids, higher than any mechanical method.
examTip.trap: **Mechanical methods buy SPEED, small AREA and weather independence — not dryness.** A belt press gives only 18-25 % against a drying bed's 40-60 %.
examTip.mnemonic: **Digestion is the PRECONDITION for open beds** — raw sludge on them is an odour nuisance that closes the works. And heavy metals in the sludge are controlled at the industrial discharge, not at the plant.

questions.stem: In a SANITARY LANDFILL, the LEACHATE that must be collected and treated is:
options: The gas generated by anaerobic decomposition of the waste
Rainwater that has run OFF the capped surface without entering the waste
Groundwater flowing beneath the site
The contaminated LIQUID formed when water percolates THROUGH the waste, dissolving and carrying away soluble and suspended contaminants
questions.solution:
**The contaminated liquid formed when water percolates THROUGH the waste**, dissolving and carrying away soluble and suspended contaminants.

> **Option (a) describes LANDFILL GAS — the other principal emission, and a quite separate problem.**

**Where leachate comes from and what it contains:**

| Source of the liquid | Note |
|---|---|
| **RAINFALL infiltrating the waste** ← | **By far the largest source — which is why the CAP matters so much** ← |
| **Moisture in the waste itself** | **Food and organic waste is mostly water** ← |
| **Water produced by the decomposition reactions** | ← |
| **Groundwater entering, if the liner has failed** | ← |

| Contaminant | Note |
|---|---|
| **Very high BOD and COD** ← | **Young leachate can exceed 20,000 mg/L BOD — some forty times raw sewage** ← |
| **AMMONIA nitrogen** | **Persistent, and the parameter that remains problematic longest** ← |
| **HEAVY METALS, chlorides, sulphates** | ← |
| **Organic micropollutants** | ← |

> **THE STRENGTH FIGURE IN THE FIRST ROW IS THE THING TO REMEMBER: leachate is not dilute contaminated water, it is an extremely strong liquid waste.**

> **Discharging it untreated to a watercourse deoxygenates the water completely and kills everything in it, and even a small volume does substantial damage.**

> **It also CHANGES with the landfill's age — young leachate is high in BOD and readily biodegradable, while old leachate is lower in BOD but high in ammonia and recalcitrant organics, and needs a quite different treatment process.**

> **A treatment plant designed for a new landfill will be treating a different liquid in twenty years, which is a real design problem for a facility whose leachate must be managed for decades after closure.**

**The engineered barriers of a sanitary landfill:**

| Element | Function |
|---|---|
| **A LINER at the base and sides** ← | **Compacted clay, a geomembrane, or both — preventing leachate reaching the groundwater** ← |
| **A LEACHATE COLLECTION layer above the liner** ← | **Graded stone with perforated pipes, draining to a sump for pumping out** ← |
| **DAILY COVER of soil over the day's waste** ← | **Controlling odour, vermin, birds, blowing litter and fire** ← |
| **A low-permeability CAP on completion** ← | **Excluding rainfall, which is the principal control on leachate VOLUME** ← |
| **GAS collection wells and pipework** | **Landfill gas is about 50 % methane** ← |
| **Groundwater MONITORING boreholes up- and down-gradient** ← | **The only way to know whether the liner is working** ← |

> **THE CAP IN THE FOURTH ROW IS THE MOST EFFECTIVE SINGLE LEACHATE CONTROL AND THE LOGIC IS WORTH STATING: leachate is produced by water entering the waste, so the way to reduce leachate is to keep the water out.**

> **Treating leachate is expensive and permanent; excluding rainfall with a capping layer and shedding it as clean surface runoff is cheap and passive.**

> **A well-capped closed landfill produces a small fraction of the leachate of an open one, and the difference persists for the whole aftercare period.**

> **This is the same principle met throughout environmental engineering: preventing contamination is far cheaper than treating it, and the intervention that reduces the VOLUME requiring treatment is worth more than an improvement in the treatment itself.**

**LANDFILL GAS, since it is the other half of the problem:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Roughly 50 % METHANE and 50 % carbon dioxide** ← | **From anaerobic decomposition of the organic fraction** ← |
| **EXPLOSIVE between about 5 and 15 % methane in air** ← | **And it MIGRATES laterally through the ground into nearby basements and services — landfill gas explosions have destroyed buildings** ← |
| **Methane is a greenhouse gas some 25 times more potent than CO₂** ← | **So uncontrolled release matters globally as well as locally** ← |
| **Can be collected and BURNT for power, or flared** ← | **Flaring converts methane to CO₂, cutting the climate impact by a factor of 25 even when the energy is not used** ← |

> **THE MIGRATION HAZARD IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE MOST IMMEDIATE DANGER AND IS OFTEN UNDERESTIMATED: gas does not simply rise from the surface, it travels sideways through permeable strata and along service trenches, and it can accumulate in a confined space hundreds of metres from the site.**

> **That is why gas monitoring extends beyond the landfill's boundary, why building on or near a former landfill requires gas protection measures, and why the location of closed and unrecorded dumps is a genuine planning issue in growing cities.**

> **In Nepal, where much municipal waste has historically gone to unengineered dumps in river valleys with no liner, no cap and no gas control, both the leachate and the gas are released entirely uncontrolled — and the first task is not to improve those sites' treatment but to stop creating new ones.**

examTip.trick: **Liquid formed when water percolates THROUGH the waste.** Option (a) is landfill GAS — the other principal emission, and a separate problem.
examTip.trap: **Young leachate can exceed 20,000 mg/L BOD — forty times raw sewage** — and its character CHANGES with age, from high-BOD to high-ammonia, needing a different process decades later.
examTip.mnemonic: **The CAP is the best leachate control** — keep the rain out rather than treat what comes through. And landfill gas MIGRATES sideways into basements hundreds of metres away; it does not just rise.

questions.stem: Among the methods of applying irrigation water to a field, the one giving the HIGHEST application efficiency is:
options: DRIP (trickle) irrigation, at about 90 per cent
Wild flooding, at about 80 per cent
Furrow irrigation, at about 95 per cent
Check basin flooding, at about 90 per cent
questions.solution:
**DRIP (trickle) irrigation, at about 90 per cent** — the highest of the common methods.

**The methods and their typical application efficiencies:**

| Method | Efficiency | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **WILD FLOODING** | **20 to 40 %** ← | **Water simply turned loose over the land — the least controlled and least efficient** ← |
| **BORDER strip** | **50 to 60 %** | **Land divided into long strips between low ridges** ← |
| **CHECK BASIN** | **50 to 70 %** ← | **Level basins bounded by bunds — the traditional Nepali and Indian method, and essential for PADDY, which needs ponding** ← |
| **FURROW** | **55 to 70 %** ← | **Water run along furrows between crop rows — suits row crops; the soil between rows stays dry** ← |
| **SPRINKLER** | **70 to 80 %** ← | **Water applied as artificial rain; suits undulating land and sandy soil** ← |
| **DRIP / trickle** | **85 to 95 %** ← | **Water delivered drop by drop directly to each plant's root zone** ← |

> **Options (b), (c) and (d) attach plausible efficiencies to the wrong methods, which is how this question is usually set — the ORDER of the methods matters more than the exact percentages.**

**Why drip is so much more efficient:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **Water is delivered ONLY to the root zone of each plant** ← | **The soil between the plants is never wetted, so it never evaporates** ← |
| **No RUNOFF and almost no deep percolation** | **The application rate is matched to the soil's intake rate** ← |
| **No EVAPORATION from a wet soil surface or from spray in the air** ← | **Sprinklers lose 5 to 20 per cent to evaporation and wind drift before the water lands** ← |
| **Application is FREQUENT and small** | **Keeping the root zone near field capacity, which is also better for the crop** ← |
| **WEEDS between the rows are not watered** | **A real secondary benefit** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE FUNDAMENTAL DIFFERENCE AND IT IS WORTH SEEING CLEARLY: every flooding method wets the WHOLE SOIL SURFACE, and a wet soil surface evaporates whether a plant is growing on it or not.**

> **Drip wets perhaps a fifth of the surface, so four fifths of the evaporation loss simply does not occur.**

> **That is not a refinement of the same process but a different one, which is why the efficiency gain is so large.**

**The other benefits of drip, and the reasons it is not universal:**

| Benefits | Note |
|---|---|
| **FERTIGATION — fertiliser dissolved in the water, delivered to the root** ← | **Far more efficient than broadcasting, and it saves fertiliser as well as water** ← |
| **Works on steep, undulating or irregular land** | **Where surface irrigation cannot** ← |
| **Can use SALINE water more safely** | **Frequent application keeps the salts moving away from the root** ← |
| **Higher yields and better quality** | **From maintaining an optimal moisture level continuously** ← |

| Limitations | Note |
|---|---|
| **HIGH capital cost per hectare** ← | **The principal barrier for a smallholder** ← |
| **EMITTERS CLOG** ← | **The critical maintenance problem — requiring FILTRATION of the supply and periodic acid or chlorine flushing** ← |
| **Requires clean water and a pressurised supply** | **Which a canal turn does not provide** ← |
| **Rodents and mechanical damage to the laterals** | ← |
| **Not suitable for PADDY** ← | **Which needs standing water for weed control and for the crop itself** ← |
| **Salts accumulate at the wetted zone's PERIPHERY** | **Needing occasional heavy leaching** ← |

> **THE EMITTER CLOGGING IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE COMMONEST CAUSE OF ABANDONED DRIP SYSTEMS AND IT IS ENTIRELY PREVENTABLE: an emitter passes a litre or two an hour through an orifice under a millimetre across.**

> **Any silt, algae, iron precipitate or biological growth blocks it, and a blocked emitter cannot be detected from the pipe — the plant simply dies.**

> **A screen or sand filter on the inlet, and a routine flushing regime, are not optional accessories but part of the system, and a drip installation supplied without them will fail within a season or two.**

> **THE PADDY EXCLUSION IN THE FIFTH ROW MATTERS ENORMOUSLY IN NEPAL, since paddy is the dominant crop: drip cannot serve it, because ponded water is part of how paddy is grown — it suppresses weeds and the variety is adapted to it.**

> **So the water-saving potential of drip applies to the vegetables, fruit, sugarcane and cash crops, and paddy must be addressed by different means — better bund maintenance, levelling, and the alternate wetting and drying technique, which reduces paddy's water use substantially without abandoning surface application.**

examTip.trick: **Wild flooding 20-40 %, border 50-60 %, check basin 50-70 %, furrow 55-70 %, sprinkler 70-80 %, DRIP 85-95 %.** The wrong options attach plausible figures to the wrong methods.
examTip.trap: **Every flooding method wets the WHOLE surface, and wet soil evaporates whether a plant is on it or not.** Drip wets a fifth of it — a different process, not a refinement.
examTip.mnemonic: **Emitters pass 1-2 litres/hour through a sub-millimetre orifice** — FILTRATION and flushing are part of the system, not accessories. And drip cannot serve PADDY, which is most of Nepal's irrigated area.

questions.stem: A soil has a field capacity of 24 per cent and a permanent wilting point of 12 per cent (both by dry weight), a dry unit weight of 1.5 g/cm³ and an effective root zone depth of 1.2 m. If irrigation is applied when 50 per cent of the available moisture has been depleted, the depth of water applied per irrigation is:
options: 54 mm
72 mm
108 mm
216 mm
questions.solution:
**108 mm.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **AVAILABLE moisture, as a fraction of dry weight** | **FC − PWP = 0.24 − 0.12 = 0.12** ← |
| **Convert to an equivalent DEPTH of water** | **d = (FC − PWP) × (γ_d/γ_w) × root depth** ← |
| **Substituting** | **= 0.12 × 1.5 × 1,200 mm** |
| **TOTAL available moisture depth** | **= 216 mm** ← (option d) |
| **At 50 per cent depletion, the depth to be replaced** | **= 216 / 2 = 108 mm** ← |

> **Option (d) 216 mm is the TOTAL available moisture — the depth that would be applied if the soil were allowed to dry to the wilting point, which is never done.**

> **Option (b) 144 mm... note that omitting the DENSITY factor gives 0.12 × 1,200 = 144 mm, and halving it gives 72 mm — which is option (b), and is the commonest error.**

**Why the DRY UNIT WEIGHT appears in the formula at all:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **Moisture content is defined by WEIGHT — mass of water divided by mass of dry soil** ← | **A dimensionless ratio** ← |
| **What the irrigator applies is a DEPTH of water over an area** ← | **A volume** ← |
| **To convert between them, the mass of dry soil per unit area is needed** ← | **Which is (dry unit weight) × (root depth)** ← |
| **Hence the γ_d/γ_w term** | **The ratio of the soil's dry density to water's — 1.5 here** ← |

> **SO THE FACTOR OF 1.5 IS A UNIT CONVERSION, NOT A CORRECTION, and omitting it understates the answer by a third — which is why it is worth understanding rather than memorising.**

> **A denser soil holds more water per metre of depth at the same moisture content, simply because there is more soil in that metre.**

**Why only 50 per cent depletion is allowed:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **Water is NOT equally available across the whole range** ← | **Near field capacity it is held loosely and the plant takes it easily; near the wilting point it is held very tightly** ← |
| **So the plant is under increasing STRESS long before the wilting point** ← | **And the yield falls even though the crop has not wilted** ← |
| **The READILY AVAILABLE moisture is therefore only part of the available moisture** ← | **Commonly taken as 50 to 60 per cent of it** ← |
| **The allowable depletion depends on the crop and its stage** | **Shallow-rooted and sensitive crops need a lower depletion; deep-rooted and tolerant ones can go further** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE POINT: the permanent wilting point is where the crop DIES, and irrigation scheduling is not about keeping the crop alive but about keeping it PRODUCTIVE.**

> **A field allowed to reach 80 per cent depletion before watering will have a living crop and a substantially reduced yield, and the loss will not be visible as anything dramatic.**

> **This is why the depletion fraction is a design decision made with the crop's economics in mind rather than its survival, and why over-irrigation and under-irrigation both cost yield — over-irrigation by waterlogging and leaching nutrients, under-irrigation by stress.**

**And the IRRIGATION INTERVAL, which follows from this figure:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Depth applied per irrigation** | **108 mm, from above** |
| **Divide by the crop's daily CONSUMPTIVE USE** | **If the crop uses 6 mm/day, interval = 108/6 = 18 days** ← |
| **Adjust for RAINFALL** | **Effective rainfall extends the interval** ← |
| **And for the APPLICATION EFFICIENCY** | **To deliver 108 mm to the root zone at 60 % efficiency, 180 mm must be applied at the field** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW COMPLETES THE CHAIN BACK TO THE GROSS REQUIREMENT AND IS THE STEP MOST OFTEN OMITTED: the 108 mm is what the SOIL must receive, not what the farmer must apply.**

> **At a realistic surface irrigation efficiency the farmer applies half again as much, and the canal must deliver more still after conveyance losses — which is how a crop needing 108 mm becomes a canal releasing 250 mm, and why the overall efficiency figure of 30 to 45 per cent met earlier is not an exaggeration.**

examTip.trick: **d = (FC − PWP) × (γ_d/γ_w) × root depth = 0.12 × 1.5 × 1,200 = 216 mm; at 50 % depletion, 108 mm.**
examTip.trap: **Do not omit the DRY DENSITY factor** — moisture content is by WEIGHT and irrigation is a DEPTH, so γ_d/γ_w is the unit conversion between them. Omitting it understates by a third.
examTip.mnemonic: **Wilting point is where the crop DIES; scheduling is about keeping it PRODUCTIVE** — hence 50-60 % depletion. And 108 mm is what the SOIL needs, not what the farmer applies.

questions.stem: A SIDE-SLOPE canal is one which is aligned:
options: ROUGHLY AT RIGHT ANGLES TO THE CONTOURS, running down the natural slope of the ground, so that it requires no cross-drainage works
Along a watershed or ridge line
Along a contour, at a gentle gradient across the slope
In a deep cutting through a ridge
questions.solution:
**Roughly AT RIGHT ANGLES to the contours**, running down the natural ground slope — so that no drainage crosses it and no cross-drainage works are needed.

**The three canal alignments:**

| Alignment | Path | Cross-drainage works | Command |
|---|---|---|---|
| **WATERSHED (ridge) canal** ← | **Along the RIDGE line separating two drainages** ← | **NONE — no drainage can cross a watershed** ← | **Commands land on BOTH sides — the ideal** ← |
| **CONTOUR canal** ← | **ALONG the contours, at a gentle gradient across the hillside** ← (option c) | **MANY — every stream flowing down the slope must be crossed** ← | **Commands on ONE side only, below the canal** ← |
| **SIDE-SLOPE canal** ← | **At right angles to the contours, DOWN the slope** ← | **NONE — it runs parallel to the drainage rather than across it** ← | **Commands very little, since the land either side is at the same level or higher** ← |

> **THE FIRST AND THIRD ROWS BOTH AVOID CROSS-DRAINAGE WORKS AND FOR THE SAME REASON: a canal that runs PARALLEL to the natural drainage lines is never crossed by them.**

> **A watershed canal runs along the top of a ridge, so all drainage flows AWAY from it. A side-slope canal runs down the slope beside the streams, so none crosses it.**

> **A CONTOUR canal, by contrast, cuts across every stream on the hillside, and each one requires an aqueduct, a super-passage or a culvert.**

**Their relative merits:**

| Alignment | Advantages | Disadvantages |
|---|---|---|
| **WATERSHED** | **No cross-drainage; commands both sides; the most economical** ← | **The ridge may wander, lengthening the canal; and a ridge may not exist where needed** ← |
| **CONTOUR** | **The only choice in hilly country where a ridge alignment is impossible** ← | **NUMEROUS and expensive cross-drainage works; one-sided command; the works are the dominant cost** ← |
| **SIDE-SLOPE** | **No cross-drainage; short and direct** ← | **Almost NO COMMAND — it is a conveyance channel, not an irrigation one; and the steep gradient risks SCOUR** ← |

> **THE SIDE-SLOPE CANAL'S LACK OF COMMAND IS THE POINT THAT DEFINES ITS USE: it cannot irrigate, because the land beside it is not below it.**

> **So it is used to CONVEY water from one place to another — from a headworks down to a lower main canal, or as a feeder — and the irrigation is done by the watershed or contour canals it feeds.**

> **Its steep gradient is also a difficulty: running down the natural slope means a gradient far steeper than a canal wants, so it must either be lined, or given drops and falls to dissipate the surplus energy.**

**Why the WATERSHED alignment is sought first, and what it implies for a project:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **In the plains — the Terai, the Indo-Gangetic plain — watershed alignments are usually available** ← | **The ground is gently undulating, with broad low ridges between drainages** ← |
| **The main canal is taken along the watershed, and branches lead off down the slopes** ← | **A branching pattern that follows the natural topography** ← |
| **In the HILLS a watershed alignment is rarely possible** | **The ridges are too steep and too narrow** ← |
| **So hill schemes are CONTOUR canals, and their cost is dominated by cross-drainage** ← | ← |

> **THE LAST ROW EXPLAINS WHY HILL IRRIGATION IS SO MUCH MORE EXPENSIVE PER HECTARE THAN PLAINS IRRIGATION, and the reason is structural rather than hydraulic:**
