> **A contour canal on a Nepali hillside may need an aqueduct or a culvert every few hundred metres, and each is a structure requiring design, materials carried to site, and maintenance.**

> **The canal itself — a lined channel a metre or two wide — is the cheap part.**

> **This is also why hill schemes so often use PIPES rather than open channels for the difficult reaches: a buried pipe crosses a gully in a single span or follows the ground through it, needs no aqueduct, is not blocked by a landslide, and loses nothing to seepage or evaporation.**

> **For small hill schemes, replacing a contour canal with a pipeline frequently costs less than the cross-drainage works alone would have — which is the same reasoning that favoured a tunnel over a hillside canal for hydropower conveyance.**

examTip.trick: **Side-slope: AT RIGHT ANGLES to the contours, down the slope. Watershed: along the ridge. Contour: along the contours.** Option (c) describes the contour canal.
examTip.trap: **Watershed and side-slope both avoid cross-drainage** — both run PARALLEL to the drainage lines. Only the CONTOUR canal cuts across every stream.
examTip.mnemonic: **A side-slope canal commands almost nothing** — it is a conveyance channel, not an irrigation one, and its steep gradient needs lining or falls. Hill schemes are contour canals, and the CROSS-DRAINAGE is the cost.

questions.stem: In the cross-section of a canal in EMBANKMENT, the DOWLA (dowel) is:
options: The horizontal shelf left between the cutting and the embankment
The strip of land from which earth was excavated for the embankment
A small SUBSIDIARY BANK provided along the INNER EDGE of the service road on top of the canal bank, to prevent vehicles from running into the canal
The spoil left over after forming the section
questions.solution:
**A small subsidiary bank along the INNER EDGE of the service road on the canal bank**, provided to stop vehicles running into the canal.

**The elements of a canal cross-section:**

| Element | Description | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **BERM** | **A horizontal shelf left at the original ground level, between the cutting's side slope and the embankment's toe** ← (option a) | **Prevents the embankment from sliding into the cutting; provides a walkway; and it WIDENS naturally as silt deposits, adding stability** ← |
| **DOWLA (dowel)** ← | **A small bank, about 0.5 m high, along the inner edge of the service road** ← | **A SAFETY barrier for vehicles, and it keeps road runoff out of the canal** ← |
| **SERVICE (inspection) ROAD** | **On the canal bank, usually the wider one** | **Access for inspection, maintenance and desilting plant; often used as a public road** ← |
| **FREEBOARD** | **The height of the bank above the full supply level** | **0.3 m for small canals to 1.0 m or more for large ones** ← |
| **SPOIL BANK** ← | **Surplus excavated earth heaped alongside a canal in CUTTING** ← (option d) | **Where there is more excavation than the embankment needs** ← |
| **BORROW PIT** ← | **The area from which earth was taken for the embankment** ← (option b) | **Where there is not enough excavation** ← |
| **Counter berm / catch water drain** | On the outer side | **Intercepting hillside runoff before it reaches the bank** ← |

> **THE BERM IN THE FIRST ROW HAS A PROPERTY WORTH NOTING BECAUSE IT IS UNUSUAL AMONG ENGINEERING FEATURES: it IMPROVES WITH AGE.**

> **Silt carried by the canal deposits along the berm, widening it and increasing the embankment's stability year by year — so an old canal's section is more stable than the one that was built.**

> **That is why a berm is provided generously at construction and why the deposits on it should not be removed during desilting: they are doing structural work.**

**THE BORROW PIT AND SPOIL BANK IN THE FIFTH AND SIXTH ROWS ARE WHERE ENVIRONMENTAL DAMAGE IS DONE, and they connect back to points made earlier:**

| Issue | Note |
|---|---|
| **BORROW PITS fill with water and become MOSQUITO breeding sites** ← | **The Anopheles habitat noted under water-related disease — created by the project itself** ← |
| **They also take land out of cultivation** | ← |
| **SPOIL BANKS obstruct natural drainage if placed carelessly** ← | **Creating waterlogging on the land behind them** ← |
| **Both should be SHAPED and DRAINED, or levelled on completion** ← | **Which costs little while the plant is on site and a great deal afterwards** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS A GENUINE AND COMMON CAUSE OF WATERLOGGING THAT IS EASILY OVERLOOKED: a continuous spoil bank alongside a canal in cutting is a small dam across the natural drainage.**

> **The land behind it cannot drain, and it waterlogs — so the canal built to irrigate the area has waterlogged part of it before delivering any water.**

> **The remedy is trivial: leave GAPS in the spoil bank at the natural drainage lines, or shape it into discontinuous heaps rather than a continuous ridge.**

> **It costs nothing at the time and is essentially uncorrectable later, which makes it exactly the sort of item that belongs in the specification rather than in the contractor's judgement.**

**And the BALANCING of earthwork, which governs the section's design:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **The BALANCING DEPTH is the depth of cutting at which the excavation exactly equals the fill needed** ← | **At that depth there is neither spoil nor borrow** ← |
| **Above it, there is surplus — a spoil bank** | ← |
| **Below it, there is a deficit — a borrow pit** | ← |
| **A canal designed at its balancing depth is the most economical** ← | **No earth is hauled in or out, and neither a spoil bank nor a borrow pit is created** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW SHOWS THAT THE ENVIRONMENTAL AND THE ECONOMIC OPTIMA COINCIDE HERE, which is not always the case and is worth taking advantage of: designing the canal to balance its earthwork eliminates the hauling cost AND the borrow pits AND the spoil banks at the same time.**

> **It is one of the more satisfying results in canal design, and it is why the balancing depth is computed as a matter of routine rather than as a refinement.**

examTip.trick: **DOWLA = a small bank along the inner edge of the service road, a vehicle safety barrier.** Option (a) is the BERM, (b) the borrow pit, (d) the spoil bank.
examTip.trap: **The BERM improves with age** — silt deposits widen it and add stability, so it is doing structural work and should not be cleared away during desilting.
examTip.mnemonic: **Leave GAPS in the spoil bank at the drainage lines** — a continuous one is a small dam that waterlogs the land the canal was built to irrigate. And design at the BALANCING DEPTH: cheapest and cleanest at once.

questions.stem: A diversion headworks is to be built across a river whose design flood is 2,500 m³/s. Using Lacey's regime relation, the WATERWAY to be provided is approximately:
questions.solution:
**About 237 m.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Lacey's regime wetted perimeter** | **P = 4.75 √Q, with Q in m³/s and P in metres** ← |
| **√2,500** | **= 50** ← |
| **P = 4.75 × 50** | **= 237.5 m** ← |
| **For a wide, shallow river, the waterway ≈ the wetted perimeter** ← | **Since P ≈ B + 2y and y is small compared with B** ← |

> **The value obtained is the river's own REGIME width — the width it would naturally adopt for that discharge — and it is taken as the waterway to be provided.**

**Why the waterway is set to the regime width rather than chosen freely:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **A river in regime has already found the width appropriate to its discharge and sediment** ← | **Constraining it to something different provokes a response** ← |
| **A waterway NARROWER than regime** ← | **Increases the velocity, causes SCOUR and deep scour holes at the piers, and raises the AFFLUX upstream** ← |
| **A waterway WIDER than regime** ← | **Reduces the velocity, causes SILTING and shoaling, the flow concentrates in one part of the width, and the structure is longer and more expensive than necessary** ← |
| **So the regime width is the equilibrium value, and departing from it in either direction has a cost** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE POINT THAT SURPRISES PEOPLE: making the waterway TOO WIDE is not merely wasteful, it is actively harmful.**

> **A river given more width than it needs does not spread out evenly. It deposits sediment across part of the opening, forms shoals, and concentrates its flow through a narrow part of the structure — which then experiences velocities and scour depths appropriate to a much narrower waterway, at an unpredictable location.**

> **So a generously wide barrage or bridge can suffer worse local scour than a correctly sized one, and the extra cost buys a worse outcome.**

**LOOSENESS FACTOR, which is how the departure is expressed:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Looseness factor = (provided waterway) ÷ (Lacey regime width)** ← | ← |
| **A factor of 1.0 is the regime condition** | ← |
| **In practice, factors between about 1.0 and 1.2 are adopted** ← | **A modest allowance for the flow not distributing perfectly, and for the piers' obstruction** ← |
| **Factors below 1.0 are used where afflux can be tolerated and scour is protected against** | **Deliberately constricting the river, with heavier protection works** ← |

> **The provided waterway must also allow for the PIERS' obstruction: the 237 m is the CLEAR waterway required, so the overall length of the barrage is that plus the total thickness of the piers and abutments.**

**And the SCOUR DEPTH, which follows from the same theory and governs the foundations:**

| Relation | Note |
|---|---|
| **Lacey's normal scour depth R = 0.47 (Q/f)^(1/3)** ← | **Measured below the highest flood level** ← |
| **Or, from the discharge per metre width: R = 1.35 (q²/f)^(1/3)** ← | **More useful where the waterway is constricted** ← |
| **Multiply by a factor for the LOCATION** ← | **1.27 R in a straight reach; 1.5 R at a moderate bend; 1.75 R at a severe bend; 2.0 R at a right-angle bend or the nose of a guide bank** ← |
| **Foundations must go BELOW the maximum scour depth, with a margin** ← | **Typically 1.5 to 2 m below it** ← |

> **THE MULTIPLIERS IN THE THIRD ROW ARE WHERE FOUNDATION DEPTHS ARE DECIDED AND THEY ARE LARGE: the scour at the nose of a guide bank is twice the normal value.**

> **Since the normal scour on a river of this size might be 6 m below HFL, the nose of the guide bund must be founded below 12 m — and the launching apron must contain enough stone to pave the face of a hole that deep as it forms.**

> **Underestimating that multiplier is the commonest cause of failure at guide banks and bridge abutments, and the failures occur during the flood that produces the scour, when nothing can be done about them.**

examTip.trick: **P = 4.75 √Q = 4.75 × 50 = 237.5 m** — the river's own regime width, taken as the clear waterway (plus the piers' thickness for the overall length).
examTip.trap: **A waterway TOO WIDE is actively harmful** — the river shoals across part of it, concentrates its flow, and produces worse local scour than a correctly sized opening. Looseness factor 1.0-1.2.
examTip.mnemonic: **Scour multipliers: 1.27 R straight, 1.5 R moderate bend, 2.0 R at a guide bank nose** — twice normal. Underestimating them is the classic cause of abutment and guide bank failure.

questions.stem: At a diversion headworks, the POND LEVEL to which the river is raised upstream of the weir must be fixed:
options: Equal to the canal's full supply level
At the highest flood level of the river
At the crest level of the weir
SUFFICIENTLY ABOVE the canal's full supply level to provide the working head needed across the canal head regulator, plus the losses through it
questions.solution:
**Sufficiently ABOVE the canal's full supply level** to provide the working head needed across the canal head regulator, together with the losses through it.

**The reasoning:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **The canal must be supplied at its designed FULL SUPPLY LEVEL (FSL)** ← | **Which is fixed by the command it must serve** ← |
| **Water flows into the canal through the head regulator, which is essentially an ORIFICE or a gated opening** ← | ← |
| **An orifice requires a HEAD DIFFERENCE to pass its discharge** ← | **No head, no flow** ← |
| **So the pond level must exceed the canal FSL by that working head plus the entry and friction losses** ← | **Typically 1.0 to 1.5 m in total** ← |

> **Option (a) is the intuitive but impossible answer — with the pond level EQUAL to the canal FSL there would be no head across the regulator and no flow at all.**

> **That is the point of the question: water does not flow from one level into the same level.**

**How the levels are fixed, in sequence:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **1. The canal's FSL at its head is determined by the COMMAND** ← | **Working backward from the highest land to be irrigated, adding the canal's slope and losses** ← |
| **2. Add the working head required across the regulator** | **Giving the POND LEVEL** ← |
| **3. The weir CREST is set at or just below the pond level** ← | **The difference being made up by SHUTTERS or GATES, which are raised in the dry season and lowered or removed in flood** ← |
| **4. The AFFLUX and the flood levels follow from the waterway and the crest level** | ← |

> **THE SHUTTERS IN THE THIRD ROW ARE THE KEY DEVICE AND THE REASON THE CREST IS NOT SIMPLY BUILT AT THE POND LEVEL, and the logic is worth following:**

> **In the DRY SEASON the river's flow is small, and the pond level must still be maintained to feed the canal — so the crest must be high.**

> **In FLOOD, a high crest would raise the upstream water level greatly, increasing the afflux and flooding land far upstream.**

> **The resolution is a LOW crest with SHUTTERS or gates on top: the shutters are raised in the dry season to hold the pond level, and dropped in flood so the flood passes over the low crest with minimal afflux.**

> **That single arrangement reconciles two irreconcilable requirements, and it is the reason barrages — which are entirely gated — have progressively replaced weirs with shutters on large rivers.**

**The consequence for the choice between a weir and a barrage:**

| Structure | Crest and control | Afflux |
|---|---|---|
| **WEIR with falling shutters** | **A relatively HIGH masonry or concrete crest, with shutters adding the last metre or so** ← | **Larger, since the crest itself obstructs the flood** ← |
| **BARRAGE** | **A LOW crest with tall GATES providing the whole of the ponding** ← | **MUCH SMALLER — the gates are lifted clear and the flood passes almost unobstructed** ← |
| **Cost** | Weir cheaper to build | **Barrage more expensive, and it requires reliable operation** ← |
| **Control** | Limited | **Full control of the upstream level at all discharges** ← |

> **THE AFFLUX ROW IS THE DECIDING CONSIDERATION ON A LARGE RIVER IN FLAT COUNTRY AND IT IS AN ECONOMIC ONE RATHER THAN A TECHNICAL ONE: afflux raises the flood level upstream, and in flat terrain a rise of even half a metre inundates a great deal of land.**

> **The cost of the land submerged, the marginal bunds needed to protect it, and the drainage problems created can far exceed the extra cost of a barrage over a weir.**

> **So on a large alluvial river in the plains the barrage is generally chosen, and on a smaller or steeper river where the afflux affects little land the weir remains appropriate.**

> **It is a good example of a structural choice determined almost entirely by the SURROUNDING TOPOGRAPHY rather than by the structure's own requirements — and of why the land acquisition and inundation assessment must be done before the type of structure is settled, not after.**

examTip.trick: **Pond level = canal FSL + the working head across the regulator + losses (about 1.0-1.5 m).** With equal levels there would be no head and no flow.
examTip.trap: **The crest is set BELOW the pond level, with SHUTTERS or gates making up the difference** — high ponding in the dry season, low obstruction in flood. Two irreconcilable requirements, one device.
examTip.mnemonic: **A BARRAGE's low crest and tall gates give a far smaller AFFLUX** — which on a flat alluvial river saves more in inundated land than the barrage costs over a weir.

questions.stem: REVETMENT (bank pitching) as a river training measure differs from a series of SPURS in that revetment:
options: ARMOURS the bank surface in place along its whole length, resisting erosion directly, whereas spurs project into the river and deflect the current away from the bank
Is placed in the middle of the river channel
Is used only on the inner bank of a bend
Requires no launching apron
questions.solution:
**Revetment ARMOURS the bank surface in place along its whole length**, resisting erosion directly, whereas spurs project into the flow and deflect the current away from the bank.

**The two approaches compared:**

| Aspect | REVETMENT (pitching) | SPURS (groynes) |
|---|---|---|
| **Principle** | **DIRECT protection — armour the bank so the current cannot erode it** ← | **INDIRECT protection — push the current away so it never reaches the bank** ← |
| **Extent** | **CONTINUOUS along the length protected** ← | **A SERIES of discrete structures with gaps between** ← |
| **Effect on the channel** | **NONE — the bank line is unchanged** ← | **The channel is narrowed and the flow deflected; silt deposits in the bays between the spurs, so the bank effectively advances** ← |
| **Cost** | **Higher per metre, since the whole face is covered** ← | **Lower per metre of bank protected, since only the spurs are built** ← |
| **Risk if one element fails** | **A local failure, repairable** ← | **A failed spur concentrates the flow at the next one, and failures can cascade** ← |
| **Best for** | **Protecting a specific asset — a town, a road, a bridge approach** ← | **Training a long reach, and reclaiming land** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW CONTAINS THE MOST INTERESTING DIFFERENCE AND IT IS OFTEN THE DECIDING ONE: spurs do not merely protect the bank, they ADVANCE it.**

> **Silt deposits in the still water between the spurs, the bays fill, vegetation establishes, and after a few seasons a new bank line has formed at the spur heads.**

> **So spurs reclaim land while protecting it, which on an eroding Terai river bank is a substantial additional benefit.**

> **Revetment holds the line and no more.**

**The construction of revetment:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **A prepared, graded bank slope** | **Typically 2:1 or flatter** ← |
| **A FILTER layer beneath the armour** ← | **Graded granular material or geotextile, satisfying the filter criteria — the most critical and most neglected element** ← |
| **The ARMOUR itself** | **Hand-placed stone pitching, dumped riprap, concrete blocks, or GABIONS** ← |
| **A LAUNCHING APRON at the toe** ← | **Loose stone that slides down the face of the scour hole as it develops, extending the protection automatically — so option (d) is false** ← |
| **A cut-off or key at the top and at each end** | **So the flow cannot get behind the armour** ← |

> **THE FILTER IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE ELEMENT ON WHICH THE WHOLE PROTECTION DEPENDS AND IT IS THE ONE MOST OFTEN OMITTED TO SAVE MONEY, and the failure mechanism deserves stating:**

> **Stone armour laid directly on a sandy bank does not stop the bank eroding. Water moves through the gaps between the stones, and the fine bank material washes out THROUGH the armour.**

> **The bank loses material from behind the stones, the stones settle into the void, the armour layer becomes discontinuous, and it fails — while looking perfectly sound from the river until it collapses.**

> **A properly graded filter, or a geotextile, retains the bank material while letting water pass, and it is the difference between protection that lasts and protection that fails in the second monsoon.**

> **This is the same filter criterion met at a dam's chimney drain, behind a retaining wall, and beneath an inverted filter — the same two conditions, in a fourth application.**

**GABIONS deserve their own note, since they are so widely used in Nepal:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Stone-filled wire mesh baskets, tied together** ← | **Flexible, permeable, and buildable entirely by hand with local stone** ← |
| **They DEFORM rather than fail** ← | **A gabion wall undermined by scour settles and continues to function, where a rigid wall would crack and collapse** ← |
| **Vegetation establishes in and through them** | **Adding strength and appearance over time** ← |
| **Their weakness is the WIRE** ← | **Abrasion by bed load, corrosion, and vandalism — once the mesh fails the stone spills and the structure unravels** ← |
| **PVC-coated or heavily galvanised wire, and a design life of 20-30 years** | ← |

> **THE FLEXIBILITY IN THE SECOND ROW IS WHY GABIONS SUIT NEPAL SO WELL: on unstable ground with unpredictable scour, a structure that can settle and deform without failing is worth more than a stronger one that cannot.**

> **The same argument favoured reinforced earth over rigid retaining walls, and it recurs wherever the ground cannot be relied upon: build something that accommodates movement, because the movement is going to happen.**

examTip.trick: **Revetment = DIRECT protection, armouring the bank in place. Spurs = INDIRECT, deflecting the current away.** Continuous versus discrete.
examTip.trap: **Spurs ADVANCE the bank** — silt fills the bays between them and a new bank line forms at the spur heads, reclaiming land as well as protecting it.
examTip.mnemonic: **Stone armour without a FILTER does not work** — the bank washes out THROUGH the stones and the armour settles into the void, looking sound until it collapses. Same filter criteria as a dam drain.

questions.stem: In the conventional hierarchy of an irrigation canal system, the channel that takes off from a DISTRIBUTARY and delivers water to the outlets is called a:
options: Main canal
MINOR
Branch canal
Watercourse
questions.solution:
**A MINOR.**

**The hierarchy, from the river downward:**

| Channel | Takes off from | Delivers to | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| **MAIN canal** | **The river, at the headworks** ← | **Branch canals** | **Carries the whole supply; NO direct irrigation from it** ← |
| **BRANCH canal** | **The main canal** | **Distributaries** | **Discharge above about 5 m³/s; little or no direct irrigation** ← |
| **DISTRIBUTARY (major)** | **A branch or the main canal** | **Minors, and some outlets** ← | **Carries 0.25 to 5 m³/s** ← |
| **MINOR (minor distributary)** ← | **A DISTRIBUTARY** ← | **The OUTLETS** ← | **Below about 0.25 m³/s** ← |
| **WATERCOURSE (field channel)** ← | **An OUTLET** ← | **The individual fields** ← | **Maintained by the CULTIVATORS, not by the irrigation department** ← |

> **THE OWNERSHIP BOUNDARY IN THE LAST ROW IS THE MOST IMPORTANT PRACTICAL FEATURE OF THE WHOLE HIERARCHY AND IT IS WORTH IDENTIFYING PRECISELY: the OUTLET is where the irrigation department's responsibility ends and the farmers' begins.**

> **Everything above the outlet is a public work, designed, built and maintained by the state. Everything below it is the cultivators' own.**

**Why that boundary causes most of the system's problems:**

| Problem | Note |
|---|---|
| **WATERCOURSES are frequently the worst-maintained part of the system** ← | **Unlined, silted, weed-choked, with breached bunds — and losses in them can exceed those in the whole canal system above** ← |
| **Nobody individually owns the whole watercourse** ← | **The head-reach farmer has no interest in the tail end of it, and the tail-ender cannot maintain the head** ← |
| **So a scheme can deliver water reliably to the outlet and still fail** ← | **The problem is entirely below the point at which the engineering was done** ← |
| **Enormous public investment above the outlet can be defeated by a hundred metres of neglected field channel** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW DESCRIBES A REAL AND WIDESPREAD OUTCOME AND IT IS WHY THE ENGINEERING VIEW OF IRRIGATION IS INCOMPLETE: a canal system that delivers its design discharge to every outlet has done everything the design asked of it, and the crops may still be short of water.**

> **This recognition produced the shift toward ON-FARM DEVELOPMENT and WATER USERS' ASSOCIATIONS — organising the cultivators of each watercourse into a body that owns, maintains and polices it collectively, with legal standing and the power to levy and enforce.**

> **Where such associations function, watercourse losses fall sharply and the tail-enders receive water. Where they do not, no amount of investment above the outlet reaches the tail.**

> **Nepal's Irrigation Policy has pursued exactly this — transferring management of smaller systems to water users' associations — and it is a recognition that the binding constraint was institutional rather than hydraulic.**

**And the design implications of the hierarchy:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **The higher channels carry LARGE discharges and irrigate nothing directly** ← | **Their design is dominated by conveyance efficiency and by the regime relations** ← |
| **The lower channels carry small discharges and are numerous** ← | **Their design is dominated by simplicity, replication and the self-cleansing velocity** ← |
| **The OUTLET is the only point of measurement and control in most systems** ← | **Which is why the outlet's flexibility and tamper-resistance matter so much** ← |
| **Losses accumulate down the hierarchy** | **Each level loses to seepage and evaporation, and the fractions multiply** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW LINKS BACK TO THE OUTLET FLEXIBILITY QUESTION AND EXPLAINS WHY IT IS SUCH A CAREFULLY STUDIED SUBJECT FOR SUCH A SMALL STRUCTURE: the outlet is the single point at which a system serving tens of thousands of hectares hands water to individual cultivators.**

> **It is the place where equity is either delivered or lost, where tampering occurs, and where the only practicable measurement can be made.**

> **A great deal of engineering thought has gone into a structure that may cost a few thousand rupees, and it is thought well spent.**

examTip.trick: **Main → branch → distributary → MINOR → outlet → watercourse.** The minor takes off from a distributary and feeds the outlets.
examTip.trap: **The OUTLET is the ownership boundary** — the department maintains everything above it, the cultivators everything below. Watercourses are often the worst-maintained part of the whole system.
examTip.mnemonic: **A scheme can deliver its full design discharge to every outlet and still fail** — the losses are below where the engineering stopped. Hence water users' associations and on-farm development.

questions.stem: MOLE DRAINS used for the subsurface drainage of agricultural land are:
options: Buried perforated clay or PVC pipes laid in a trench
Open ditches excavated across the field
UNLINED CHANNELS formed in the subsoil by dragging a torpedo-shaped device through it, relying on the CLAY's own cohesion to keep them open
Vertical wells sunk into the aquifer
questions.solution:
**Unlined channels formed in the subsoil by dragging a torpedo-shaped "mole" through it**, relying on the clay's own cohesion to keep the channel open.

**How they are formed:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **A bullet- or torpedo-shaped MOLE PLOUGH, typically 75 to 100 mm in diameter, is drawn through the subsoil at 400 to 600 mm depth** ← | **Behind a vertical blade, towed by a tractor or a winch** ← |
| **It forms a smooth, unlined CHANNEL** ← | **No pipe, no gravel, no trench** ← |
| **An EXPANDER follows the mole, compacting and smoothing the channel wall** ← | **Making it more stable and durable** ← |
| **The blade's slot above the channel also cracks and fissures the soil** ← | **Which improves the soil's permeability and helps water reach the mole — a valuable secondary effect** ← |
| **Moles are drawn at 2 to 4 m spacing, discharging into a collector pipe or an open ditch** | ← |

> **THE ATTRACTION IS COST AND SPEED: a mole drain requires no materials at all — no pipe, no gravel, no geotextile — and a tractor can form hundreds of metres in an hour.**

> **Compared with a piped tile system, which requires trenching, pipes, a graded gravel surround and careful laying, the cost is a small fraction.**

**The essential requirement, which limits their use severely:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **The subsoil MUST be a stable CLAY of adequate plasticity** ← | **The channel is held open by the clay's own cohesion — nothing else supports it** ← |
| **Clay content generally above about 30 to 35 per cent** ← | ← |
| **They FAIL COMPLETELY in sandy, silty or unstable soils** ← | **The channel simply collapses, often within days** ← |
| **The soil must be MOIST when moling — plastic enough to form, not so wet that it flows** ← | **A narrow window, and the timing of the operation is critical** ← |
| **The surface should be dry enough to carry the tractor** | **Which conflicts with the requirement above** ← |

> **THE CONFLICT IN THE LAST TWO ROWS IS THE PRACTICAL DIFFICULTY OF THE TECHNIQUE: the subsoil must be moist and the topsoil dry, which occurs for only a short period after the winter and before the ground dries out.**

> **Moling done outside that window either fails to form a channel at all, or the tractor cannot operate, or the channel collapses.**

> **So the operation is confined to a few weeks a year, which limits how much land can be treated in a season.**

**Their durability, and the honest comparison:**

| Aspect | MOLE drains | PIPED (tile) drains |
|---|---|---|
| **Cost** | **A small fraction** ← | **High — materials, trenching, laying** ← |
| **LIFE** | **2 to 10 years, then they must be re-formed** ← | **50 years or more** ← |
| **Soils** | **Stable CLAY only** ← | **Any soil, with a suitable filter** ← |
| **Depth** | **Shallow — 400 to 600 mm** | **1.0 to 2.0 m** ← |
| **Renewal** | **Simply re-mole, at low cost** ← | **Cannot be renewed; must be replaced** ← |

> **THE LIFE COMPARISON LOOKS DECISIVE AGAINST MOLE DRAINS AND IS NOT, because of the last row: a mole drain is CHEAP TO RENEW.**

> **Re-moling every five years at a small cost may be economically better than a permanent piped system at many times the capital cost, particularly for a farmer who cannot finance the latter.**

> **The comparison must be made on the whole-life cost, and where the soil suits moling the answer is often the temporary system repeatedly renewed rather than the permanent one built once.**

> **That is a general result worth carrying beyond this topic: a cheap solution renewed regularly can beat an expensive permanent one, and comparing them on DESIGN LIFE alone gives the wrong answer.**

**And a related technique worth knowing, since it uses the same idea:**

> **SUBSOILING is the same operation performed for a different purpose: a deep tine is drawn through the subsoil to BREAK UP a compacted layer — a plough pan, or compaction from machinery traffic — without forming a drainage channel.**

> **It improves infiltration and root penetration, and its effect is temporary in the same way, because the soil re-compacts under continued traffic.**

> **Both techniques address the same underlying problem: an impermeable layer in the subsoil that prevents water moving down and roots moving through, and which is created as often by farming itself as by nature.**

examTip.trick: **A torpedo-shaped mole dragged through the subsoil forms an UNLINED channel held open by the clay's own cohesion** — no pipe, no gravel, no trench.
examTip.trap: **They need a stable CLAY subsoil (30-35 % clay) and fail completely in sand or silt.** And the subsoil must be moist while the surface is dry enough for a tractor — a window of a few weeks.
examTip.mnemonic: **A 5-year life is not the objection it appears** — re-moling is cheap, and a temporary system repeatedly renewed can beat a permanent one. Compare WHOLE-LIFE cost, never design life alone.

questions.stem: CONJUNCTIVE USE of surface water and groundwater in an irrigation command means:
options: Using surface water in the monsoon and abandoning it thereafter
Using groundwater exclusively, to avoid canal seepage
Mixing canal water with groundwater to improve its quality

Operating the canal and the groundwater as a SINGLE PLANNED SYSTEM — pumping groundwater in the dry season and relying on canal supply in the wet, so that canal seepage RECHARGES the aquifer that is later pumped
questions.solution:
**Operating the canal supply and the groundwater as a SINGLE PLANNED SYSTEM** — canal water in the wet season, pumped groundwater in the dry, with the canal's seepage recharging the aquifer that is later pumped.

**Why the combination works so well:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **The canal's SEEPAGE, otherwise a pure loss, becomes RECHARGE** ← | **The water "lost" from the canal is stored in the aquifer and recovered by pumping — so it is not lost at all** ← |
| **The aquifer acts as a free, enormous RESERVOIR** ← | **With no dam, no submergence, no resettlement, no evaporation and no sedimentation** ← |
| **Pumping LOWERS the water table, preventing WATERLOGGING and salinity** ← | **The problem the canal itself created is solved by the pumping** ← |
| **Groundwater is available ON DEMAND** | **Unlike a canal turn, which arrives when the rotation dictates** ← |
| **The canal supplies the wet season's bulk demand cheaply; the wells supply the dry season's reliability** | **Each does what it is best at** ← |

> **THE FIRST AND THIRD ROWS TOGETHER MAKE THIS ONE OF THE MOST ELEGANT IDEAS IN WATER RESOURCES ENGINEERING, and it is worth setting out plainly:**

> **An unlined canal has two problems — it LOSES water to seepage, and that seepage WATERLOGS the command.**

> **Conjunctive use turns both into benefits. The seepage becomes aquifer storage, and pumping that storage out lowers the water table and cures the waterlogging.**

> **The two defects cancel each other, and the scheme ends with more usable water and a lower water table than either component alone would give.**

> **It is a rare case in which the right answer to two problems is to let them solve each other rather than to fix either.**

**The AQUIFER AS A RESERVOIR comparison, which is the strongest argument:**

| Aspect | Surface reservoir | Aquifer storage |
|---|---|---|
| **Capital cost** | **Very high — a dam** ← | **NIL — it exists already** ← |
| **Land submerged** | **Large; and resettlement** ← | **NONE** ← |
| **EVAPORATION loss** | **Substantial — metres per year from the surface** ← | **NEGLIGIBLE** ← |
| **SEDIMENTATION** | **Progressive, and it destroys the storage** ← | **NONE** ← |
| **Distribution** | **Requires a canal network** | **The water is already beneath the point of use** ← |
| **Recovery cost** | **Gravity — nearly free** ← | **PUMPING energy — the one real disadvantage** ← |
| **Risk of catastrophic failure** | **Dam break** ← | **NONE** ← |

> **THE ONLY COLUMN IN WHICH THE SURFACE RESERVOIR WINS IS THE RECOVERY COST, and that is a genuine and continuing expense — but it is set against every other item favouring the aquifer.**

> **In a region with a suitable aquifer, storing water underground is very often the better engineering, and the fact that it requires no visible structure has probably delayed its adoption more than any technical objection.**

**The requirement that makes or breaks it:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **Pumping must be BALANCED against recharge over the long term** ← | **Otherwise the water table falls year on year and the resource is mined rather than used** ← |
| **Which requires MONITORING of water levels across the command** ← | **The essential feedback, and the item usually missing** ← |
| **And REGULATION of pumping — which is very hard** ← | **Thousands of individual private tube wells, each rational in isolation, collectively over-abstracting** ← |
| **The energy for pumping must be affordable but not free** ← | **Free or heavily subsidised power removes any restraint on abstraction and guarantees over-pumping** ← |

> **THE LAST TWO ROWS DESCRIBE WHY CONJUNCTIVE USE SO OFTEN FAILS IN PRACTICE DESPITE BEING TECHNICALLY EXCELLENT, and it is a tragedy of the commons in its textbook form:**

> **The aquifer is a shared resource. Each farmer's own pumping has a negligible effect on the water table and a large effect on their own crop, so each rationally pumps as much as they can.**

> **Collectively they exhaust it, and the falling water table then raises everyone's pumping cost until the shallow wells fail and only those who can afford to deepen continue — which is inequitable as well as unsustainable.**

> **Subsidised electricity makes it worse by removing the only self-limiting mechanism.**

> **The engineering is sound and the institutions are the binding constraint — which is the same conclusion reached about waterlogging, about watercourse maintenance, and about road maintenance funding, and it is probably the most important recurring lesson in the whole of water resources practice.**

examTip.trick: **Canal in the wet season, pumped groundwater in the dry, with canal SEEPAGE recharging the aquifer** — the two components planned as one system.
examTip.trap: **It turns two defects into benefits** — seepage becomes storage, and pumping the storage cures the waterlogging the seepage caused. The problems cancel each other.
examTip.mnemonic: **An aquifer beats a surface reservoir on every count except PUMPING COST** — no dam, no submergence, no evaporation, no sedimentation, no dam break. But it needs monitoring and regulated abstraction, or it is mined.

questions.stem: During the construction of a dam across a river, a DIVERSION TUNNEL together with upstream and downstream COFFERDAMS is provided in order to:
options: Store water for the construction works
Carry the river's flow AROUND the dam site and keep the foundation excavation DRY while the dam is being built
Generate power during construction
Dispose of the excavated spoil
questions.solution:
**To carry the river's flow AROUND the dam site and keep the foundation excavation dry** while the dam is built.

**The arrangement:**

| Element | Function |
|---|---|
| **DIVERSION TUNNEL (or a diversion channel, or a flume)** ← | **Carries the river around or past the works** ← |
| **UPSTREAM cofferdam** ← | **Blocks the river's own channel and directs the flow into the diversion** ← |
| **DOWNSTREAM cofferdam** | **Prevents tailwater backing up into the excavation** ← |
| **DEWATERING pumps** | **Removing seepage and rainfall from within the enclosure** ← |
| **On completion, the tunnel is PLUGGED** ← | **Often converted afterwards into a low-level outlet, a bottom sluice, or part of the power waterway** ← |

> **THE CONVERSION IN THE LAST ROW IS GOOD PRACTICE AND WORTH KNOWING: a diversion tunnel is an expensive temporary work, and designing it so that it becomes a permanent bottom outlet, sluice or penstock recovers much of its cost.**

> **It requires the tunnel's alignment and size to be planned for both purposes from the outset, which is a coordination problem rather than a technical one — and where it is not done, a large tunnel is built, used for three years and then filled with concrete.**

**The central decision — the DIVERSION DESIGN FLOOD:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **The diversion works are TEMPORARY, in use for perhaps 2 to 5 years** ← | **So they are NOT designed for the probable maximum flood** ← |
| **They are designed for a flood of modest return period** ← | **Commonly 20 to 50 years, depending on the consequence of overtopping** ← |
| **This is a deliberate acceptance of RISK** ← | **There is a real probability that the diversion will be overtopped during construction** ← |
| **The consequence must therefore be considered and planned for** ← | **What happens if the site floods? Is it a delay, or a disaster?** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS AN UNUSUAL AND INSTRUCTIVE PIECE OF ENGINEERING JUDGEMENT AND IT IS WORTH DWELLING ON: nowhere else in dam engineering is a significant probability of failure knowingly accepted.**

> **The permanent spillway is designed for the probable maximum flood because a failure would be catastrophic. The diversion works are designed for a 25-year flood because a failure means a flooded excavation, lost time and damaged plant — serious, but recoverable.**

> **Designing the diversion for the PMF would require a tunnel several times larger, used for three years and then abandoned — and the cost of that would exceed the expected cost of the flooding it would prevent.**

> **So the return period is chosen by explicit economic comparison of the diversion's cost against the expected damage, which is exactly the kind of analysis that the permanent works' catastrophic consequences forbid.**

**And the STAGED diversion, which is used on wide rivers:**

| Stage | Note |
|---|---|
| **Stage 1: a cofferdam encloses HALF the river's width** ← | **The river continues through the other half, and the dam is built in the enclosed half** ← |
| **Stage 2: the cofferdam is moved to the other half** ← | **The river is passed through openings or sluices left in the part already built** ← |
| **Advantage** | **NO diversion tunnel is needed at all — a very large saving on a wide river** ← |
| **Requirement** | **The river must be wide enough to be halved, and the first-stage structure must be designed with openings to pass the flood** ← |

> **STAGED DIVERSION IS THE STANDARD APPROACH FOR A BARRAGE OR A WIDE CONCRETE DAM AND IT AVOIDS THE DIVERSION WORKS ENTIRELY, which is why barrages on the great alluvial rivers are built this way.**

> **In a narrow rocky gorge, halving the river is impossible and a tunnel is unavoidable — so the diversion method follows directly from the site's geometry, and it is one of the first things settled in planning a dam's construction.**

> **The CLOSURE — the moment the upstream cofferdam is completed and the river is forced into the diversion — is the most critical operation of the whole construction period, because it must be completed faster than the rising water can wash the cofferdam away.**

> **It is timed for the driest part of the year, planned in detail, and executed continuously once begun; and a closure attempted at the wrong season, or interrupted, has been lost more than once.**

examTip.trick: **Diversion tunnel carries the river past the site; upstream cofferdam directs the flow into it; downstream cofferdam keeps tailwater out.** Plug it afterwards, ideally converting it to a permanent outlet.
examTip.trap: **The diversion is designed for a 20-50 year flood, NOT the PMF** — a deliberate acceptance of risk, because overtopping means lost time rather than catastrophe. The only place in dam work where that is done.
examTip.mnemonic: **STAGED diversion halves the river and needs no tunnel at all** — standard for wide barrages, impossible in a narrow gorge. And CLOSURE is the most critical operation of the whole job.

questions.stem: The LEVELLISED COST OF ENERGY (LCOE) of a hydropower project is:
options: The tariff at which the power is actually sold
The capital cost divided by the installed capacity
The annual operating cost divided by the annual energy generated
The PRESENT VALUE of all costs over the project's life DIVIDED by the present value of all the energy generated — giving a cost per kWh that can be compared directly between technologies
questions.solution:
**The present value of all COSTS over the project's life divided by the present value of all the ENERGY generated** — giving a single cost per kWh comparable between technologies.

**What it includes and why:**

| Included | Note |
|---|---|
| **Capital cost, including interest during construction** ← | **Discounted to present value** ← |
| **All operating, maintenance and replacement costs over the life** | ← |
| **Fuel, where applicable** | **Zero for hydro, solar and wind — which is their central advantage** ← |
| **Decommissioning** | ← |
| **DIVIDED BY the discounted energy output over the whole life** ← | **Note that the ENERGY is discounted too, which surprises people** ← |

> **THE DISCOUNTING OF THE ENERGY IN THE LAST ROW IS ESSENTIAL AND IS OFTEN OMITTED IN CARELESS CALCULATIONS: a kWh generated in year 30 is worth less in present-value terms than one generated in year 1, exactly as a rupee is.**

> **Dividing discounted costs by UNDISCOUNTED energy understates the LCOE substantially, and it flatters long-lived projects in particular — which is precisely the class that hydropower belongs to.**

**Option (b) — capital cost per kW — is the figure most often quoted and it is a poor basis for comparison:**

| Comparison | Capital cost per kW | LCOE |
|---|---|---|
| **Hydropower** | **HIGH — perhaps 1,500 to 3,000 US$/kW** ← | **LOW, because there is no fuel and the plant lasts 50 to 100 years** ← |
| **Diesel generation** | **LOW — a few hundred US$/kW** ← | **VERY HIGH, because fuel dominates the whole-life cost** ← |
| **Solar PV** | **Moderate and falling** | **Moderate; but the CAPACITY FACTOR is low, so the energy per kW installed is small** ← |

> **THE CONTRAST IN THE FIRST TWO ROWS IS THE REASON LCOE EXISTS: ranking these technologies by capital cost per kW puts diesel first and hydro last, and ranking them by LCOE reverses the order entirely.**

> **A diesel set is cheap to buy and ruinous to run. A hydropower plant is expensive to build and nearly free to operate for a century.**

> **Only a whole-life measure captures that, and any comparison based on capital cost alone will systematically favour the technology with the highest running cost — which is exactly the wrong answer, and exactly the decision that a shortage of capital pushes people toward.**

**The parameters LCOE is most sensitive to:**

| Parameter | Effect |
|---|---|
| **The DISCOUNT RATE** ← | **The single most influential assumption for a capital-intensive, long-lived project** ← |
| **The CAPACITY FACTOR (or annual energy)** | **Directly in the denominator** ← |
| **The economic LIFE assumed** ← | **And for hydro, whether the CONCESSION period or the physical life is used makes an enormous difference** ← |
| **Construction TIME and cost overrun** | **Interest during construction compounds, so delay is very expensive** ← |
| **Fuel price, where applicable** | ← |

> **THE DISCOUNT RATE'S DOMINANCE IN THE FIRST ROW IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING BECAUSE IT DECIDES ARGUMENTS RATHER THAN INFORMING THEM: a hydropower project's costs are almost all incurred at the start and its benefits spread over decades.**

> **A HIGH discount rate makes those distant benefits nearly worthless and the immediate costs fully weighted, so it makes hydropower look expensive.**

> **A LOW discount rate does the opposite.**

> **Comparing hydro against a gas turbine at 12 per cent and at 6 per cent can reverse the ranking, without a single physical fact changing — which is why the discount rate used must be stated with any LCOE figure, and why LCOE comparisons quoted without it should be treated with suspicion.**

> **THE CONCESSION PERIOD POINT IN THE THIRD ROW MATTERS PARTICULARLY IN NEPAL, and it connects to the licensing question: the plant physically lasts a century, and the developer has 35 years.**

> **Computing LCOE over 35 years gives a much higher figure than over 100, and the tariff must be set on the 35-year basis because that is the developer's horizon.**

> **So the transferred asset's remaining 65 years of nearly free generation is a large benefit accruing to the state, and it does not appear in the tariff calculation at all — which is a fair way to view the arrangement, and one that makes the tariff look less expensive than it first appears.**

examTip.trick: **Present value of all COSTS ÷ present value of all ENERGY.** The energy is discounted too — dividing discounted costs by undiscounted energy understates the LCOE badly.
examTip.trap: **Capital cost per kW (option b) reverses the ranking** — diesel is cheap to buy and ruinous to run; hydro is the opposite. Only a whole-life measure captures it.
examTip.mnemonic: **The DISCOUNT RATE decides the argument** — high rates make hydro's distant benefits worthless, low rates favour it. Any LCOE quoted without its discount rate and life is not comparable to anything.

questions.stem: The MASS CURVE (Rippl diagram) of inflow is used in reservoir planning to determine:
options: The STORAGE CAPACITY required to meet a given demand, by finding the largest cumulative DEFICIT between the inflow and the demand
The peak flood discharge for spillway design
The sediment load entering the reservoir
The evaporation loss from the reservoir surface
questions.solution:
**The STORAGE CAPACITY required to meet a given demand**, found as the largest cumulative deficit between the inflow and the demand.

**How it works:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Plot the CUMULATIVE inflow volume against time** ← | **A curve that always rises, steeply in the wet season and gently in the dry** ← |
| **Plot the CUMULATIVE demand as a straight line** ← | **Straight if the demand is uniform; its SLOPE is the demand rate** ← |
| **Where the mass curve is STEEPER than the demand line, the reservoir is FILLING** ← | **Inflow exceeds demand** ← |
| **Where it is FLATTER, the reservoir is EMPTYING** ← | **Demand exceeds inflow — and this is the period the storage must cover** ← |
| **Draw demand lines TANGENT to the curve at each summit** ← | **The summits are where the reservoir is full** ← |
| **The MAXIMUM VERTICAL INTERCEPT between a tangent and the curve below it is the required STORAGE** ← | ← |

> **THE SLOPE INTERPRETATION IN THE THIRD AND FOURTH ROWS IS THE KEY TO READING THE DIAGRAM AND MAKES EVERYTHING ELSE FOLLOW: the slope of the mass curve at any point IS the inflow rate at that time.**

> **So comparing the curve's slope with the demand line's slope tells you immediately whether the reservoir is filling or emptying, and the largest gap that opens up between a full-reservoir tangent and the curve is the volume the reservoir must hold.**

**WHY THE MASS CURVE IS USED RATHER THAN THE FLOW DURATION CURVE, which is the important comparison:**

| Aspect | FLOW DURATION curve | MASS curve |
|---|---|---|
| **Preserves CHRONOLOGY?** | **NO — the order is discarded** ← | **YES — it is cumulative in time** ← |
| **Tells you HOW MUCH water and for what fraction of time** | **YES** ← | Yes |
| **Tells you HOW LONG the deficit lasts CONSECUTIVELY** ← | **NO** ← | **YES — which is exactly what storage sizing requires** ← |
| **Used for** | **Run-of-river design discharge and firm power** ← | **STORAGE capacity** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE WHOLE REASON BOTH CURVES EXIST: storage must cover the LENGTH of the dry period, not merely its severity.**

> **A river that is low for 30 scattered days needs almost no storage; the same river low for 30 CONSECUTIVE days needs a month's supply held back.**

> **The flow duration curve cannot distinguish those two cases, and the mass curve can — which is why a reservoir cannot be sized from a flow duration curve however carefully it is read.**

**The practical requirements and limitations:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The record must be LONG — at least 25 to 40 years, and preferably more** ← | **Because the design condition is the WORST drought in the record** ← |
| **The storage obtained is that needed for the worst drought OBSERVED** ← | **Not the worst POSSIBLE — a longer record would probably contain a worse one** ← |
| **Two or more successive dry years may govern** ← | **In which case the critical period spans years, and a short record will miss it entirely** ← |
| **EVAPORATION and seepage losses, and the DEAD storage, must be ADDED** ← | **The mass curve gives the live storage requirement only** ← |
| **Sequent peak analysis is the same method arranged for computation** | **The standard modern form, easily programmed** ← |

> **THE SECOND AND THIRD ROWS TOGETHER STATE THE METHOD'S HONEST LIMITATION AND IT IS A SERIOUS ONE: the mass curve sizes the reservoir for the worst drought in the RECORD.**

> **A 30-year record contains the worst 30-year drought, and the reservoir will fail in a worse one — which will eventually occur.**

> **And multi-year droughts are the dangerous case: two consecutive poor monsoons can require several times the storage that any single dry season demands, and a 20-year record may contain no such sequence at all while a 60-year record contains two.**

> **So the record length is not a matter of convenience but the principal determinant of the design's reliability, and the appropriate response to a short record is not a more careful analysis of it but an explicit allowance for the drought it does not contain.**

> **This is also why RELIABILITY is stated explicitly in modern reservoir planning — "a firm yield with 90 per cent reliability" — rather than pretending that a reservoir sized on the historic minimum will never fail.**

examTip.trick: **Cumulative inflow against time, with the demand as a straight line; the maximum vertical intercept between a summit tangent and the curve is the storage required.** The curve's SLOPE is the inflow rate.
examTip.trap: **Storage cannot be sized from a FLOW DURATION curve** — it discards chronology, and storage depends on how LONG the deficit lasts consecutively, not just how severe it is.
examTip.mnemonic: **It sizes for the worst drought in the RECORD, not the worst possible** — and MULTI-YEAR droughts govern, which a short record may not contain at all. Record length is the real determinant of reliability.

questions.stem: A peaking run-of-river plant has a design discharge of 30 m³/s and is to generate at full capacity for 6 hours each day. If the river's dry-season flow is a steady 10 m³/s, the DAILY PONDAGE volume required is:
questions.solution:
**432,000 m³.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Discharge drawn during generation** | **30 m³/s** |
| **Discharge arriving from the river** | **10 m³/s, continuously** ← |
| **DEFICIT that must come from storage while generating** | **30 − 10 = 20 m³/s** ← |
| **Duration of generation** | **6 h = 21,600 s** |
| **Pondage required** | **20 × 21,600 = 432,000 m³** ← |

> **Option (d) 648,000 m³ is 30 × 21,600 — the whole volume drawn during the 6 hours, forgetting that the river continues to supply 10 m³/s throughout.**

> **Only the DEFICIT has to be stored, which is the point of the question.**

**Checking that the pond can actually refill, which the arithmetic must always confirm:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **During the 18 non-generating hours, the river's inflow is stored** | **10 × 18 × 3,600 = 648,000 m³** ← |
| **Which comfortably exceeds the 432,000 m³ drawn down** ← | **So the pond refills each night with a surplus** ← |
| **Total daily river volume** | **10 × 86,400 = 864,000 m³** |
| **Total daily draw** | **30 × 21,600 = 648,000 m³** ← |
| **Surplus, which spills** | **216,000 m³ per day** ← |

> **THE REFILL CHECK IS ESSENTIAL AND IS OFTEN OMITTED: pondage is only useful if the pond can be refilled in the non-generating hours.**

> **If the plant tried to generate for 12 hours a day at 30 m³/s, it would need 12 × 3,600 × 20 = 864,000 m³ of pondage, and the river's whole daily volume is 864,000 m³ — so it would exactly consume the entire flow and the pond could never refill any surplus.**

> **Beyond that point the plant simply cannot peak at all, and the daily generating hours are limited by the river's total daily volume divided by the design discharge — here 864,000/30 = 28,800 s = 8 hours.**

> **So this plant could peak for at most 8 hours a day even with unlimited pondage, and asking for 6 is within that limit with a margin.**

**PONDAGE against STORAGE, which is the distinction the question rests on:**

| Term | Period regulated | Volume | Structure |
|---|---|---|---|
| **PONDAGE** | **DAILY or weekly** ← | **Small — hours of flow** ← | **A pond behind the diversion weir, or an enlarged forebay** ← |
| **STORAGE** | **SEASONAL or annual** ← | **Large — months of flow** ← | **A reservoir behind a dam** ← |

> **THE SCALE DIFFERENCE IS ENORMOUS AND IT IS WHY PONDAGE IS SO ATTRACTIVE: 432,000 m³ is a pond a few hundred metres across and a few metres deep, which can often be created simply by raising the diversion weir a little or by excavating a basin beside the headrace.**

> **Seasonal storage for the same plant would require tens of millions of cubic metres, a high dam, a submerged valley and resettlement.**

> **Yet pondage delivers a large share of the commercial benefit, because it converts the plant's output from whatever the river happens to give into power delivered AT THE SYSTEM PEAK, when it is worth several times as much.**

**Why that matters so much in Nepal:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **The system's peak demand is in the EVENING** ← | **A few hours of high demand, when lighting and cooking coincide** ← |
| **A plain run-of-river plant generates a flat output all day** ← | **Producing surplus energy at 3 a.m. that nobody wants, and no more than average at the peak** ← |
| **A PROR plant with pondage shifts its output INTO the peak** ← | **Same annual energy, far higher value** ← |
| **And it can be paid a peak tariff for it** | **Which is why PROR plants command a better power purchase agreement** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE COMMERCIAL POINT AND IT IS WORTH GRASPING: pondage does not create energy, it MOVES it in time.**

> **Since electricity's value varies by a factor of two or three between the small hours and the evening peak, moving energy from one to the other is worth a great deal for a very modest civil work — which makes pondage one of the highest-return additions available to a run-of-river scheme.**

> **It is also why a plant designed without pondage can rarely be given it later: the pond must be part of the headworks layout from the outset, and there is usually nowhere to put it afterwards.**

examTip.trick: **Only the DEFICIT is stored: (30 − 10) × 6 × 3,600 = 432,000 m³.** Option (d) forgets that the river keeps supplying 10 m³/s while the plant generates.
examTip.trap: **Always check the REFILL** — and note that the daily generating hours are capped at (daily river volume ÷ design discharge) = 8 h here, however much pondage is provided.
examTip.mnemonic: **Pondage does not create energy, it MOVES it into the evening peak** — where it is worth two or three times as much. The highest-return civil addition to an ROR scheme, and it cannot be retrofitted.

questions.stem: In checking the stability of a concrete gravity dam against SLIDING, the SHEAR FRICTION FACTOR is used in preference to the simple sliding factor because it:
options: Ignores the uplift pressure, giving a simpler calculation
Accounts for the SHEAR STRENGTH (cohesion) of the concrete-rock contact and of the rock itself, IN ADDITION to the frictional resistance
Applies only to dams founded on soil
Is always more conservative than the sliding factor
questions.solution:
**Because it accounts for the SHEAR STRENGTH (cohesion) of the contact and of the rock, IN ADDITION to the frictional resistance.**

**The two checks:**

| Check | Expression | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **SLIDING FACTOR** | **ΣH / ΣV — the ratio of the horizontal to the vertical forces** ← | **Must be less than the coefficient of friction μ (typically 0.65 to 0.75). It relies on FRICTION ALONE** ← |
| **SHEAR FRICTION FACTOR (SFF)** | **SFF = (μ ΣV + c A) / ΣH** ← | **Adds the COHESIVE shear resistance c A of the contact area — required to be 3 to 5** ← |

> **THE SIMPLE SLIDING FACTOR IGNORES COHESION ENTIRELY, and for a concrete dam bonded to a sound rock foundation that is a large omission: the concrete-rock bond has real shear strength, and the rock itself has more.**

> **A dam that fails the simple sliding check can be perfectly safe when its shear strength is properly counted, which is why the shear friction factor is the governing check in modern practice.**

> **Option (d) is therefore wrong in an interesting way: the shear friction factor is LESS conservative in the sense that it credits resistance the simple factor ignores — but it demands a much higher numerical value (3 to 5, against a sliding factor comfortably below 1), so the two are not directly comparable.**

**The four failure modes of a gravity dam, and the check for each:**

| Mode | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **OVERTURNING about the toe** | **The resultant must fall within the base; factor of safety 1.5 to 2 on the moments** ← |
| **SLIDING along the base or a horizontal joint** ← | **Sliding factor < μ; shear friction factor 3 to 5** ← |
| **CRUSHING (compressive failure)** | **The maximum compressive stress at the toe must not exceed the allowable stress of concrete or rock** ← |
| **TENSION at the heel** | **No tension permitted — the resultant must lie within the MIDDLE THIRD of the base** ← |

> **THE NO-TENSION REQUIREMENT IN THE LAST ROW IS THE ONE THAT USUALLY GOVERNS THE PROFILE AND IT IS THE MOST DEMANDING, and its reason connects to the uplift problem:**

> **Tension at the heel would open a crack. Once open, the crack fills with water at full reservoir pressure, which acts as additional UPLIFT over the cracked length and drives the crack further.**

> **The process is self-propagating, so a small tensile crack does not stay small — which is why the no-tension rule is applied absolutely rather than with a factor of safety, and why the middle-third rule met in the eccentric loading question reappears here as the governing condition of a major structure.**

**THE UPLIFT'S ROLE IN THE SLIDING CHECK IS WORTH SPELLING OUT because it is where option (a) misleads:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Uplift REDUCES ΣV** ← | **The effective vertical force is the weight MINUS the uplift** ← |
| **Reducing ΣV reduces the frictional resistance μ ΣV proportionately** ← | **So uplift attacks the sliding resistance directly** ← |
| **It does NOT reduce the cohesive term c A** | **Cohesion does not depend on the normal force** ← |
| **So uplift is more damaging to the friction term than to the cohesion term** ← | ← |

> **THAT ASYMMETRY IS A GOOD REASON TO COUNT THE COHESION RATHER THAN IGNORE IT: on a dam with substantial uplift, the frictional resistance may be badly eroded while the cohesive resistance is untouched, and a check that ignores cohesion therefore understates the dam's real security by a large margin.**

> **It is also why the grout curtain and the drainage holes, which reduce the uplift, improve the sliding resistance as well as the overturning and no-tension checks — one measure improving every check at once, which is why they are always provided.**

**And the practical point about the cohesion value:**

> **The cohesion of the concrete-rock contact depends entirely on how well the foundation was PREPARED and how the first lift was placed.**

> **A surface cleaned to sound rock, with all loose material and drill cuttings removed, washed, and covered with a rich mortar or a bedding layer immediately before the first concrete, develops a genuine bond.**

> **A surface with a layer of mud, drill spoil or laitance left on it develops almost none — and the design's cohesive term, which may be carrying much of the sliding resistance, simply is not there.**

> **Foundation cleaning before the first pour is therefore one of the most consequential and least glamorous operations in dam construction, and it is inspected accordingly: on a major dam the foundation is formally accepted, surface by surface, before any concrete is permitted.**

examTip.trick: **SFF = (μΣV + cA)/ΣH, required to be 3 to 5** — it credits the COHESIVE shear strength of the contact, which the simple sliding factor ΣH/ΣV ignores entirely.
examTip.trap: **Four modes: overturning, sliding, crushing, TENSION — and no-tension usually governs.** A tensile crack fills with water at full pressure and propagates itself, so the rule is absolute.
examTip.mnemonic: **Uplift erodes the FRICTION term and not the COHESION term** — so ignoring cohesion badly understates a dam with high uplift. And the cohesion exists only if the foundation was properly CLEANED before the first pour.

questions.stem: A ZONED earth dam differs from a HOMOGENEOUS one in that the zoned dam:
options: Is built entirely of a single well-graded material
Uses a thin upstream concrete or asphalt membrane as its water barrier
Has no internal drainage
Has a relatively IMPERVIOUS CENTRAL CORE flanked by more PERVIOUS SHELLS, so that each material is placed where its properties are most useful
questions.solution:
**It has a relatively IMPERVIOUS central core flanked by more PERVIOUS shells** — placing each material where its properties are most useful.

**The three types of embankment dam:**

| Type | Construction | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **HOMOGENEOUS** | **A single material throughout, usually with a small internal drain or a rock toe** ← | **LOW dams (below about 10 m) where only one material is available** ← |
| **ZONED (composite)** ← | **An impervious CORE, transition/filter zones, and pervious SHELLS** ← | **Most large embankment dams — the standard type** ← |
| **DIAPHRAGM type** ← | **A pervious embankment with a thin impervious MEMBRANE — concrete, asphalt or geomembrane — on the upstream face or as an internal wall** ← (option b) | **Where no suitable clay exists on site** ← |

> **THE ZONED DAM IS THE STANDARD FOR ANY SUBSTANTIAL EMBANKMENT AND THE REASON IS A DIVISION OF LABOUR BETWEEN THE MATERIALS, which is worth setting out:**

| Zone | Material | Its job |
|---|---|---|
| **CORE** | **Clay or a well-graded material with clay fines — IMPERVIOUS** ← | **Stops the water. It contributes little to stability, being weak** ← |
| **FILTER / TRANSITION zones** | **Graded sand and gravel, satisfying the filter criteria** ← | **Prevents the core's fines from migrating into the shell, and controls seepage safely** ← |
| **SHELLS** | **Rockfill, gravel or sand — PERVIOUS and STRONG** ← | **Provides the STABILITY and the weight. It holds no water back at all** ← |
| **Riprap / slope protection** | Rock on the upstream face | **Against wave action** ← |

> **THE CONTRAST BETWEEN THE FIRST AND THIRD ROWS IS THE WHOLE IDEA: the material that stops water is weak, and the material that provides strength is permeable.**

> **A homogeneous dam must use one material for both jobs, so it is a compromise: permeable enough to be strong and stable is too permeable to hold water, and impervious enough to hold water is too weak for steep slopes.**

> **Zoning lets each material do the job it is good at — the clay core holds the water and needs no strength because the shells support it, and the rockfill shells provide steep stable slopes and need no imperviousness because the core handles that.**

> **The result is a dam with a smaller cross-section, steeper slopes and less material than a homogeneous dam of the same height, built from materials that are individually unsuitable.**

**The FILTER ZONES in the second row are the critical detail:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Without a filter, the core's fine particles migrate into the coarse shell under the seepage gradient** ← | **PIPING — and it hollows out the core from within** ← |
| **The filter must satisfy both criteria — retain the core's fines, and pass the water freely** ← | **The same two conditions met at the chimney drain, behind a retaining wall, and beneath a revetment** ← |
| **Several graded layers may be needed between a fine core and a coarse rockfill** ← | **No single grading can bridge the gap** ← |
| **The transition also prevents the shell's stones puncturing into the soft core** | **A mechanical function as well as a hydraulic one** ← |

> **THIS IS THE FOURTH APPEARANCE OF THE FILTER CRITERIA IN THIS CHAPTER'S SUBJECT MATTER, and the repetition is the point: whenever water flows from a fine material into a coarse one, a filter is required, and the two conditions are always the same.**

> **It is one of the small number of ideas in geotechnical engineering that recurs in almost every application, and recognising it as one idea rather than several saves a great deal of memorising.**

**The CORE's position, which is a genuine design choice:**

| Position | Advantages | Disadvantages |
|---|---|---|
| **CENTRAL vertical core** | **Higher contact pressure between core and foundation, so less risk of leakage there; shorter core; access to both shells during construction** ← | **The core must be placed simultaneously with the shells, so construction is more complex** ← |
| **INCLINED or upstream core** ← | **The shells can be built FIRST and the core placed later; the downstream shell stays dry, so it is fully effective; and the phreatic line is drawn far forward** ← | **A longer core; lower contact pressure; and it is more vulnerable to a drawdown** ← |

> **THE CONSTRUCTION SEQUENCE ADVANTAGE OF THE INCLINED CORE IN THE SECOND ROW IS OFTEN DECISIVE IN PRACTICE AND IS WORTH KNOWING: clay core placement is weather-dependent and slow, and rockfill placement is neither.**

> **An inclined core lets the rockfill shells be placed through a monsoon while the core waits for dry weather, whereas a central core must keep pace with the shells and holds up the whole embankment.**

> **On a Himalayan site with a four-month wet season, that difference can be a whole construction year — which is a scheduling consideration determining a structural configuration, and a good illustration of how buildability shapes design on large civil works.**

examTip.trick: **Impervious CORE stops the water; pervious SHELLS provide the strength; FILTER zones between them.** Option (b) is the diaphragm type, (a) the homogeneous one.
examTip.trap: **The material that stops water is weak and the strong material is permeable** — zoning lets each do what it is good at, giving steeper slopes and less material than a homogeneous dam.
examTip.mnemonic: **An INCLINED core lets the rockfill shells be built through the monsoon while the core waits for dry weather** — on a Himalayan site that can be a whole construction year.

questions.stem: A CONTINUOUS-FLUSHING settling basin at a run-of-river hydropower headworks differs from an intermittently flushed one in that the continuous type:
options: Has a system of HOPPERS and FLUSHING DUCTS that carry the deposited sediment away WITHOUT interrupting the plant's operation, at the cost of a continuous small loss of water
Requires the plant to be shut down for cleaning
Removes only the coarse gravel fraction
Needs no flushing arrangement at all
questions.solution:
**It has hoppers and flushing ducts that remove the deposited sediment WITHOUT interrupting generation**, at the cost of a small continuous loss of water.

**The two arrangements compared:**

| Aspect | INTERMITTENT flushing | CONTINUOUS flushing |
|---|---|---|
| **Operation** | **The basin fills with sediment, is then ISOLATED and flushed** ← | **Sediment is removed continuously from hoppers as it settles** ← |
| **Effect on generation** | **The basin (or one of two bays) must be TAKEN OUT of service** ← | **NONE — the plant runs throughout** ← |
| **Number of bays needed** | **TWO or more, so one can be flushed while the other works** ← | **ONE may suffice** ← |
| **Water lost to flushing** | **A large volume, for a short period** ← | **A small volume, continuously — typically 5 to 10 per cent of the design discharge** ← |
| **Structure** | **Simpler and cheaper** ← | **More complex — hoppers, ducts, gates and a controlled outfall** ← |
| **Suits** | **Moderate sediment loads; where a shutdown or a spare bay is acceptable** | **HEAVY sediment loads, where intermittent flushing would be needed too often** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE DECIDING CONSIDERATION AND IT IS WHY CONTINUOUS SYSTEMS ARE COMMON IN NEPAL: with a Himalayan sediment load, a basin sized for intermittent flushing may fill in a matter of HOURS during a monsoon flood.**

> **Flushing it then means stopping generation several times a day, in the season when the river is full and the plant should be earning most — which is commercially unacceptable.**

> **A continuous system gives up 5 to 10 per cent of the flow permanently in exchange for uninterrupted generation, and on a monsoon-fed plant that trade is strongly favourable.**

**Why the settling basin exists at all, restated because the reason is specific:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Himalayan rivers carry very hard, ANGULAR quartz and feldspar sand** ← | **Not soft silt — abrasive mineral grains** ← |
| **At turbine velocities this acts as a cutting abrasive** ← | **Eroding runner buckets, guide vanes, nozzles and needles** ← |
| **A Pelton needle and nozzle can be destroyed in a single monsoon** ← | **And efficiency falls measurably as the profiles wear** ← |
| **So particles above a threshold size must be removed** | **Typically 0.2 mm for a low-head plant, and 0.1 mm or finer for a HIGH-head Pelton** ← |

> **THE THRESHOLD IN THE LAST ROW TIGHTENS WITH HEAD AND THE REASON IS THE VELOCITY: erosion rate rises very steeply with velocity — roughly as the third power.**

> **A Pelton jet at 400 m head moves at nearly 90 m/s, and a particle in it does enormously more damage than the same particle at 20 m/s in a low-head Kaplan.**

> **So the high-head plant needs a much finer removal, which means a much LARGER basin — and the settling basin for a high-head scheme is often one of the largest and costliest structures in the whole headworks.**

**The design of the basin itself:**

| Parameter | Note |
|---|---|
| **Sized on the SETTLING VELOCITY of the threshold particle** ← | **The basin must be long enough for that particle to reach the floor before the water reaches the outlet** ← |
| **Flow velocity reduced to 0.2 to 0.4 m/s** ← | **Low enough for settlement, high enough to avoid depositing everything** ← |
| **The inlet TRANSITION must be gradual** ← | **A sudden expansion produces jetting and eddies, the flow short-circuits through part of the basin, and the effective volume is a fraction of the actual** ← |
| **A high TRAP EFFICIENCY for the design particle** | **Typically 80 to 95 per cent** ← |
| **Preceded by a GRAVEL TRAP** ← | **Which removes the coarse fraction that would otherwise fill the basin rapidly** ← |

> **THE INLET TRANSITION IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE ELEMENT MOST OFTEN COMPROMISED FOR WANT OF SPACE AND IT IS THE ONE THAT DECIDES WHETHER THE BASIN WORKS: a settling basin's performance depends entirely on the flow being slow and UNIFORM across its full width and depth.**

> **An abrupt inlet sends a jet down the centre, the water at the sides barely moves, and the sediment-laden jet passes through in a fraction of the design detention time.**

> **The basin is then a large, expensive structure with a small effective volume, and no amount of flushing improves it.**

> **This is why physical or numerical modelling of the inlet transition is standard for a significant plant, and why a long, gently expanding approach is worth the length it consumes.**

examTip.trick: **Continuous flushing removes sediment from hoppers WITHOUT stopping the plant**, at a cost of 5-10 % of the flow. Intermittent flushing needs the bay out of service, hence two bays.
examTip.trap: **Removal threshold tightens with HEAD** — 0.2 mm for low head, 0.1 mm or finer for a high-head Pelton — because erosion goes as roughly the CUBE of velocity, and a Pelton jet moves at 90 m/s.
examTip.mnemonic: **The INLET TRANSITION decides whether the basin works** — an abrupt inlet jets down the centre and the sediment passes through in a fraction of the design detention time. No flushing regime fixes that.

questions.stem: In a low-head hydropower plant, a RISE in the TAILRACE water level during a river flood:
options: Increases the net head and hence the power output
Has no effect, since the head is measured at the intake
REDUCES the NET HEAD and therefore the power output, and can in an extreme flood reduce it to the point where generation must stop
Increases the discharge through the turbine
questions.solution:
**It REDUCES the net head and therefore the power output**, and in an extreme flood can reduce it to the point where generation must stop.

**Why:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **The GROSS head is the difference between the UPSTREAM water level and the TAILRACE water level** ← | **Both ends matter — which disposes of option (b)** ← |
| **The NET head is the gross head less the losses in the waterway** | ← |
| **A rise in the tailrace RAISES the lower end of the head** ← | **So the difference — the head available — SHRINKS** ← |
| **Power P = ρ g Q H η, so power falls in proportion to H** ← | ← |

> **THE PHRASE "LOW-HEAD PLANT" IN THE QUESTION IS THE ESSENTIAL QUALIFICATION AND IT IS WHERE THE PRACTICAL SIGNIFICANCE LIES:**

| Plant | Gross head | Tailwater rise of 2 m | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| **HIGH head, 400 m** | **400 m** | **2 m** | **A 0.5 % loss — negligible** ← |
| **LOW head, 8 m** | **8 m** | **2 m** | **A 25 % LOSS — severe** ← |

> **THE SAME ABSOLUTE RISE IS TRIVIAL FOR A PELTON PLANT AND CRIPPLING FOR A LOW-HEAD KAPLAN, and that is the whole point.**

> **A low-head plant's head is of the same order as the river's own flood variation, so its output is at the mercy of the tailwater — and the worst case is a flood, when the river is carrying the most water and the plant can use the least of it.**

> **That is a genuinely awkward outcome: the plant is starved of head exactly when it has abundant flow, and its annual energy is reduced in precisely the season that should be its best.**

**How the difficulty is addressed:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **Set the powerhouse and the turbine LOW enough to keep an adequate submergence and head at high tailwater** ← | **But not so low that the draft tube is drowned in ordinary conditions** ← |
| **Design the TAILRACE CHANNEL generously** ← | **A short, wide, low-friction tailrace keeps the level down; a long, narrow, silted one raises it** ← |
| **Keep the tailrace CLEAR of silt and vegetation** ← | **A maintenance item with a direct effect on output, and it is often neglected because the loss is gradual and invisible** ← |
| **Accept a reduced output, or shut down, in extreme floods** | **And account for it in the energy estimate** ← |
| **Site the outfall where the river's flood level is lowest** | **Sometimes worth a longer tailrace** ← |

> **THE TAILRACE MAINTENANCE IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE MOST NEGLECTED ITEM AND THE EASIEST TO PUT RIGHT: a tailrace channel that silts up or grows vegetation over a few seasons raises the tailwater level by a few tens of centimetres.**

> **On a low-head plant that is a direct and permanent loss of output, and it accumulates so gradually that nobody attributes the falling generation to it.**

> **Clearing the tailrace is cheap, and the output recovers immediately — which makes it one of those maintenance tasks whose value is invisible until it is measured.**

**And the DRAFT TUBE's role, which is worth connecting here:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **The draft tube RECOVERS the velocity head leaving the runner** ← | **Converting kinetic energy back into pressure by a gradual expansion** ← |
| **It also allows the runner to be set ABOVE the tailwater** | **While still using the full head down to the tailwater level** ← |
| **Its importance rises as the head FALLS** ← | **On a low-head Kaplan, the velocity head leaving the runner can be a substantial fraction of the total head — so recovering it is essential** ← |
